questions.text:
A company is building a generative AI(GenAI) application that uses Amazon Bedrock APIs to process complex customer inquiries. During peak usage periods, the application experiences intermittent API timeouts that cause issues such as broken response chunks and delayed data delivery. The application struggles to ensure that prompts remain within token limits when handling complex customer inquiries of varying lengths. Users have reported truncated inputs and incomplete responses. The company has also observed foundation model(FM) invocation failures.

The company needs a retry strategy that automatically handles transient service errors and prevents overwhelming Amazon Bedrock during peak usage periods. The strategy must also adapt to changing service availability and support response streaming and token-aware request handling.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Implement a standard retry strategy that uses a 1-second fixed delay between attempts and a 3-retry maximum for all errors. Handle streaming response timeouts by restarting streams. Cap token usage for each session.

Implement an adaptive retry strategy that uses exponential backoff with a 2-second initial maximum interval and a maximum of 5 retries for transient errors. Use error rates exceeded a predefined threshold. Implement a streaming response handler that monitors for chunk delivery timeouts. Configure the handler to buffer successfully received chunks and intelligently resume streaming from the last received chunk when connections are re-established.

Use the AWS SDK to configure a simple retry strategy in nested mode. Wrap Amazon Bedrock API calls in try-catch blocks that handle timeout exceptions. Return cached completions for failed streaming requests. Enforce a global token limit for all users. Add jitter-based retries logic to introduce randomness in retry intervals between requests. Restart streaming chunks from the point of failure. Maintain a small in-memory buffer of the most recent chunks to minimize redundant data transfer.

Set Amazon Bedrock client request timeouts to 30 seconds. Implement client-side load shedding. Buffer partial results and skip new requests when the application performance begins to degrade Set static token usage caps for all requests. Configure exponential backoff retries, dynamic chunk sizing, and context-aware token limits.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

The requirement specifies an adaptive retry strategy that handles transient errors, prevents overwhelming Bedrock, adapts to changing service availability, and supports streaming and token-aware handling. Option B is the only choice that combines:
  • Adaptive retry with exponential backoff — the AWS SDK's adaptive retry mode dynamically adjusts the rate of API calls based on observed throttling, exactly matching the "adapt to changing service availability" requirement.
  • Bounded retries (max 5) on transient errors only — prevents retry storms while still recovering from ThrottlingException, ServiceUnavailable, and ModelStreamErrorException.
  • Stream-resumption with buffered chunks — preserves partial responses when chunk delivery times out, addressing the "broken response chunks and delayed data delivery" pain points.

This pattern aligns with AWS Well-Architected Reliability pillar guidance (REL05) for retrying with exponential backoff and jitter while implementing graceful degradation for streaming workloads.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Fixed 1-second delay with only 3 retries is non-adaptive and will hammer Bedrock during throttling. Restarting streams loses all already-received chunks.
  • C: "Nested mode" is not a real SDK retry mode. Returning cached completions for streaming responses can leak stale or wrong content. A single global token cap ignores per-request context.
  • D: Setting a hardcoded 30s client timeout doesn't help with throttling. Static token caps ignore varying prompt complexity. The strategy combines exponential backoff with load shedding, but client-side load shedding without adaptive throttling signals overreacts.

questions.text:
A healthcare company is using Amazon Bedrock to develop a real-time patient care AI assistant to respond to queries for separate departments that handle clinical inquiries, insurance verification, appointment scheduling, and insurance claims. The company wants to use a multi-agent architecture. The company must ensure that the AI assistant is scalable and can onboard new features for patients. The AI assistant must be able to handle thousands of parallel patient interactions. The company must ensure that patients receive appropriate domain-specific responses to queries.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Isolate data for each agent by using separate knowledge bases. Use IAM Identity Center to control access to each knowledge base. Deploy a supervisor agent to perform natural language client classification on patient inquiries. Configure the supervisor agent to route queries to specialized collaborator agents (e.g. clinical, claims, insurance) based on classification. Configure each specialized collaborator agent to use Retrieval-Augmented Generation(RAG) with the agent's department-specific knowledge base.

Create a separate supervisor agent for each department. Configure individual collaborator agents to perform natural language intent classification for each specialty domain within each department. Integrate each collaborator agent with department-specific knowledge bases only. Implement manual handoff processes between the supervisor agents.

Isolate data for each department in separate knowledge bases. Use IAM filtering to enforce access by using a general-purpose agent. Configure multiple action groups within the general-purpose agent to perform individual department functions. Implement role-based routing logic within the general-purpose agent's instructions.

Implement multiple independent supervisor agents that run in parallel to respond to patient queries for each specific department. Configure each collaborator agent to support specialty within each department. Use external routing logic to merge responses from multiple supervisor agents.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

Amazon Bedrock multi-agent collaboration is purpose-built for this exact pattern: one supervisor agent that classifies/routes a user request and dispatches it to specialized collaborator agents, each owning its domain knowledge base via Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).
Option A delivers: 1. Data isolation per department — each collaborator agent uses its own Bedrock Knowledge Base (separate S3 prefixes / vector indexes), satisfying healthcare data segregation requirements (HIPAA aligned). 2. Centralized intelligent routing — the supervisor agent uses an FM to classify intent and route, eliminating the brittleness of hand-coded rules. 3. Scalability — Bedrock Agents is fully managed and serverless; supervisor + collaborator orchestration scales to thousands of concurrent sessions automatically. 4. Extensibility — adding a new department only requires registering a new collaborator agent with the supervisor.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Multiple supervisors with manual handoff destroys the single-entry-point experience and complicates routing — multi-agent collaboration is meant to abstract this.
  • C: One general-purpose agent stuffed with many action groups becomes prompt-bloated, hits context window limits, and loses domain specialization. IAM filtering is not how Bedrock KB access is segmented in agents.
  • D: Parallel independent supervisors with external merging duplicates work, increases cost, and risks contradictory responses. There is no need to "merge" — only one department owns a given query.

questions.text:
A company uses Amazon Bedrock to generate technical content for customers. The company has recently experienced a surge in hallucination outputs when the company's model generates summaries of long technical documents. The model outputs include inaccurate or fabricated details. The company's current solution uses a large foundation model(FM) with a basic one-shot prompt that includes the full document in a single input.

The company needs a solution that will reduce hallucinations and meet factual accuracy goals. The solution must process more than 1,000 documents each hour and deliver summaries in fewer than 3 seconds for each document.

Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements?(Select TWO.)
opts: Implement zero-shot chain-of-thought(CoT) instructions that require step-by-step reasoning with explicit fact verification before the model generates summaries.
Use Retrieval Augmented Generation(RAG) with an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Apply semantic chunking and tuned embeddings to ground summaries in source content.
Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails to block any generated output that matches patterns that are associated with hallucinated content.
Increase the temperature parameter in Amazon Bedrock.
Prompt the Amazon Bedrock model to summarize each full document in one pass.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A, B

  • *B — RAG with semantic chunking and tuned embeddings** is the strongest hallucination mitigation because it forces the model to ground its summaries in retrieved, verifiable source passages instead of relying on its parametric memory. Semantic chunking preserves topical coherence inside chunks, and tuned (domain-adapted) embeddings improve recall on technical jargon — critical for accurate summarization at 1000+ docs/hour.

  • *A — Zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) with explicit fact verification** improves factual accuracy by making the model decompose its reasoning and explicitly check claims against the source before emitting the summary. This is a well-documented technique to reduce confabulation, and zero-shot CoT (as opposed to few-shot with long exemplars) keeps prompt length low — important for the <3s latency target.

Together, A + B provide grounding (retrieval) + verification (reasoning), which is the canonical two-pronged defense against hallucination.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • C: Bedrock Guardrails filter denied topics, PII, profanity, and contextual grounding violations — but they cannot detect arbitrary "hallucination patterns" via static patterns. Hallucinations are semantic, not lexical. (Note: the newer Contextual Grounding check helps, but the option specifies pattern matching, which is wrong.)
  • D: Higher temperature increases randomness and hallucinations — the exact opposite of what's needed. Lower temperature (closer to 0) is what reduces drift.
  • E: This is the current failing approach. Stuffing 1000s of long docs into one-shot prompts exceeds optimal context utilization and is the root cause of the surge in hallucinations.

questions.text:
A financial services company is building a customer support application that retrieves relevant financial regulation documents from a database based on semantic similarities to user queries. The application must integrate with Amazon Bedrock to generate responses. The application must be able to search documents that are in English, Spanish, and Portuguese. The application must filter documents by metadata such as publication date, regulatory agency, and document type.

The database stores approximately 10 million document embeddings. To minimize operational overhead, the company wants a solution that minimizes management and maintenance effort. The application must provide low-latency responses for real-time customer interactions.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use Amazon OpenSearch Serverless to provide vector search capabilities and metadata filtering. Connect to Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to enable Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capabilities that use an Anthropic Claude foundation model(FM).

Deploy an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database with the pgvector extension. Define tables to store embeddings and metadata. Use SQL queries to perform similarity searches. Send retrieved documents to Amazon Bedrock to generate responses.
Use Amazon S3 Vectors to store a vector index and non-filterable metadata fields. Integrate S3 Vectors with Amazon Bedrock to enable Retrieval Augmented Generation(RAG) capabilities.

Set up an Amazon Neptune Analytics graph database. Configure a vector index that has appropriate dimensionality to store document embeddings. Use Amazon Bedrock to perform graph-based retrieval and to generate responses.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

The requirements are: semantic vector search, metadata filtering, multilingual content, 10M embeddings, low latency, and minimal operational overhead. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless (vector engine) + Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the canonical AWS-managed RAG stack:
  • Serverless — no cluster sizing/patching/upgrades; auto-scales OCUs.
  • Native vector + metadata filtering — k-NN with pre/post-filtering on arbitrary metadata fields (date, agency, type).
  • Bedrock Knowledge Base integration — Bedrock handles ingestion (chunking, embedding via Titan Multilingual / Cohere) and query orchestration; the application calls RetrieveAndGenerate for end-to-end RAG.
  • Multilingual — Bedrock supports Titan Text Embeddings V2 and Cohere Embed Multilingual, which handle English/Spanish/Portuguese in the same vector space.
  • Scales to 10M+ vectors with low single-digit-ms retrieval latency.


Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Aurora pgvector works, but the company must define schemas, manage the instance, write SQL similarity queries, and orchestrate the RAG flow themselves. Higher operational overhead — violates the "minimize management" requirement.
  • C: Amazon S3 Vectors is cost-optimized for infrequent queries and offers non-filterable metadata for cheap storage. Spec says "filter by publication date, regulatory agency, and document type" — S3 Vectors filterable metadata is limited (10 keys, smaller size). Also S3 Vectors is sub-second but generally not as low-latency as OpenSearch for real-time chat.
  • D: Neptune Analytics excels at graph + vector hybrid workloads. Pure document semantic search without graph relationships is overkill, costlier, and harder to operate than OpenSearch Serverless.

questions.text:
A company is implementing a serverless inference API by using AWS Lambda. The API will dynamically invoke multiple AI models hosted on Amazon Bedrock. The company must include a solution that can switch between model providers without modifying or redeploying Lambda code in real time. The design must include safe rollout of configuration changes and validation and rollback capabilities.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Store the active model provider in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Configure a Lambda function to read the parameter at runtime to determine which model to invoke.
Store the active model provider in AWS AppConfig. Configure a Lambda function to read the configuration at runtime to determine which model to invoke.
Configure an Amazon API Gateway REST API to route requests to separate Lambda functions. Hardcode each Lambda function to a specific model provider. Switch the integration target manually.

Store the active model provider in a JSON file hosted on Amazon S3. Use AWS AppConfig to reference the S3 file as a hosted configuration source. Configure a Lambda function to read the file through AppConfig at runtime to determine which model to invoke.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

  • *AWS AppConfig** is purpose-built for dynamic runtime configuration with:
  • Safe deployment strategies — linear, exponential, or canary rollouts over a time window.
  • Validators — JSON Schema or Lambda-based validation that runs before any deployment can proceed.
  • Automatic rollback — alarm-triggered rollback via CloudWatch alarms attached to a deployment.
  • Lambda extension layer — caches config locally with TTL polling, minimizing latency and API calls.

Storing the active Bedrock model provider in AppConfig lets the Lambda fetch the current value at invocation time. Operators can switch providers (e.g., from Anthropic Claude to Amazon Nova) by deploying a new AppConfig version — no code redeploy, with built-in validation and rollback. This precisely matches every stated requirement.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: SSM Parameter Store supports dynamic reads but lacks deployment strategies, validators, and automatic rollback. It's a key-value store, not a config-deployment system.
  • C: Requires code redeploys and manual integration-target swaps in API Gateway — opposite of the requirement to switch in real time without modifying Lambda code.
  • D: Over-engineered. AppConfig can host the configuration directly ("Hosted Configuration"); routing through S3 adds latency and a needless artifact. It also blurs ownership and complicates IAM/versioning.

questions.text:
A company is building a video analysis platform on AWS. The platform will analyze a large video archive by using Amazon Rekognition and Amazon Bedrock. The platform must comply with predefined privacy standards. The platform must also use secure model I/O, control foundation model(FM) access patterns, and provide an audit of who accessed what and when.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Configure VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock model API calls. Implement Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for harmful or unauthorized content in prompts and responses. Use Amazon Bedrock model IAM roles to track model invocation for auditing purposes. Configure Amazon CloudWatch to capture API call metrics and AWS KMS keys(SSE-KMS).

Define access control by using IAM with attribute-based access control (ABAC) for granular permissions to specific Amazon Bedrock model API calls. Use Amazon GuardDuty to monitor Amazon Bedrock for harmful events. Capture invocation logs in Amazon S3 with AWS KMS encryption. Enable AWS CloudTrail to detect anomalies in user behavior. Configure VPC interactions with the video archive. Use Amazon Macie to detect and report on the presence of sensitive personal data in the video archive. Use Amazon CloudWatch alarms to detect and alert on suspicious user actions or API calls.

Restrict access to services by using IAM roles. Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) for video archive storage. Use Amazon Inspector to scan for vulnerabilities. Use AWS Config to ensure access to logs by region for compliance auditing.

Configure AWS CloudTrail Insights to capture API call patterns across accounts and detect anomalous activity in Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Rekognition, Amazon S3, and AWS KMS. Enable AWS Config to check for unintended model and configuration changes. Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys(SSE-KMS) for video archive storage in Amazon S3. Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to query CloudTrail logs and to identify unusual access patterns to detect unauthorized use of unapproved foundation models (FMs). Use Amazon CloudWatch logs metrics filters to alert on suspicious activity.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: D

The platform must: 1. Audit who accessed what and when → CloudTrail logs every Bedrock/Rekognition/S3/KMS API call. 2. Detect anomalous / unauthorized FM use → CloudTrail Insights detects deviations from baseline API call patterns; CloudWatch Logs Insights queries CloudTrail logs to identify access to unapproved models. 3. Detect configuration drift → AWS Config tracks resource state changes (model invocation logging settings, IAM policies, KMS keys). 4. Secure model I/O at rest → SSE-KMS on S3 video archive. 5. Alert on suspicious activity → CloudWatch metric filters + alarms.
This option assembles the standard AWS security observability stack (CloudTrail + Config + CloudWatch + KMS) and explicitly targets shadow-AI / unauthorized FM usage detection — the exact threat called out by "control foundation model access patterns" and the audit requirement.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: "Amazon Bedrock model IAM roles to track model invocation for auditing" is wrong — IAM roles authorize, they do not audit. Auditing is CloudTrail's job. Also conflates KMS key configuration with metrics. Missing detection of unauthorized FM access.
  • B: GuardDuty does not monitor Bedrock for "harmful content" — that's the job of Guardrails. Macie scans S3 for PII in text, not videos (Rekognition would extract text first). The mix-and-match of services here doesn't cleanly address audit of FM access.
  • C: Inspector is for EC2/ECR/Lambda vulnerability scanning — not relevant to FM access auditing. No CloudTrail mention means no audit trail. Insufficient.

questions.text:
A healthcare company wants to develop a proof-of-concept application that uses Amazon Bedrock to automatically summarize medical documents. The company has 3 weeks to validate the application's accuracy. The application must comply with the company's data privacy policies. The application must include manual review metrics to evaluate summarization accuracy and processing time.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Create a dataset that includes 80-100 anonymized patient records. Implement Retrieval Augmented Generation(RAG) with a secure knowledge base. Use a judge model to automate accuracy metrics across the foundation models(FMs).

Fine-tune a single foundation model(FM) on patient records. Deploy the FM on Amazon Bedrock. Use Amazon Bedrock Agents to configure the FM as an agent. Conduct user testing on 500 company staff members.

Select the most powerful available AWS foundation model(FM). Create a chat interface by using Converse APIs. Test the application on 50-100 actual patient records by using only qualitative feedback from customers. Use a custom web interface to gather real-world performance data.

Use the Amazon SDK to deploy multiple agents that connect to multiple knowledge bases that contain specialized medical documents. Compare the responses of the agents. Evaluate the integration of the agents with the company's existing systems.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

For a 3-week PoC focused on accuracy validation with privacy compliance and manual review metrics, option A is the right minimum-viable approach:
  • Small anonymized dataset (80–100) — respects healthcare privacy (de-identified per HIPAA Safe Harbor) and is feasible in 3 weeks; large enough to be statistically meaningful for a PoC.
  • RAG with a secure knowledge base — grounds summaries in the actual source documents (critical for medical accuracy), and Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports KMS-encrypted, VPC-private storage.
  • LLM-as-a-judge for automated accuracy metrics — Bedrock Model Evaluation supports automatic evaluation jobs that use a judge model to score outputs (relevance, faithfulness, summarization quality). This complements human review and meets the "accuracy + processing-time metrics" requirement within the time budget.


Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Fine-tuning a model on patient records is slow, expensive, and risks PHI being embedded in model weights — a privacy violation. Testing on 500 staff in 3 weeks is unrealistic for a PoC.
  • C: "Most powerful FM" is vague and ignores cost/latency tradeoffs. Qualitative-only feedback fails the explicit "accuracy metrics" requirement. Using real (non-anonymized) patient data without compliance controls likely violates HIPAA.
  • D: Multi-agent + multi-KB + integration with existing systems is too much scope for a 3-week PoC. Comparing agent responses doesn't itself produce accuracy metrics.

questions.text:
An ecommerce company is using Amazon Bedrock to build a generative AI(GenAI) application. The application uses AWS Step Functions to orchestrate a multi-agent workflow to produce detailed product descriptions. The workflow consists of three sequential states: a description generator, a technical specifications validator, and a brand voice consistency checker. Each state produces intermediate reasoning traces and outputs that are passed to the next state. The application uses an Amazon S3 bucket for process storage and to store outputs.

During testing, the company discovers that outputs between Step Functions states frequently exceed the 256 KB quota and cause workflow failures.

A GenAI Developer needs to revise the application architecture to efficiently handle the Step Functions 256 KB quota and maintain workflow observability. The revised architecture must preserve the existing high reasoning capacity and acting(ReAct) pattern.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
opts: Store intermediate outputs in Amazon DynamoDB. Pass only references between states. Create a Map state that retrieves the complete data from DynamoDB when required for each agent's processing step.

Configure an Amazon Bedrock integration to use the S3 bucket URI in the input parameter for large outputs. Use the ResultPath field to track the agent's state while maintaining the agent's processing capabilities.

Use AWS Lambda functions to compress outputs to less than 256 KB before each agent state. Configure each agent task to decompress the data before processing and to compress results before passing them to the next agent state.

Configure a separate Step Functions state machine to handle each agent's outputs. Use Amazon EventBridge to coordinate the execution flow between state machines. Use S3 references for the outputs as event data.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

Step Functions enforces a hard 256 KB limit on the size of state input/output payloads. The recommended AWS pattern when payloads exceed this limit is the "claim check" / "pointer" pattern: store the large payload in a backing store and pass only a small reference (key/ID) between states.
Option A implements exactly this pattern with DynamoDB as the store: - Each agent writes its full output (reasoning trace + result) to a DynamoDB item. - The state output passed to the next state is a tiny reference (table + key). - Subsequent agent states read the full payload by key. - Map state can fan out reads when needed. - DynamoDB is serverless, single-digit-ms latency, scales automatically — least operational overhead. - Preserves the ReAct loop because each agent still has full access to prior reasoning traces; only the transport changes.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Misleading wording — Step Functions and Bedrock do not natively support a "use S3 URI for large output" parameter that solves the 256 KB cap automatically. Bedrock returns the model output inline; you still must externalize it yourself. The mechanism described doesn't exist.
  • C: Compression adds Lambda functions to encode/decode at every state — significant operational overhead, brittle (compression ratios vary, hard to guarantee <256 KB), and degrades observability since logs see compressed blobs.
  • D: Splitting into multiple state machines coordinated by EventBridge fundamentally breaks the single orchestrated ReAct workflow and increases complexity. Doesn't directly solve the per-state payload limit — EventBridge has its own size limits too.

questions.text:
A company is developing a customer support application that uses Amazon Bedrock foundation models (FMs) to provide real-time AI assistance to the company's employees. The application must display AI-generated responses character by character as the responses are generated. The application supports up to 2 thousand concurrent users with response latency between 15 to 45 seconds each.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Configure an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API with an AWS Lambda integration. Configure the WebSocket API to invoke the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModelWithResponseStream API and stream incremental response chunks to clients by using existing WebSocket connections.
Implement an Amazon API Gateway REST API with an AWS Lambda integration. Configure the REST API to invoke the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel API and return complete responses to clients.
Implement front frontend client connections to Amazon Bedrock by using IAM user credentials and the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API without any intermediate gateway or proxy layer.

Configure an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API with an AWS Lambda function. Configure the API to handle complete responses in an Amazon DynamoDB table and serve the responses through multiple paginated GET requests to frontend clients.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

To stream AI output character-by-character to the browser as it's generated, the connection must be: - Long-lived and bidirectional, capable of carrying many small messages over the 15–45s generation window. - Compatible with Bedrock's InvokeModelWithResponseStream which emits Server-Sent-Event-style chunks.
  • *API Gateway WebSocket API + Lambda** is the canonical AWS solution:
  • WebSocket maintains a persistent connection per client (supports up to ~10K simultaneous connections per region by default, with quota increases for 2K concurrent users).
  • Lambda calls InvokeModelWithResponseStream and for each chunk uses PostToConnection (@connections management API) to push the chunk back to the specific client via the existing connection.
  • No polling, no head-of-line blocking, response visible incrementally — perfect UX for chat.


Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: REST API returns only after the full response is generated (15–45s of waiting). Also, API Gateway REST integration has a hard 29-second timeout for default integrations, which fails for 45-second responses. No character-by-character UX.
  • C: Embedding IAM user credentials in front-end clients is a critical security anti-pattern. Also doesn't scale, can't be revoked per-user, and exposes Bedrock API quotas directly to browsers. Never do this.
  • D: Storing full response then paginating with GETs is the opposite of streaming — adds latency, eliminates real-time feel, costs more, and is unnecessarily complex.

questions.text:
A company is developing a generative AI(GenAI) application that uses Amazon Bedrock foundation models (FMs). The application has several custom tool integrations. The application has experienced unexpected token consumption surges despite consistent user traffic. The company needs a solution that uses Amazon CloudWatch to monitor InputTokenCount metrics and OutputTokenCount metrics. The solution must detect unusual patterns in tool usage and identify which specific tool integrations cause abnormal token consumption. The solution must also automatically adjust thresholds as traffic patterns change.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Create Amazon CloudWatch Logs to capture model invocation logs. Create CloudWatch dashboards based on InputTokenCount metrics and OutputTokenCount metrics. Configure static CloudWatch alarms with fixed thresholds for each tool integration.
Store model invocation logs in an Amazon S3 bucket. Use AWS Athena queries to analyze token consumption patterns by using scheduled Amazon Athena queries that generate reports on tool usage patterns.

Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs to capture model invocation logs. Create CloudWatch metric filters to extract tool-specific invocation patterns. Configure CloudWatch alarms that use anomaly detection to dynamically adjust thresholds based on historical data.

Store model invocation logs in an Amazon S3 bucket. Create AWS Lambda function to process logs in real time. Manually update Amazon CloudWatch alarm thresholds based on token consumption trends that the Lambda function detects.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C

The question explicitly requires: 1. Use CloudWatch (rules out S3/Athena-centric designs). 2. Identify which specific tool integration causes spikes — extracting per-tool metrics from invocation logs requires CloudWatch metric filters that parse log events and emit dimensioned custom metrics. 3. Automatically adjust thresholds as patterns change — this is exactly CloudWatch Anomaly Detection, which uses a machine-learning model trained on the metric's history to compute a dynamic expected band; alarms fire on deviations.
Option C combines all three: - Enable Bedrock Model Invocation Logging → CloudWatch Logs. - Metric filters parse each log event for the toolUseId / tool name and emit Custom/Bedrock/TokenCount metrics dimensioned by tool. - CloudWatch Anomaly Detection alarms on each tool's metric automatically learn the normal range and alert on outliers without manual threshold tuning.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Static thresholds with fixed values violates the "automatically adjust thresholds" requirement. As traffic changes, static thresholds either over-alert or miss anomalies.
  • B: Athena over S3 logs is reactive and batch-oriented; scheduled queries do not provide real-time detection, and the requirement explicitly mandates CloudWatch-based monitoring.
  • D: Manual threshold updates is the antithesis of "automatically adjust thresholds." Adds operational overhead and lag.

questions.text:
A company is developing a generative AI (GenAI) application by using Amazon Bedrock. The application will analyze patterns and relationships in the company's data. The application will process millions of new data points daily across AWS Regions in Europe, North America, and Asia before storing the data in Amazon S3.

The application must comply with local data protection and storage regulations. Data residency and processing must occur within the same continent. The application must also maintain audit trails of the application's decision-making processes and provide data classification capabilities.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Deploy the application in each Region with local IAM policies. Use Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference to distribute the workload. Use Amazon CloudWatch to log AI decision-making processes and data processing activities. Manually track compliance certifications across Regions.

Use SCPs with AWS Organizations to manage location-specific permissions. Use AWS CloudTrail immutable logs to audit the decision-making processes. Import a custom model into Amazon Bedrock and deploy the model in each Region.

Use Amazon S3 Object Lock with Region-specific S3 bucket policies. Pre-process the data points within the Region based on geographic origin before sending the data points to Amazon Bedrock. Use Amazon Macie to classify the data. Use AWS CloudTrail immutable logs to audit the decision-making processes.

Create separate AWS accounts for each Region with individual compliance frameworks. Use Amazon SageMaker AI with custom monitoring to track model performance and compliance with data residency requirements. Create manual reports for each regulatory jurisdiction.
questions.exp:
Correct answer:

The scenario requires four distinct controls: (1) keeping data and processing within the same continent (data residency), (2) immutable audit trails of decision-making, (3) data classification, and (4) compliance scale across many Regions. Option C is the only one that uses purpose-built AWS services for each requirement:
  • S3 Object Lock + Region-specific bucket policies enforce WORM-style residency at the storage layer so data never crosses continents.
  • Pre-processing inside the Region of origin keeps the inference call to Amazon Bedrock local — Bedrock is a Regional service, so calling the Bedrock endpoint in eu-west-1 keeps inference data in the EU. Cross-Region inference (option A) deliberately routes traffic to other Regions for capacity, which violates residency.
  • Amazon Macie is AWS's managed PII/PHI data-classification service for S3 — directly satisfies the "data classification capabilities" requirement.
  • AWS CloudTrail with log file integrity validation / Object Lock on the trail bucket produces immutable audit trails of API calls including InvokeModel, giving traceable decision-making logs.


…

questions.text:
A company is building a generative AI (GenAI) application that produces content based on a variety of internal and external data sources. The company wants to ensure that the generated output is fully traceable. The application must support data source registration and enable metadata tagging to attribute content to its original source. The application must also maintain audit logs of data access and usage throughout the system.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use AWS Lake Formation to catalog data sources and control access. Apply metadata tags directly in Amazon S3. Use AWS CloudTrail to monitor API activity.
Use AWS Glue Data Catalog to register and tag data sources. Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs to monitor access patterns and application behavior.
Store data in Amazon S3 and use object tagging for attribution. Use AWS Glue Data Catalog to register schema information. Use AWS CloudTrail to log access to S3 buckets.
Use AWS Glue Data Catalog to register data sources and apply metadata tags to attribute data sources. Use AWS CloudTrail to log access and activity across services.
questions.exp:
Correct answer:

The three requirements are: (1) source registration, (2) metadata tagging for attribution, (3) audit logs across the whole system.
  • AWS Glue Data Catalog is AWS's central technical metadata store. It registers tables/databases for any source (S3, JDBC, Redshift, Kinesis, RDS, on-prem JDBC, etc.) and supports custom tag-style properties on databases, tables, and columns, which is exactly the attribution model required.
  • AWS CloudTrail captures management and (optionally) data events across services — Glue, S3, Bedrock, Lambda, etc. — giving a single, unified audit trail of data access and usage. The phrase "across services" in the option matches CloudTrail's role-of-record.

Together, Glue Data Catalog (registration + tagging) plus CloudTrail (cross-service audit) satisfy every traceability requirement.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Lake Formation is fine for fine-grained access control, but applying metadata tags "directly in Amazon S3" only gives object tags — it misses schema/source registration. The option also limits CloudTrail to "API activity" rather than data-access audit across services.
  • B: CloudWatch Logs captures application logs; it is not an audit trail of who-accessed-what. Without CloudTrail you lose the immutable, signed audit record AWS expects for compliance.
  • C: Mixes S3 object tagging (attribution) with Glue Data Catalog for schema only — splitting metadata across two systems. CloudTrail scope is restricted to "S3 buckets," so cross-service access (Bedrock, Glue) is not audited.

questions.text: A company deploys multiple Amazon Bedrock based generative AI (GenAI) applications across multiple business units for customer service, content generation, and document review. Some applications show unpredictable token consumption patterns. The company requires a comprehensive observability solution that provides real-time visibility into token usage patterns across multiple models. The observability solution must support custom team dashboards for multiple stakeholder groups and provide alerting capabilities for token consumption across all the foundational models that the company's applications use. Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
opts: Use Amazon CloudWatch usage metrics to monitor token consumption. Add custom CloudWatch metrics for cross-application analysis. Set up Amazon QuickSight dashboards that show token usage trends and usage patterns across FMs.

Use Amazon CloudWatch logs and Amazon Athena to query Amazon Bedrock invocation logs for token consumption patterns and usage analytics by application. Create custom queries to identify high-usage scenarios and configure scheduled reports.
Create custom Amazon CloudWatch dashboards that combine native Amazon Bedrock token and invocation CloudWatch metrics. Set up CloudWatch alarms to monitor token usage thresholds.
Create dashboards that show token usage trends and patterns across the company's FMs by using an Amazon Bedrock zero-ETL integration with Amazon Redshift.

Implement Amazon EventBridge rules to capture Amazon Bedrock model invocation events. Route token usage data to an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream that targets Amazon OpenSearch Serverless. Use OpenSearch dashboards to analyze usage patterns.
questions.exp:
Correct answer:

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Requires enabling Bedrock invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs / S3, then building Athena tables, queries, and scheduled reports — substantial operational overhead and not real-time (queries run on stored logs).
  • D: There is no "Amazon Bedrock zero-ETL integration with Amazon Redshift." Bedrock metrics don't flow to Redshift through a zero-ETL feature; this is a fabricated capability.
  • E: EventBridge → Firehose → OpenSearch Serverless → OpenSearch Dashboards is a full custom pipeline (multiple services to configure, secure, monitor). Bedrock doesn't natively emit per-invocation events to EventBridge for every model call either. Highest operational overhead of all the options.

questions.text: A medical device company wants to feed reports of medical procedures that used the company's devices into an AI assistant. To protect patient privacy, the AI assistant must replace patient personally identifiable information (PII) only to surgeons. The AI assistant must redact PII for engineers. The AI assistant must remove only medical reports that are less than 3 years old. The company stores reports in an Amazon S3 bucket as soon as each report is published. The company has already set up an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. The AI assistant uses Amazon Cognito to authenticate users. Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Enable Amazon Macie PII detection on the S3 bucket. Use an S3 trigger to invoke an AWS Lambda function for the reports. Configure the Lambda function to delete outdated documents from the bucket and to invoke knowledge base syncing.

Invoke an AWS Lambda function to sync the S3 bucket and the knowledge base when a new report is uploaded to the bucket. Use a second Lambda function to remove documents from Amazon S3 that are older than 3 years from the Cognito user group. Set up an S3 Lifecycle configuration to remove the report data when older than 3 years.

Set up an S3 Lifecycle configuration on the bucket to remove reports that are older than 3 years. Schedule an AWS Lambda function to run daily syncs between the bucket and the knowledge base. When users interact with the AI assistant, set the ApplyGuardrail configuration that matches the user's Cognito user group to redact PII from the agent's responses if appropriate.

Create a second knowledge base. Set up an S3 Lifecycle configuration on the bucket to remove reports that are older than 3 years. Invoke an AWS Lambda function that syncs the bucket with the knowledge base when reports are uploaded to the bucket. Use Amazon Comprehend to detect and redact PII from reports stored in the bucket. When users interact with the AI assistant, redirect the model to the appropriate knowledge base depending on the user's Cognito user group.
questions.exp:
Correct answer:

The question (note that the wording is intentionally tricky — "replace ... only to surgeons" = show PII to surgeons, "redact PII for engineers" = hide PII from engineers) has three concerns:
  • Role-based PII redaction — surgeons see PII, engineers do not.
  • 3-year retention — delete documents older than 3 years.
  • Sync the knowledge base so deleted/new documents are reflected.

Option C handles each with the right managed primitive:
  • S3 Lifecycle rule is the canonical way to expire objects after N days (here ~1095 days) — fully managed, no Lambda code to maintain.
  • Scheduled Lambda for KB sync triggers StartIngestionJob on the Bedrock Knowledge Base, picking up new files and removing references to expired ones.
  • Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with ApplyGuardrail API selected at runtime per Cognito group is the supported pattern for dynamic, per-user policy enforcement. The application reads the caller's Cognito group claim and applies the engineer guardrail (with PII masking enabled — SensitiveInformationPolicyConfig set to ANONYMIZE) or the surgeon guardrail (PII pass-through). One knowledge base, one model — different guardrail per group.


…

questions.text: A financial services company needs to pre-process unstructured data such as customer transcripts, financial reports, and documentation. The company stores the unstructured data in Amazon S3 to support an Amazon Bedrock application. The company must validate data quality, create auditable metadata, monitor data metrics, and customize text chunking to optimize foundation model (FM) performance. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
opts: Set up an AWS Glue Data Wrangler to create a data flow. Configure Amazon CloudWatch metrics and alarms to monitor data quality. Use a custom AWS Lambda function to pre-process the data. Load processed data into Amazon Bedrock.

Set up an AWS Glue crawler to catalog data sources. Create AWS Glue ETL jobs to run custom transformation scripts. Use AWS Glue Quality to validate data quality. Load processed data into Amazon Bedrock.
Use Amazon Comprehend to extract entities. Create an AWS Lambda function to chunk text. Use Amazon Athena to query and validate data quality.

Create an AWS Step Functions workflow to orchestrate data pre-processing tasks. Run custom code on Amazon EC2 instances to process the data. Use Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor to monitor data quality. Load processed data into Amazon Bedrock.
questions.exp:
Correct answer:

The requirements decompose to: (1) catalog the unstructured S3 data, (2) custom chunking transformation, (3) data quality validation, (4) auditable metadata, (5) data metrics, all with LEAST development effort.
  • AWS Glue Crawler automatically catalogs S3 sources into the Glue Data Catalog, supplying auditable metadata (databases, tables, schema, classifiers).
  • AWS Glue ETL jobs (Spark or Python shell) provide a managed runtime for custom chunking transformations — no servers to manage.
  • AWS Glue Data Quality (DQ) is the native rules-based engine for declarative data-quality checks (DQDL). It emits results to CloudWatch metrics and EventBridge — covering quality + monitoring without custom code.
  • Output is written back to S3 for ingestion into a Bedrock Knowledge Base.

This is a single-service solution using Glue's purpose-built components.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: "AWS Glue Data Wrangler" is not the right name — SageMaker Data Wrangler is the visual tool, and it focuses on tabular ML prep, not chunked-text prep for FMs. Adding custom Lambda + custom CloudWatch alarms increases development effort and is not Glue's data-quality engine.
  • C: Comprehend extracts entities, not arbitrary chunks. A Lambda for chunking adds custom code. Athena queries don't validate data quality the way Glue DQ does. No source cataloging.
  • D: Step Functions + EC2 + SageMaker Model Monitor is the heaviest option: EC2 to patch/scale, Model Monitor is for ML model drift (not raw data pre-processing), Step Functions adds orchestration code. Highest dev effort.

questions.text:
A healthcare company uses Amazon Bedrock to deploy an application that generates summaries of clinical documents. The application experiences inconsistent response quality with occasional factual hallucinations. Recently, accuracy has dropped by 40%. A GenAI developer must implement a near real-time monitoring solution to detect quality issues, identify abnormal token consumption and provide early warnings of cost anomalies. The solution must require minimal custom development work and maintenance overhead.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Configure Amazon CloudWatch metrics to monitor input/InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount metrics to detect anomalies. Store model invocation logs in an Amazon S3 bucket. Use AWS Glue and Amazon Athena to monitor the logs.

Run Amazon Bedrock evaluation jobs that run for each new report is uploaded to the bucket. Use a second AWS Lambda function to process events from CloudWatch metrics. Configure Amazon CloudWatch alarms to track Lambda function errors and trigger notifications.

Configure Amazon Bedrock to store model invocation logs in an Amazon S3 bucket. Enable text output logging. Configure Amazon CloudWatch alarms based on the logs to monitor for quality issues. Configure a Lambda function to send usage notifications.

Configure Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for contextual grounding checks. Configure Amazon CloudWatch metrics to track usage patterns. Use Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor to detect alarms for model quality.
questions.exp:
Correct answer:

The core requirement is near real-time detection of hallucinations (a quality/grounding problem) plus token/cost anomaly alerts, with minimal custom development.
  • Amazon Bedrock Guardrails — Contextual Grounding Check is the purpose-built feature for hallucination detection. It scores each model response on (a) Grounding — does the response derive from the source/context? (b) Relevance — does it address the question? Responses below configurable thresholds are filtered or flagged. This is native to Bedrock — no custom code.
  • CloudWatch metrics (InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, Invocations) already exist for token / cost anomaly alarms; CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms catch unusual spend automatically.
  • SageMaker Model Monitor can be wired to track ongoing quality alerts (data quality, model quality, bias drift) and feed into CloudWatch alarms.

Combined, D is the answer that directly tackles the hallucination problem via the right managed feature.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Token-count metrics detect cost anomalies but do nothing for hallucinations (a semantic quality problem). Glue + Athena over logs is batchy, not near real-time.
  • B: Bedrock model evaluation jobs are offline/batch evaluations — not near-real-time. Wiring "Lambda errors → notifications" is unrelated to quality monitoring. The architecture is incoherent.
  • C: Invocation logging + Lambda alarms on log content requires writing custom log-parsing logic ("text output logging" doesn't classify hallucinations). High custom-dev overhead and no native grounding check.

questions.text:
A company is designing a solution that uses foundation models (FMs) to support multiple AI workloads. Some FMs need to be invoked on demand in real time. Other FMs require consistent high-throughput access for batch processing.

The solution must support hybrid deployment patterns across cloud infrastructure and on-premises infrastructure to comply with data residency and compliance requirements. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
opts: Use AWS Lambda to orchestrate low-latency FM inference by invoking FMs hosted in Amazon EC2 to asynchronous endpoints.
Configure provisioned throughput in Amazon Bedrock to ensure consistent performance for high-volume workloads.
Deploy FMs to Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints with support for edge deployment by using Amazon SageMaker Neo. Orchestrate the FMs by using AWS Lambda to support hybrid deployment.
Use Amazon Bedrock with auto-scaling to handle unpredictable traffic surges.
Use Amazon SageMaker JumpStart to host and invoke the FMs.
questions.exp:
Correct answer:

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Lambda + EC2-hosted FMs on asynchronous endpoints contradicts the "low-latency, real-time" need. Self-managing FMs on EC2 is also operationally heavy and not the AWS-recommended pattern.
  • D: Bedrock on-demand has internal scaling but no customer-controlled auto-scaling configuration, and it cannot satisfy on-prem residency. Doesn't address hybrid at all.
  • E: JumpStart is a model catalog/launcher for SageMaker — it can deploy FMs but does not by itself provide hybrid/on-prem capability or guaranteed throughput. Incomplete answer.

questions.text:
A financial services company needs to build a sentiment analysis system that uses Amazon Bedrock to process quarterly reports. The system must analyze financial data, perform sentiment analysis, and validate compliance across batches of reports. Each batch contains 5 reports. Each report requires multiple foundation model (FM) calls. The solution must finish the analysis within 10 seconds for each batch. Current sequential processing takes 45 seconds for each batch.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use AWS Lambda functions with provisioned concurrency to process each analysis type sequentially. Configure the Lambda function timeouts to 10 seconds with exponential backoff.

Use AWS Step Functions with a Parallel state to invoke separate AWS Lambda functions for each analysis type simultaneously. Configure Amazon Bedrock provisioned throughput to maintain consistent performance and to reduce response latency.

Create an Amazon SQS queue to buffer analysis requests. Deploy multiple AWS Lambda functions with reserved concurrency. Configure an Amazon Bedrock client throttling mechanism to track execution time and resolve service errors.

Deploy an Amazon ECS cluster that runs containers that process the analysis. Use a load balancer to distribute batch workloads. Configure an auto-scaling policy based on CPU utilization to handle demand fluctuations.
questions.exp:
Correct answer:

Mathematically: sequentially the workload takes 45 s; target is ≤10 s. We need ~5× speed-up, meaning the FM calls must be parallelised and each call must hit predictable latency.
  • AWS Step Functions Parallel state fans out to multiple branches that each invoke a Lambda concurrently — naturally executing the multiple FM calls per report and the 5 reports per batch in parallel.
  • Each Lambda calls Bedrock with Provisioned Throughput to avoid on-demand throttling and to produce consistent, low-variance latency so the parallel branches reliably finish under 10 s.
  • The combination directly fixes the two bottlenecks: serialization (Step Functions Parallel) and per-call latency variance (Provisioned Throughput).


Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Still sequential. Provisioned concurrency only removes Lambda cold starts — it does not parallelise the workflow. 10-second timeouts cause failures, not speed-ups.
  • C: SQS adds queuing latency; reserved concurrency limits how many Lambdas can run but doesn't orchestrate parallel fan-out. "Bedrock client throttling mechanism" is not a real native feature, and tracking execution time doesn't reduce it.
  • D: ECS + ALB is high operational overhead (cluster, scaling policy on CPU which is irrelevant since the bottleneck is external Bedrock latency, not CPU). Cannot reliably bring 45 s → 10 s without fanning out FM calls.

questions.text:
An ecommerce company is building an internal platform to develop generative AI applications by using Amazon Bedrock foundation models (FMs). Developers need to select models based on evaluations that are aligned to ecommerce use cases. The platform must deploy accuracy metrics for text generation and summarization in dashboards. The company has multiple business units that use standardized evaluation inputs.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
opts: Import the datasets to an Amazon S3 bucket. Provide appropriate IAM permissions and cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) policies to give the evaluation jobs the necessary access to the datasets.
Import the datasets to an Amazon S3 bucket. Provide appropriate IAM permissions and a VPC endpoint configuration to give the evaluation jobs access to the datasets.
Configure an AWS Lambda function to create model evaluation jobs in a schedule in the Amazon Bedrock console. Provide the URI of the S3 bucket that contains the datasets as an input.

Configure the evaluation framework to compute the required knowledge (RIK) score for text generation and BERT Score for summarization. Configure a second Lambda function to create the data evaluation jobs in SageMaker AI. Establish a centralized dashboard by using Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights dashboard.

Use Amazon SageMaker Clarify on a schedule to create model evaluation jobs. Use source frameworks to create and run standardized evaluations. Publish results to Amazon CloudWatch metrics. Use the worst score values per model to drive model selection and identify the worst-performing models. Configure Amazon CloudWatch Logs dashboards to share the results across the platform and publish a custom Amazon CloudWatch Logs dashboard.
questions.exp:
Correct answer:

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: A VPC endpoint adds networking complexity that isn't required for S3 dataset access from Bedrock / SageMaker evaluation jobs (they can read via the public endpoint with IAM). Higher operational overhead than the simpler IAM + CORS pattern.
  • C: Bedrock model evaluation jobs are not natively scheduled by Lambda invoking the console; this would require custom code, error handling, and IAM. Higher overhead than Clarify schedules.
  • D: "RIK score" is not a recognised metric. Adding a second Lambda to start "data evaluation jobs in SageMaker AI" duplicates work. CloudWatch Logs Insights dashboards are query-based and not built for metric dashboards — wrong tool.

questions.text:
A company is using Amazon Bedrock and Anthropic Claude 3 Haiku to develop an AI assistant. The AI assistant normally processes 10,000 requests each hour but experiences surges of up to 30,000 requests each hour during peak usage periods. The AI assistant must respond within 2 seconds while operating across multiple AWS Regions. The company observes that during peak usage periods, the AI assistant experiences throughput bottlenecks that cause increased latency and occasional request timeouts. The company must resolve the performance issues.

Which solution will meet this requirement?
opts: Purchase provisioned throughput and sufficient model units (MUs) in a single Region. Configure the application to retry failed requests with an exponential backoff.
Implement token batching to reduce API overhead. Use Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference profiles to automatically distribute traffic across Regions available.
Set up auto-scaling AWS Lambda functions in each Region. Implement client-side round-robin request distribution. Purchase one model unit (MU) of provisioned throughput as a backup.
Implement batch inference for all requests by using Amazon S3 buckets across multiple Regions. Use Amazon SQS to set up an asynchronous retrieval process.
questions.exp:
Correct answer:

The bottleneck is real-time on-demand throughput during 3× surges with a hard 2-second SLA across multiple Regions.
  • Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference profiles are the purpose-built feature for exactly this scenario: a single inference profile (e.g., us.anthropic.claude-3-haiku-*) transparently routes invocations to multiple Regions in the profile's geography. Bedrock balances load and uses the aggregated quota across Regions, smoothing surges and raising effective throughput without requiring the application to maintain Region-aware routing logic. This directly resolves the "throughput bottleneck" and the multi-Region requirement.
  • It preserves latency because Bedrock chooses an in-geography Region that can serve quickly, and reduces throttling that was causing timeouts.
  • Token batching (sending fewer, larger requests where appropriate) reduces per-call overhead, complementing the throughput gain.


Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Provisioned throughput in a single Region violates the multi-Region requirement. Exponential backoff also adds latency, hurting the 2-second SLA. PT helps with capacity but doesn't address geographic distribution.
  • C: Lambda auto-scaling doesn't increase Bedrock-side throughput (Bedrock quotas are the constraint, not Lambda). Client-side round-robin is brittle and ignores Region health. One MU of PT is a token amount — insufficient as backup.
  • D: Batch inference is asynchronous (results delivered to S3 later) — incompatible with a 2-second real-time SLA. SQS adds queueing latency. Wrong mode of inference for an interactive AI assistant.

questions.text:
A media company is launching a platform that allows thousands of users every hour to upload images and text content. The platform uses Amazon Bedrock to process the uploaded content to generate creative compositions.

The company needs a solution to ensure that the platform does not process or produce inappropriate content. The platform must not expose personally identifiable information (PII) in the compositions. The solution must integrate with the company's existing Amazon S3 storage workflow. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST infrastructure management overhead?
opts: Enable the Enhanced Monitoring tool. Use an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to filter traffic to the platform.

Use Amazon Comprehend PII detection to pre-process the data. Create a CloudWatch alarm to monitor for Amazon Comprehend PII detection events. Create an AWS Step Functions workflow that includes an Amazon Rekognition image moderation step.

Use an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API with request validation templates to screen content before storing the uploaded content in Amazon S3. Use Amazon SageMaker AI to build custom content moderation models that process content before sending the processed content to Amazon Bedrock.

Create an Amazon Cognito user pool that uses pre-authentication AWS Lambda functions to run content moderation checks. Use Amazon Textract to filter text content and Amazon Rekognition to filter image content before sending users to upload content to the platform.

Create an AWS Step Functions workflow that uses built-in Amazon Bedrock guardrails to filter content. Use Amazon Comprehend PII detection to pre-process the content. Use Amazon Rekognition image moderation.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

Option B uses fully managed AWS AI services purpose-built for the exact tasks: Amazon Comprehend's PII detection API redacts/identifies personally identifiable entities in text, and Amazon Rekognition's DetectModerationLabels API flags unsafe imagery. Coordinating them in an AWS Step Functions workflow leverages a serverless orchestrator that integrates natively with S3 events. None of these components require provisioning servers, training custom models, or maintaining infrastructure, so this satisfies the "LEAST infrastructure management overhead" constraint.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: "Enhanced Monitoring" with a CloudWatch alarm only filters/observes metric traffic — it cannot detect PII in text or moderate image content. It does not meet the functional requirement at all.
  • C: API Gateway request validation can only validate JSON schemas/parameters, not screen semantic content. Building custom SageMaker moderation models requires data labeling, training, hosting, and continuous tuning — the highest possible infrastructure overhead.
  • D: Cognito pre-authentication Lambda triggers run during sign-in, not on content upload. Textract is for extracting text from documents (forms/tables), not moderating text. The architecture also runs moderation client-side before upload, which is unreliable.
  • E: Bedrock Guardrails apply to model input/output during Bedrock InvokeModel calls — they do not run as a standalone "Step Functions task" on arbitrary S3 objects. Also redundantly stacks Comprehend + Guardrails for the same text task.

questions.text:
A media company is launching a platform that allows thousands of users every hour to upload images and text content. The platform uses Amazon Bedrock to process the uploaded content to generate creative compositions.

The company needs a solution to ensure that the platform does not process or produce inappropriate content. The platform must not expose personally identifiable information (PII) in the compositions. The solution must integrate with the company's existing Amazon S3 storage workflow. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST infrastructure management overhead?
opts: Enable the Enhanced Monitoring tool. Use an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to filter traffic to the platform.

Use Amazon Comprehend PII detection to pre-process the data. Create a CloudWatch alarm to monitor for Amazon Comprehend PII detection events. Create an AWS Step Functions workflow that includes an Amazon Rekognition image moderation step.

Use an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API with request validation templates to screen content before storing the uploaded content in Amazon S3. Use Amazon SageMaker AI to build custom content moderation models that process content before sending the processed content to Amazon Bedrock.

Create an Amazon Cognito user pool that uses pre-authentication AWS Lambda functions to run content moderation checks. Use Amazon Textract to filter text content and Amazon Rekognition to filter image content before sending users to upload content to the platform.

Create an AWS Step Functions workflow that uses built-in Amazon Bedrock guardrails to filter content. Use Amazon Comprehend PII detection to pre-process the content. Use Amazon Rekognition image moderation.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

Combining Amazon Comprehend (managed PII detection on text) with Amazon Rekognition (managed image moderation) and orchestrating them through AWS Step Functions delivers all the requirements with zero servers to manage. Step Functions integrates natively with S3 events, Comprehend, and Rekognition, so the company can wire detection into the existing S3 storage workflow declaratively. The CloudWatch alarm provides operational visibility into PII findings so the team can investigate spikes without managing additional infrastructure.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: A CloudWatch alarm cannot inspect image or text content — it only reacts to numeric metrics. No moderation or PII detection is actually performed.
  • C: API Gateway request validation is restricted to JSON schema/parameters and cannot screen file contents. Custom SageMaker moderation models impose maximum infrastructure overhead (training pipelines, endpoints, drift monitoring).
  • D: Cognito pre-authentication Lambda runs once during sign-in, not on uploads. Textract extracts text from documents — it is not a text moderation engine.
  • E: Bedrock Guardrails are scoped to InvokeModel/Converse calls; they cannot be plugged in as a Step Functions task to filter raw S3 assets. The option also doubles up Guardrails + Comprehend on the same text.

questions.text: A financial services company uses multiple foundation models (FMs) through Amazon Bedrock for its generative AI (GenAI) applications. To comply with new regulations for GenAI use and ensure financial data, the company needs a token management solution that proactively alerts when applications approach model-specific token limits. The solution must also process more than 5,000 requests each minute and maintain token usage metrics to allocate costs across business units. Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Develop model-specific tokenizers in an AWS Lambda function. Configure the Lambda function to estimate the token consumption before sending requests to Amazon Bedrock. Configure the Lambda function to publish metrics to Amazon CloudWatch and trigger alarms when requests approach thresholds. Store detailed token usage in Amazon DynamoDB to report costs.

Implement Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with built-in token usage policies. Capture metrics on rejected requests. Configure Amazon EventBridge rules to trigger notifications based on Amazon Bedrock Guardrails events. Use Amazon CloudWatch dashboards to visualize token usage trends across business units.

Deploy an Amazon SQS dead-letter queue for failed requests. Configure an AWS Lambda function to analyze token-related failures. Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to generate reports on token usage patterns based on error logs from Amazon Bedrock API responses.

Use Amazon API Gateway to create a proxy in front of Amazon Bedrock APIs. Configure request throttling based on custom usage plans with predefined token quotas. Configure API Gateway to reject requests that exceed token limits.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

Different Bedrock foundation models use different tokenizers (Anthropic vs. Cohere vs. Meta vs. Amazon Titan), so reliable pre-flight token estimation requires running the matching tokenizer client-side before invocation. A Lambda function can call the appropriate tokenizer (e.g., Anthropic's count_tokens, tiktoken for Cohere/Llama variants, etc.), publish per-tenant/per-model metrics to CloudWatch (which alarms when usage approaches the per-model quota), and persist detailed usage into DynamoDB for low-latency chargeback reports. At 5,000+ rpm, both Lambda and DynamoDB scale easily, and CloudWatch alarms are the supported AWS pattern for proactive notification before account-level Bedrock quotas are hit.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Bedrock Guardrails do not provide "token usage policies." Guardrails filter content (denied topics, PII, harmful categories) — they do not track or alert on token quotas.
  • C: A DLQ + log-analysis pattern is reactive — it only notices throttling after requests already fail. It cannot proactively alert before limits are hit, and CloudWatch Logs Insights is too slow for high-volume cost reporting.
  • D: API Gateway throttles by request count (RPS/burst), not by tokens. It has no visibility into the model's tokenizer or token consumption, so it cannot enforce per-model token quotas or generate accurate cost attribution.

questions.text: A bank is developing a generative AI (GenAI)-powered AI assistant that uses Amazon Bedrock to assist the bank's website users with account inquiries and financial guidance. The bank must ensure that the AI assistant does not reveal any personally identifiable information (PII) in customer interactions. The AI assistant must not send PII in prompts to the GenAI model. The AI assistant must not respond to customer requests to provide investment advice. The bank must collect audit logs of all customer interactions, including any images or documents that are transmitted during customer interactions. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?
opts: Use Amazon Macie to detect and redact PII in user inputs and in the model responses. Apply prompt engineering techniques to force the model to avoid investment advice topics. Use AWS CloudTrail to capture conversation logs.

Use an AWS Lambda function and Amazon Comprehend to detect and redact PII. Use Amazon Comprehend topic modeling to predict the AI assistant from discussing investment advice topics. Set up custom metrics in Amazon CloudWatch to capture customer conversations.

Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails to apply a sensitive information filter to redact PII in user inputs. Set up a topic policy in the Guardrails configuration to prevent the AI assistant from discussing investment advice topics. Use the Converse API to log model invocations. Enable delivery and image logging to Amazon S3.

Use regex scripts to match patterns for PII. Apply prompt engineering techniques to prevent the AI assistant from discussing investment advice topics. Enable Amazon S3 logging, delivery logging, and image logging in Amazon S3.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails offer purpose-built, fully managed policies that satisfy every requirement at once: 1. The sensitive information filter can mask or block PII entities in both inputs and outputs. 2. Denied/topic policies let you declaratively prevent the model from responding about "investment advice," with natural-language descriptions instead of brittle regex. 3. Bedrock model invocation logging (configurable on the Bedrock service) captures full request/response payloads — including image inputs — to S3 and/or CloudWatch with one toggle.
This is delivered as managed configuration on Bedrock — no Lambdas, no Macie jobs, no SageMaker — which is the lowest operational effort solution.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Amazon Macie scans S3 buckets for PII; it does not redact in-flight prompts or model responses. CloudTrail records API control-plane events, not prompt/response payloads, so it cannot satisfy the audit requirement.
  • B: Comprehend topic modeling discovers themes in a corpus; it cannot prevent a live model from producing investment advice. Custom CloudWatch metrics cannot store the conversation payloads either. Significant Lambda glue is required — high operational effort.
  • D: Regex-based PII matching is fragile, misses many entity formats, and prompt engineering alone cannot guarantee the model refuses investment advice. "S3 logging" of model traffic still requires building the logging pipeline yourself.

questions.text: A financial technology company is using Amazon Bedrock to build an assessment system for the company's customer service AI assistant. The AI assistant must provide financial recommendations that are factually accurate, compliant with conversationally appropriate. The company needs to combine automated quality evaluations at scale with targeted human reviews of critical interactions. What solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Configure a pipeline in which financial experts manually score all responses for accuracy, compliance, and conversational quality. Use Amazon SageMaker notebooks to analyze results to identify improvement areas.

Configure Amazon Bedrock evaluations that use Anthropic Claude Sonnet as a judge model to assess response accuracy and appropriateness. Configure custom Amazon Bedrock automated evaluations to evaluate the responses. Add Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) human reviews for flagged critical interactions.

Create an Amazon Lex bot to manage the customer service interactions. Configure AWS Lambda functions to check responses against a static compliance database. Configure interns in the bot that call the Lambda functions to check the responses. Add an additional intent to collect user feedback.

Use reports across data sources for PII. Apply prompt engineering techniques to avoid returning PII in investment advice topics to customers. Enable model invocation logging, delivery logging, and image logging in Amazon S3.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

The requirement is a hybrid evaluation pipeline: automated quality scoring at scale plus targeted human review for critical interactions. - Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation supports automatic evaluation jobs (including LLM-as-a-judge) where a strong model such as Claude Sonnet scores another model's outputs on dimensions like correctness, relevance, and toxicity. - Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) provides a managed human-review workflow: when an interaction meets a "critical" condition (e.g., low confidence, high-risk topic), it is routed to private reviewers with a custom worker UI for adjudication. Together they form the canonical AWS pattern for "scale + selective human oversight."

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: 100% human review does not "scale" and ignores the explicit requirement for automated quality evaluation. Operationally infeasible.
  • C: Amazon Lex builds chatbots; it does not perform quality evaluation of generated responses. A static compliance database cannot judge factual accuracy or conversational appropriateness of LLM output.
  • D: Discusses PII, prompt engineering, and logging — none of which evaluate response quality or supply human review. Off-topic.

questions.text: A company has set up an Amazon Q Developer Pro licenses for all developers at the company. The company maintains a list of approved resources that developers must use when developing applications. The approved resources include internal libraries, proprietary algorithmic techniques, and sample code with approved styling. A new team of developers is using Amazon Q Developer to create a new Java-based application. The company must ensure that the new developer team uses the company's approved resources. The company does not want to make project-level modifications. Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Create a Git repository that contains all of the approved internal libraries, algorithms, and code samples. Include the Git repository in the application project locally as an IP workspace. Ensure that the developers use the workspace context to receive suggestions from the Git repository.

In the project root folder, create a folder named amazonqrules. Add the approved internal libraries, algorithms, and code samples to the folder. Configure the developers to use the Amazon Q chat to reference approved rules during development.
Create a folder in the application project named rules. Store the guidelines and code in the folder for Amazon Q Developer to reference product code suggestions.
Create an Amazon Q Developer customization that includes the approved data sources. Ensure that the developers use the customization to develop the application.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: D

  • *Amazon Q Developer customizations let an administrator securely connect approved source-code repositories so Amazon Q's inline suggestions and chat draw from the company's private libraries, patterns, and APIs. Customizations are administered at the account level**, applied to entitled users via IAM Identity Center groups — no per-project file changes are needed, satisfying the "does not want to make project-level modifications" constraint. The new Java team simply uses Amazon Q Developer with the customization enabled and will receive suggestions that respect the approved internal libraries and styles.


Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Adding a Git repo as a local workspace requires modifying every project to include it, violating the "no project-level modifications" rule. Amazon Q's workspace context is not equivalent to a customization for influencing suggestions across teams.
  • B: There is no amazonqrules convention — this is fabricated. Even if it existed, adding a folder is a project-level modification.
  • C: A rules folder in each project is again a per-project modification, and Amazon Q Developer does not consume an arbitrary rules folder as a source of approved patterns.

questions.text: A finance company is developing an AI assistant to help clients plan investments and manage their portfolios. The company identifies several high-risk conversation patterns such as requests for specific stock recommendations or guaranteed returns. High-risk conversation patterns could lead to regulatory violations if the company cannot implement appropriate controls. The company must ensure that the AI assistant does not provide inappropriate financial advice, generate content about competitors, or make claims that are not factually grounded in the company's approved financial guidance. The company wants to use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to implement a solution. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select THREE.)
opts: Add the high-risk conversation patterns to a denied topics guardrail.
Configure a content filter guardrail to filter prompts that contain high-risk conversation patterns.
Configure a content filter guardrail to filter prompts that contain competitor names.
Add the names of competitors as custom word filters. Set the input and output actions to block.
Set a low grounding score threshold.
Set a high grounding score threshold.
questions.exp:
