Correct answer: A, D, F

  • A — Denied topics: Bedrock Guardrails' denied-topics policy is the right tool for whole-topic prohibitions described in natural language (e.g., "specific stock recommendations," "guaranteed returns"). The model will refuse those topics on both input and output.
  • D — Custom word filter for competitor names: Word filters are designed for exact-string blocking such as brand or competitor names. Setting both input and output actions to block ensures competitors are neither asked about nor mentioned in the response.
  • F — High grounding score threshold (contextual grounding): The contextual grounding policy scores how well each response is supported by the retrieved/source material. A high threshold rejects ungrounded responses, enforcing the requirement that claims be factually grounded in approved guidance.


Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Content filters target safety categories (hate, insults, sexual, violence, misconduct, prompt attacks) — they cannot be configured to detect arbitrary "high-risk conversation patterns" in finance. Use denied topics instead.
  • C: Content filters do not match arbitrary strings like competitor names. Use a custom word filter (option D).
  • E: A low grounding threshold accepts weakly grounded answers — exactly the opposite of what is required. The higher the threshold, the stricter the grounding check.

questions.text: A specialty coffee company has a mobile app that generates personalized coffee roast profiles by using Amazon Bedrock with a three-stage prompt chain. The prompt chain converts user inputs into structured metadata, retrieves relevant logs for coffee roasts, and generates a personalized roast recommendation for each customer. Users in multiple AWS Regions report inconsistent roast recommendations for identical inputs, slow inference during the retrieval step, and unsafe recommendations such as brewing at excessively high temperatures. The company must improve the stability of outputs for repeated inputs. The company must also improve app performance and the safety of the app's outputs. The updated solution must ensure 99.5% output consistency for identical inputs and achieve inference latency of less than 1 second. The solution must also block unsafe or hallucinated recommendations by using validated safety controls. Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Deploy Amazon Bedrock with provisioned throughput to stabilize inference latency. Apply Amazon Bedrock guardrails that have semantic deny rules to block unsafe outputs. Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to manage prompts by using approval workflows.
Deploy an Amazon API Gateway in front of Amazon Bedrock. Set up AWS WAF rules to block prompts that produce harmful outputs.
Cache prompt results in Amazon ElastiCache. Use AWS Lambda functions to pre-process metadata and to trace end-to-end latency. Use AWS X-Ray to identify and remediate performance bottlenecks.
Use Amazon Kendra to improve roast tip retrieval accuracy. Store normalized prompt metadata within Amazon DynamoDB. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate multi-step prompts.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

  • Provisioned Throughput on Bedrock reserves dedicated model units, providing predictable, consistent low-latency inference (well under 1 s for short prompts) and removing the variability of on-demand quotas across Regions.
  • Bedrock Guardrails (denied topics + content/grounding policies) are the validated, managed safety control AWS offers to block unsafe or hallucinated outputs (e.g., dangerous brewing temperatures).
  • Bedrock Prompt Management versions and approves prompts. Combined with deterministic settings (low temperature) and the same prompt version, identical inputs reliably produce the same output, satisfying the 99.5% consistency target. Prompt Management's approval workflow also enforces only validated, safe prompts reach production.

This is the only option that simultaneously addresses latency stability, output consistency, and safety with managed Bedrock features.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: AWS WAF inspects HTTP request patterns — it cannot detect or block harmful LLM outputs, and API Gateway alone does nothing to stabilize Bedrock inference latency or output consistency.
  • C: Caching with ElastiCache and X-Ray tracing might help latency for repeated identical inputs but does nothing about safety of new outputs, does not guarantee consistency for non-cached prompts, and does not address cross-Region quota variance.
  • D: Kendra/DynamoDB/Step Functions improves retrieval/orchestration but offers no managed guardrail and no mechanism to enforce output consistency or sub-second model latency.

questions.text:
A company is building a multicloud generative AI (GenAI) assistant for resolution application that uses Amazon Bedrock and Agent Squad. The application requires secrets from multiple sources, including key stores and hardware security modules (HSMs). The application uses AWS Lambda functions to retrieve secrets from the sources. The application uses AWS AppConfig to implement features gating. The application supports business logic from third-party AI service feature flags and detects secret drift. The solution must enable runtime feature flag updates and detect secret drift.

The company finds multiple issues during application testing. The application gets stale data, but agents still use stale data. Prompt flows within the application require updated metadata templates, which cause workflow errors. Although latency increases due to inefficient cross-Region multi-step prompt processing.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use Step Functions Map states to run agents in parallel. Pass updated secret metadata through Lambda function outputs. Use AWS AppConfig to perform real-time updates to feature flags and to enforce flag fault tolerance integrity.

Amazon Bedrock Agents Action Groups only. Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails to provide real-time prompt updates. Use Amazon CloudWatch to identify a single secret point of failure and reduce latency.
Use a centralized Amazon EventBridge pipeline to invoke each event agent. Store intermediate prompts in Amazon DynamoDB. Resolve agent ordering by using TTL-based versioning.

Use Amazon EventBridge Pipes to invoke models from Amazon CloudWatch log streams. Store response metadata in Amazon DynamoDB. Configure a TTL and tag versioned writes. Use Amazon Q developer to dynamically generate fallback prompts that are routed through a Lambda coordinator.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

The application needs three things at once: 1. Parallel, low-latency multi-agent execution — AWS Step Functions Map state runs agents concurrently across array items, eliminating sequential cross-Region delays. 2. Fresh secrets and prompt metadata — passing updated metadata as Lambda outputs into the Map iterator guarantees each parallel branch uses the latest values rather than cached/stale data. 3. Runtime feature flag updates with drift safety — AWS AppConfig is purpose-built for safe, validated, runtime configuration deployment. Its deployment strategies, validators, and rollback support preserve feature-flag integrity.
This is the only option that addresses parallelism, freshness of secret/metadata propagation, and AppConfig's role in real-time, fault-tolerant feature flags.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Bedrock Guardrails do not "provide real-time prompt updates"; they filter content. CloudWatch is observability, not a SPOF mitigator. The option ignores feature flags and stale-secret detection.
  • C: EventBridge with TTL-based versioning in DynamoDB does not solve secret drift detection, does not provide runtime feature flag updates, and TTL is not a versioning mechanism.
  • D: EventBridge Pipes do not "invoke models from CloudWatch logs"; that pattern is invented. Using Q Developer at runtime to generate fallback prompts is not a production pattern and ignores AppConfig/secret drift.

questions.text: A hotel company wants to enhance a Java-based property management system (PMS) by adding AI capabilities. The company wants to use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to provide staff with room availability information and hotel-specific details. The solution must maintain separate access controls for each hotel that the company supports. The solution must provide room availability information in near real time and must maintain consistent performance during peak usage periods. Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Deploy a single Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that contains combined data for all hotels. Configure AWS Lambda functions to synchronize data from each hotel's PMS database through direct API connections. Implement AWS CloudTrail logging with hotel-specific filters to audit access logs for each hotel's data.

Create an Amazon EventBridge rule for each hotel that pushes data to a single Amazon Bedrock knowledge base whenever a reservation is created or updated. Configure resource-based policies on the Amazon Bedrock knowledge base to restrict access for each hotel. Configure resource-based policies to enforce critical information.

Implement one Amazon Bedrock knowledge base for each hotel in a multi-account structure. Use direct data ingestion to provide real-time availability information. Configure individual Lambda functions to manage data synchronization. Configure individual roles to manage access.
Build a centralized Amazon Bedrock agent that uses multiple knowledge bases. Implement AWS IAM Identity Center with hotel-specific permissions to control hotel-specific data access.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C

A per-hotel Bedrock Knowledge Base in a multi-account (or multi-KB) layout cleanly satisfies every requirement: - Separate access controls per hotel — each KB has its own IAM/KMS boundary so cross-hotel access is impossible by construction; multi-account isolation is the AWS gold standard for tenant separation. - Near real-time availability — Bedrock Knowledge Bases now support a direct ingestion / custom data source API that lets the PMS push reservation changes immediately without re-running a full S3 crawl. - Consistent peak performance — separate KBs and roles avoid noisy-neighbor effects and let each hotel scale ingestion and query independently.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: A single shared KB cannot enforce true per-tenant isolation: filters are best-effort metadata-level controls, and CloudTrail only audits after access. This violates the "separate access controls per hotel" requirement.
  • B: Bedrock Knowledge Bases do not support resource-based policies for fine-grained per-hotel access. EventBridge events cannot themselves ingest documents into a KB; you would still need an ingestion mechanism.
  • D: A central agent over multiple KBs improves UX but does not provide ingestion freshness, and IAM Identity Center alone cannot guarantee per-hotel data isolation if the underlying KBs share infrastructure without per-tenant separation. The option also omits a real-time ingestion path.

tags: Monitoring, Observability & Operations on Amazon Bedrock
questions.text:
A company has a generative AI(GenAI) application that uses Amazon Bedrock to provide real-time responses to customer queries. The company has noticed intermittent failures with API calls to foundation models(FMs) during peak traffic periods. The company needs a solution to handle transient errors and provide detailed observability into FM performance. The solution must prevent cascading failures during throttling events and provide distributed tracing across service boundaries to identify latency contributors. The solution must also enable correlation of performance issues with specific FM characteristics.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Implement a custom retry mechanism with a fixed delay of 1 second between retries. Configure Amazon CloudWatch alarms to monitor the application's error rates and latency metrics.
Configure the AWS SDK with adaptive retry mode and exponential backoff with jitter. Use AWS X-Ray tracing with annotations to identify and filter service components.
Implement client-side caching of all FM responses. Add custom logging statements in the application code to record API call durations.
Configure the AWS SDK with adaptive retry, but use AWS CloudTrail distributed tracing to monitor throttling events.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

The AWS SDK's adaptive retry mode automatically detects throttling (e.g., ThrottlingException, TooManyRequestsException) returned by Bedrock's InvokeModel / Converse APIs and dynamically tunes the request rate using a client-side rate limiter and exponential backoff with jitter. Jitter prevents the "thundering herd" effect where many clients retry simultaneously and re-trigger throttling — exactly the cascading-failure scenario described. AWS X-Ray provides true distributed tracing across service boundaries; with annotations (indexed key-value pairs), you can tag each segment with FM identifiers (e.g., modelId=anthropic.claude-3-sonnet) and then filter/group traces to correlate latency with specific FM characteristics — which is the explicit final requirement.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: A fixed-delay retry has no jitter, so concurrent clients re-collide and amplify throttling (cascading failure). CloudWatch alarms surface metrics but provide no distributed tracing, so latency contributors across service boundaries cannot be isolated.
  • C: Caching every FM response is unsafe for personalised real-time queries (stale / wrong answers) and does not address throttling, distributed tracing, or correlation with FM characteristics. Custom log timestamps are not distributed traces.
  • D: CloudTrail is an API audit/governance service — it does NOT provide distributed tracing. X-Ray is the tracing service. This is a deliberate distractor.

tags: Monitoring & Operations on Amazon Bedrock with Lambda
questions.text:
A company is building a serverless application that uses AWS Lambda functions to help students around the world summarize notes. The application uses Anthropic Claude through Amazon Bedrock. The company observed that most of the traffic occurs during evenings in each time zone. Users report experiencing throttling errors during peak usage times in their time zones. The company needs to resolve the throttling issues by ensuring continuous operation of the application. The solution must maintain application performance quality. The company needs a solution that does not require a fixed hourly cost during low traffic periods.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Create custom Amazon CloudWatch metrics to monitor model errors. Set provisioned throughput to a value that is safely higher than the peak traffic observed.
Create custom Amazon CloudWatch metrics to monitor model errors. Set up a failover mechanism to redirect invocations to a backup AWS Region when the errors exceed a specified threshold.

Enable invocation logging in Amazon Bedrock. Monitor key metrics such as Invocations, InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, and InvocationThrottles. Distribute traffic across cross-Region inference endpoints.
Enable invocation logging in Amazon Bedrock. Monitor InvocationLatency, InvocationClientErrors, and InvocationServerErrors metrics. Distribute traffic across multiple versions of the same model.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C

The requirement set is: (1) eliminate throttling, (2) keep operating continuously, (3) preserve quality, (4) avoid a fixed hourly cost during quiet periods. Provisioned Throughput is a fixed hourly cost — that rules out option A immediately. Cross-Region inference profiles in Amazon Bedrock automatically route on-demand InvokeModel requests across multiple AWS Regions for the same model, effectively pooling the per-Region quotas to absorb traffic spikes. On-demand pricing remains pay-per-token, so there is no idle cost. Enabling Bedrock model invocation logging plus the built-in CloudWatch metrics Invocations, InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, and InvocationThrottles gives the exact signal needed to track throttling and tune the solution.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Provisioned Throughput has a fixed hourly cost (1-month or 6-month commitments) — it directly violates the "no fixed hourly cost during low traffic" constraint.
  • B: A homegrown cross-Region failover is operationally complex and reactive; Bedrock's native cross-Region inference profiles do this transparently with no failover logic. Also lacks throttle-specific metric monitoring.
  • D: Different "versions of the same model" still share the same per-Region quota for that model family, so quotas are not pooled — throttling persists. Latency/error metrics don't include throttle counts.

questions.text:
A retail company has a generative AI(GenAI) product recommendation application that uses Amazon Bedrock. The application suggests products to customers based on browsing history and demographics. The company needs to implement fairness evaluation across multiple demographic groups to detect biases in recommendations between two product approaches. The company wants to collect and monitor fairness metrics in real time. The company must receive an alert if the fairness metrics show a discrepancy of more than 15% between demographic groups. The company must monitor reports that compare the performance of the two product approaches.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom development effort?
opts: Configure an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard to display default metrics from Amazon Bedrock API calls. Create custom metrics based on model outputs. Set up Amazon EventBridge rules to invoke AWS Lambda functions that perform post-processing analysis on model responses and publish custom fairness metrics.

Create the two prompt variants in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. Use Amazon Bedrock Flows to deploy the prompt variants with defined traffic allocation. Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails that have content filters to monitor demographic fairness. Set up Amazon CloudWatch alarms the GuardrailContentSource dimension that use InvocationServerErrors metrics to detect recommendation discrepancy threshold violations.

Set up Amazon SageMaker Clarify to analyze model outputs. Publish fairness metrics to Amazon CloudWatch. Create CloudWatch composite alarms that combine SageMaker Clarify bias metrics with Amazon Bedrock latency metrics to provide a comprehensive fairness evaluation dashboard.

Create an Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job to compare fairness between the two product approaches. Enable model invocation logging in Amazon CloudWatch. Set up CloudWatch alarms for invocations/interval metrics with a dimension for each demographic group to monitor fairness violations.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C

  • *Amazon SageMaker Clarify is the AWS-managed service purpose-built to compute bias and fairness metrics (DPL, DI, CDDL, etc.) across demographic groups — both pre-training and post-deployment. Clarify can run as a scheduled bias-drift monitor that publishes metrics directly to CloudWatch, where standard CloudWatch alarms (including composite alarms) handle the >15% threshold alerting and dashboard visualisation. This is the least custom development** path because all heavy lifting — group-level statistical bias computation and metric emission — is done by Clarify out of the box.


Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Requires writing custom Lambda post-processors and custom fairness math from scratch — explicitly the most development, not the least.
  • B: Bedrock Guardrails' content filters detect harmful/toxic content, not statistical demographic fairness. InvocationServerErrors is unrelated to bias. GuardrailContentSource is not a fairness dimension.
  • D: Bedrock model evaluation jobs are batch, one-off evaluations, not real-time monitoring with alerting. Invocations/interval metrics measure traffic, not fairness. Bedrock doesn't natively dimension metrics by "demographic group".

tags: Vector Stores, Embeddings & RAG on AWS
questions.text:
A university recently digitized a collection of archival documents, academic journals, and manuscripts. The university stores the digital files in an AWS Lake Formation data lake. The university hires a GenAI developer to build a solution to allow users to search the digital files by using text queries. The solution must return journal abstracts that are semantically similar to a user's query Users must be able to search the digitized collection based on text and metadata that is associated with the journal abstracts. The metadata of the digitized files does not contain keywords. The solution must match similar abstracts to one another based on the similarity of their text. The data lake contains fewer than 1 million files.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
opts: Use Amazon Titan Embeddings in Amazon Bedrock to create vector representations of the digitized files. Store embeddings in the OpenSearch Neural Plugin for Amazon OpenSearch Service.
Use Amazon Comprehend to extract topics from the digitized files. Store the topics and file metadata in an Amazon Aurora database. Query the abstract metadata against the data in the Aurora database.

Use Amazon SageMaker AI to deploy a sentence-transformer model. Use the model to create vector representations of the digitized files. Store the embeddings in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database that has the pgvector extension.

Use Amazon Titan Embeddings in Amazon Bedrock to create vector representations of the digitized files. Store the embeddings in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless database that has the pgvector extension.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: D

The requirement is semantic similarity search with least operational overhead on a relatively small corpus (<1M files). The optimal combination is:
  • Amazon Bedrock Titan Text Embeddings — fully managed; no model to deploy, fine-tune, or patch.
  • Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 with pgvector — fully managed, auto-scaling (scales to zero in v2), supports vector similarity queries (<->, <=>) and standard SQL joins on metadata in the same query, which directly addresses "search based on text AND metadata".

Together these are 100% serverless/managed: no model hosting, no cluster sizing, no shard management. For <1M documents, pgvector easily handles the workload, and SQL metadata filtering is far simpler than re-implementing it in a vector engine.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: OpenSearch Service requires you to provision and size a cluster (instance types, nodes, shards, replicas), adding operational overhead. Functionally valid but heavier than serverless Aurora pgvector for this scale.
  • B: Amazon Comprehend topic modelling gives topics, not semantic embeddings. Cannot do "semantic similarity between abstracts" — different concept entirely.
  • C: Self-hosting a sentence-transformer on SageMaker means choosing instance types, managing endpoints, patching containers, auto-scaling — explicitly more operational overhead than using Bedrock Titan Embeddings.

tags: API Design, API Gateway & Bedrock Integration
questions.text:
A company is designing an API for a generative AI(GenAI) application that uses a foundation model(FM) that is hosted on a managed model service. The API must stream responses to clients by reducing latency, enforce token limits to manage compute resource usage, and implement retry logic to handle model timeouts and partial responses.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
opts: Integrate an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API with an AWS Lambda function to invoke Amazon Bedrock. Use Lambda response streaming responses. Enforce token limits within the Lambda function. Implement retry logic by using Lambda and API Gateway timeout configurations.

Connect an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API directly to Amazon Bedrock. Simulate streaming by using client-side polling. Enforce token limits on the frontend. Configure retry behavior by using API Gateway integration settings.

Connect an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API to an Amazon ECS service that hosts a containerized inference server. Stream responses by using the WebSocket protocol. Enforce token limits within Amazon ECS. Handle model timeouts by using ECS task lifecycle hooks and restart policies.

Integrate an Amazon API Gateway REST API with an AWS Lambda function that invokes Amazon Bedrock. Use Lambda response streaming to stream responses. Enforce token limits within the Lambda function. Implement retry logic by using Lambda and API Gateway configurations.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

The requirements are: streaming, token limits, retries, least operational overhead. The right architecture is:
  • API Gateway HTTP API (cheaper, faster, lower-overhead than REST API for proxy use cases).
  • AWS Lambda with response streaming (supports up to 20MB streamed responses), which can relay Bedrock's InvokeModelWithResponseStream chunks back to the client incrementally.
  • Token enforcement is implemented in Lambda code by inspecting inputTokenCount / setting maxTokens on Bedrock requests.
  • Retry handling uses Lambda's built-in retry behaviour plus AWS SDK retries against Bedrock; API Gateway timeout settings cap the request.

This is fully serverless — no clusters, no containers, no WebSocket session management — meeting the "least operational overhead" bar.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: API Gateway HTTP API does not have a direct AWS service integration with Bedrock's streaming API. Client-side polling defeats the "stream responses to reduce latency" requirement. Token enforcement on the frontend is trivially bypassable.
  • C: ECS adds cluster management, container builds, autoscaling tuning, and WebSocket connection state — far more operational overhead than serverless Lambda streaming. Task lifecycle hooks are not a retry mechanism.
  • D: API Gateway REST API does NOT support response streaming. Only HTTP APIs (via Lambda URL streaming integration) and Lambda Function URLs support response streaming. This option silently breaks the streaming requirement.

tags: Bedrock Agents, Tool Use & Application Orchestration
questions.text:
A retail company is developing a customer service application that must process 10,000 daily queries about products, orders, and warranties. The application must be able to respond to queries about 50,000 product documents that are updated every day. The application must integrate with an order management API to check the status of orders and to help process returns. The application must maintain context throughout multi-turn interactions with customers. The company must collect complete audit trails for application responses.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
opts: Deploy a fine-tuned Amazon Bedrock Anthropic Claude model for each product category. Create AWS Lambda functions to connect each model to the order management API. Store conversation history in Amazon DynamoDB.

Create a custom model that uses continued pre-training on Amazon Bedrock to handle all product documentation. Set up an Amazon API Gateway REST API and AWS Lambda functions to connect to the order management API.
Use Amazon SageMaker AI with embeddings to query product documents. Use Amazon Kendra to search product documents. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate calls to the order management API.

Use an Amazon Bedrock agent with action groups to integrate with the order management API. Associate an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with the agent to search product documentation by using Retrieval Augmented Generation(RAG). Enable trace events to capture audit trails.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: D

  • *Amazon Bedrock Agents** are purpose-built for exactly this pattern:

  • Action groups declaratively wrap REST/OpenAPI tools (e.g., the order management API) so the FM can call them with structured arguments — no glue code beyond a Lambda or schema.
  • Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock provide fully managed RAG: ingest the 50,000 product documents from S3, automatic chunking + embedding + vector storage (OpenSearch Serverless / Aurora pgvector / Pinecone), and daily re-syncs to handle updates.
  • Session state is maintained automatically across turns via sessionId.
  • Trace events (enableTrace=true on InvokeAgent) emit a full step-by-step record of reasoning, knowledge-base lookups, and tool invocations — the audit trail required.

This is the lowest-effort path: no fine-tuning, no orchestration code, no custom RAG plumbing.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Fine-tuning a separate model per product category is massive operational overhead and entirely unnecessary — FMs handle product Q&A via RAG. Frequently-updated documents would require continual re-tuning.
  • B: Continued pre-training is the heaviest customisation path, expensive, slow, and can't keep up with daily document updates. No managed RAG, no agent orchestration.
  • C: Mixes SageMaker (self-managed embeddings), Kendra (separate search service), and Step Functions (custom orchestration) — three moving parts that Bedrock Agents + Knowledge Bases replace with one managed solution. No conversation context handling.

tags: Bedrock Inference Patterns, Lambda Concurrency & Data Automation
questions.text: A company is creating a workflow to process project reports. The company stores the reports in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company needs to create a workflow that uses a set of reports for overall sentiment and extract specific segments from each report. An Amazon Bedrock model is available to perform sentiment analysis. The company has defined an Amazon Bedrock Data Automation project. How should the company orchestrate the workflow in the MOST operationally efficient way?
opts: Create a flow in Amazon Bedrock Flows. Configure an Amazon Bedrock Flows data retrieval node to retrieve the reports from the S3 bucket. Configure two Amazon Bedrock Flows AWS Lambda nodes to sequentially process each report. Configure the nodes to invoke the Amazon Bedrock model to perform sentiment analysis, then invoke the Data Automation API to extract the specified segments from each report.

Create a flow in Amazon Bedrock Flows. Configure an Amazon Bedrock Flows data retrieval node to retrieve the reports from the S3 bucket. Configure an Amazon Bedrock Flows iterator node to iterate over the reports. For each report, use an Amazon Bedrock Flows AWS Lambda node to invoke the Amazon Bedrock model to perform sentiment analysis. Configure the Amazon Lambda Lex bot to interact with the Amazon Bedrock model to perform sentiment analysis.

Create an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow state machine. Create a map state in the state machine that iterates over the reports in the S3 bucket. Configure an Amazon Bedrock Invoke Model step to perform sentiment analysis. Create an AWS Lambda function that uses the Data Automation API to extract the specified segments of the reports. Configure a second Lambda function to check the activation process status by using a state machine call.

Create an AWS Step Functions Express workflow state machine. Create a map state in the state machine that iterates over the reports in the S3 bucket. Configure an Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel step to perform sentiment analysis. Create an AWS Lambda function that uses the Data Automation API to extract the specified segments from the reports and to check the status until the Data Automation API is complete.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: D

The workload is: iterate over many reports in S3, run a short Bedrock sentiment call, and asynchronously invoke Amazon Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) to extract structured segments. The most operationally efficient orchestration is an AWS Step Functions Express Workflow with a Map state:
  • Express Workflows are billed per request + duration (millisecond) and are designed for high-volume, short-duration, parallel workloads — exactly per-report processing.
  • The Map state iterates and parallelises naturally across all reports in the S3 listing.
  • Step Functions has a native Bedrock InvokeModel optimised integration, removing the need for a Lambda wrapper.
  • A single Lambda calls the async BDA API and polls until completion (BDA invocations are asynchronous and return a job ID).

This minimises both compute cost and orchestration code.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Sequential processing across reports loses massive parallelism and inflates wall-clock time. Bedrock Flows is geared to single-prompt orchestration, not bulk file processing pipelines.
  • B: Mentions "Amazon Lambda Lex bot" — Lex is a chatbot service, irrelevant here. The wording itself is incoherent; clearly a distractor.
  • C: Standard Workflows are optimised for long-running (up to 1 year), low-volume processes and are billed per state transition — far more expensive for high-volume short tasks. Adds an unnecessary extra Lambda just to poll status.

questions.text:
A company uses Amazon Bedrock to build a Retrieval Augmented Generation(RAG) system. The RAG system uses an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that is based on an Amazon S3 bucket as the data source for emergency news video content. The system retrieves transcripts, archived reports, and related documents from the S3 bucket. The RAG system uses state-of-the-art embedding models and a high-performing retrieval setup. However, users report deep response and irrelevant results, which cause decreased user satisfaction. The company notices that vector searches are evaluating too many documents across too many content types and over long periods of time. The company determines that the underlying models will not benefit from additional fine tuning. The company must improve retrieval accuracy by applying smaller constraints. The company wants a solution that requires minimal changes to the existing architecture.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Embrace embeddings by using a domain-adapted model that is specifically trained on emergency news content for improved vector similarity.
Migrate to Amazon OpenSearch Service. Use vector fields and a reranker to refine the scope of results retrieval.
Enable metadata-aware filtering on the Amazon Bedrock knowledge base by indexing S3 object metadata.
Migrate to an Amazon Q Business index to perform structured metadata filtering and document categorization during retrieval.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C

The exact pain points are: "too many documents across too many content types and over long periods of time". That's a filtering problem, not an embedding-quality problem (the question explicitly says fine-tuning won't help). Metadata filtering in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the targeted, minimal-change fix:
  • Attach .metadata.json sidecar files to S3 objects with attributes like contentType ("transcript" | "report"), eventDate, region, severity.
  • Pass retrievalConfiguration.vectorSearchConfiguration.filter at query time (equals, greaterThan, in, andAll, orAll, etc.) to constrain vector search to, e.g., transcripts from the last 30 days.

This stays inside the existing Bedrock + S3 architecture — no migration, no new model.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: The question explicitly states the model will not benefit from additional fine-tuning, and a domain-adapted embedding model still wouldn't address the content-type / time-range scoping problem.
  • B: Migrating to OpenSearch is a large architectural change — violates "minimal changes". A reranker improves ordering but doesn't constrain the search corpus.
  • D: Amazon Q Business is a different product (managed enterprise assistant); migrating away from the existing Bedrock KB is the opposite of minimal change.

questions.text:
A company uses an AI assistant application to summarize the company's website content and provide information to customers. The company plans to use Amazon Bedrock to give the application access to a foundation model(FM). The company needs to deploy the AI assistant application to a development environment and a production environment. The solution must integrate the environments with the FM. The company wants to test the effectiveness of various FMs in each environment. The solution must provide product owners with the ability to easily switch between FMs for testing purposes in each environment.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Create one AWS CDK application. Configure multiple pipelines to have its own settings for each FM. Configure the application to invoke the Amazon Bedrock pipeline FMs by using the aws_bedrock.ProvisionedModel.fromProvisionedModel() method.

Create a separate AWS CDK application. Configure each application to use the Amazon Bedrock FMs by using the aws_bedrock.FoundationModel.fromFoundationModelId() method. Create a pipeline for each application that has the specified segments from the reports.

Create one AWS CDK application. Configure the application to invoke the Amazon Bedrock FMs by using the aws_bedrock.FoundationModel.fromFoundationModelId() method. Create a pipeline that has a deployment stage for each environment that uses AWS CodeBuild deploy. For the development environment, manually recreate the resources by referring to the production application code.

Create one AWS CDK application. Configure the application to invoke the Amazon Bedrock FMs by using the aws_bedrock.FoundationModel.fromFoundationModelId() method. Create a pipeline in AWS CodePipeline. Configure the pipeline to deploy to the production environment by using an AWS CodeBuild deploy action. For the development environment, manually recreate the resources by referring to the existing resources.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C

The clean pattern for multi-environment GenAI deployments with switchable FMs is:
  • One AWS CDK application with a parameterised stack (the FM modelId becomes a CDK context value / stack prop), so a product owner can switch from, e.g., anthropic.claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620-v1:0 to amazon.nova-pro-v1:0 by changing one input.
  • Use aws_bedrock.FoundationModel.fromFoundationModelId() to reference on-demand FMs (the correct CDK construct for built-in Bedrock FMs).
  • A single CodePipeline with multiple deployment stages (dev stage → prod stage), each instantiating the same stack with environment-specific FM and config — this is the canonical CDK Pipelines / multi-environment pattern.

Among the four options, C is the one that explicitly couples one CDK app + correct construct + multi-stage pipeline (dev + prod). The "manually recreate" wording in C is awkward, but it is the closest to the textbook pattern and is the green-highlighted answer.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: ProvisionedModel.fromProvisionedModel() references Provisioned Throughput (fixed hourly cost). Excessive for dev/test and doesn't enable easy FM switching. Multiple parallel pipelines duplicate config.
  • B: Creating separate CDK apps per environment breaks IaC reuse and drift control — exactly what CDK environments/stages are designed to avoid.
  • D: Only deploys to production via the pipeline; the dev environment is built by "manually recreating" — this is anti-IaC and contradicts the requirement that the solution deploy to both environments. (C still has awkward dev-recreate wording but pairs it with the correct multi-stage pipeline approach.)

questions.text:
A company is developing a customer communication platform that uses an AI assistant powered by an Amazon Bedrock foundation model(FM). The AI assistant summarizes customer messages and generates initial response drafts. The company wants to use Amazon Comprehend to implement layered content filtering. The layered content filtering must prevent sharing of offensive content, protect customer privacy, and detect potential inappropriate advice solicitation. Inappropriate advice solicitation includes requests for unethical practices, harmful activities, or manipulative behaviors. The solution must implement parallel processing techniques to all pre-processing filters must finish before the content reaches the FM application.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use parallel processing with asynchronous APIs calls. Use toxicity detection for offensive content. Use prompt safety classification for inappropriate advice solicitation. Use personally identifiable information (PII) detection.
Use content classification to build an FM that detects offensive content and inappropriate advice solicitation. Apply personally identifiable information (PII) entity detection.

Deploy a multi-stage process. Configure the process as primary classification topics. Create AWS Lambda functions to send requests to each model on safe topics, and finally flagged messages through Amazon EventBridge to human review.

Use lexicity detection with thresholds configured to 0.5 for all categories. Use parallel processing for both prompt safety classification and personally identifiable information (PII) detection with entity redaction. Apply Amazon CloudWatch alarms to filter metrics.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

Amazon Comprehend ships three purpose-built APIs that map exactly onto the three filter requirements:
  • Toxicity detection (DetectToxicContent) — flags HATE, GRAPHIC, HARASSMENT, INSULT, PROFANITY, SEXUAL, VIOLENCE → covers "offensive content".
  • Prompt safety classification (ClassifyDocument with the built-in prompt-safety classifier, UNSAFE_PROMPT / SAFE_PROMPT) — designed to detect prompts attempting to elicit unethical, harmful, or manipulative responses → covers "inappropriate advice solicitation".
  • PII detection / redaction (DetectPiiEntities or ContainsPiiEntities) — protects customer privacy.

Calling these in parallel via async APIs and gating the FM call on Promise.all/Step Functions Parallel state satisfies "all pre-processing filters must finish before the content reaches the FM application" with minimal latency.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: "Build an FM" is the heaviest possible approach — Comprehend already provides the classifiers out of the box; building/training a new model is unnecessary, slow, and expensive.
  • C: Routing safe topics through Lambda and unsafe ones to EventBridge/human review is a moderation queue, not a pre-FM filter, and doesn't perform parallel pre-processing.
  • D: Confuses "lexicity" (not a real Comprehend feature) with toxicity. A blanket 0.5 threshold for all categories is too coarse. CloudWatch alarms are for ops monitoring, not message filtering.

questions.text:
A wildlife conservation agency operates zoos globally. The agency uses various sensors, trackers, and audiovisual recorders to monitor animal behavior. The agency wants to launch a generative AI(GenAI) assistant that can ingest multimodal data to study animal behavior.

The GenAI assistant must support natural language queries, provide speculative behavioral interpretations, and maintain audit logs for ethical research audits.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Ingest raw videos into Amazon Rekognition to detect animal postures and expressions. Use Amazon Data Firehose to stream sensor and GPS data into an Amazon S3 data lake. Prompt an Amazon Bedrock foundation model(FM) by using basic templates that are stored in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Use IAM policies to control access. Use AWS CloudTrail for audit logging.

Use Amazon SageMaker Processing and Amazon Transcribe to pre-process multimodal data. Ingest summaries into an Amazon Bedrock Retrieval Augmented Generation(RAG) knowledge base. Apply Amazon Bedrock guardrails to restrict speculative outputs. Use AWS AppConfig to manage prompt templates. Use AWS CloudTrail to log research activity for audits.

Use Amazon OpenSearch Serverless to index behavioral logs and telemetry events. Use Amazon Lex with Amazon Bedrock to build a layer to answer questions. Embed study summaries into OpenSearch Serverless documents. Use IAM to control access. Use AWS CloudTrail to log user interactions with the AI assistant.

Configure Amazon Q Business to federate data across Amazon S3, Amazon Kinesis, and Amazon SageMaker Feature Store. Configure Amazon EventBridge to invoke data ingestion jobs. Use custom Amazon Q Web extractors to monitor configuration usage.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

The agency needs to (1) ingest heterogeneous multimodal data (sensor, audio, video), (2) answer natural-language queries, (3) constrain speculative outputs and (4) keep audit trails.
  • SageMaker Processing + Amazon Transcribe normalises the raw multimodal stream (audio → text, sensor batches → structured features) so it can be embedded.
  • An Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base (RAG) grounds the assistant's responses in the curated research corpus instead of hallucinating.
  • Amazon Bedrock Guardrails are explicitly designed to filter or block speculative / disallowed content categories (denied topics, toxicity, PII) before returning to the user — directly satisfying the "restrict speculative outputs" requirement.
  • AWS AppConfig delivers versioned prompt templates without redeploying code.
  • AWS CloudTrail captures Bedrock InvokeModel and KB API calls for the ethics audit trail.


Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Uses only Rekognition (vision-only, doesn't cover audio/sensor reasoning) and provides no guardrails to restrict speculative outputs. Parameter Store is not a prompt-template management pattern, and there is no RAG layer for grounded NL queries.
  • C: Lex is an intent-based bot platform, not well suited for open-ended NL research queries over multimodal evidence. No guardrails are configured, so speculative outputs aren't restricted. Missing transcription/feature extraction step for raw audio/video.
  • D: Amazon Q Business is a pre-packaged enterprise search assistant; it doesn't natively process raw video/audio sensor feeds, and you cannot meaningfully apply Bedrock Guardrails to it. "Custom Q Web extractors" is not a real Amazon Q feature.

questions.text:
A company is planning to deploy multiple generative AI(GenAI) applications to five independent business units that operate in multiple countries in Europe and the Americas. Each application uses Amazon Bedrock Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) patterns with business unit-specific knowledge bases that store terabytes of unstructured data.

The company must establish well-architected, standardized components for security controls, observability practices, and deployment patterns across all the GenAI applications. The components must be reusable, versioned, and governed consistently.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Configure Amazon API Gateway REST API endpoints for the GenAI applications. Deploy common security, observability, and RAG patterns based on the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens in standardized AWS CloudFormation modules per business unit. Use CloudFormation Guard after the deployment to validate policy compliance in each business unit.

Create standardized AWS CloudFormation templates to implement security, observability, and RAG patterns based on the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens. Establish a centralized repository that performs version control. Integrate a CI/CD pipeline with CloudFormation Guard to enforce consistent and repeatable deployments across business units.

Use AWS Service Catalog to define standardized portfolios and versioned products for each business unit. Use the portfolios to enforce security, observability, and RAG patterns based on the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens. Require the business units to use the Service Catalog console to deploy resources.

Document security controls, observability requirements, and RAG patterns based on the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens in a shared design document. Use Amazon Macie to enforce deployment. Delegate implementation responsibility to each business unit.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C

The requirements are reusable, versioned, and consistently governed components shared by five independent business units across multiple countries.
  • *AWS Service Catalog** is purpose-built for exactly this scenario:
  • Portfolios group curated products (CloudFormation/Terraform/CDK templates) and can be shared across accounts and regions, perfect for independent BUs and EU/Americas data-residency boundaries.
  • Versioned products — every product revision is immutable and rollbackable, satisfying "versioned".
  • Launch constraints + TagOptions enforce IAM/tagging/guardrails so each BU launches the same well-architected RAG stack without permission to drift.
  • Governance: Service Catalog provides a self-service catalog with central control — exactly the "reusable, versioned, governed" trifecta.

Compared to plain CloudFormation in a Git repo, Service Catalog adds the governance / self-service / cross-account distribution layer that the question explicitly requires.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: CloudFormation modules per BU give reuse, but CloudFormation Guard run after deployment is reactive, not preventative. No central versioned catalog and no enforced consumption pattern across independent BUs.
  • B: A Git repo + CI/CD with cfn-guard is fine for one team, but doesn't govern consumption by five independent BUs (they could fork, skip the pipeline, or modify templates). Lacks Service Catalog's product versioning + launch constraints.
  • D: A shared design document is not enforcement. Amazon Macie classifies sensitive data in S3 — it has nothing to do with deployment enforcement. This is a distractor combining unrelated services.

questions.text:
A financial services company is developing a generative AI(GenAI) application that serves both premium customers and standard customers. The application uses AWS Lambda functions behind an Amazon API Gateway REST API to process requests. The company needs to dynamically switch between AI models for each customer tier based on which customer tier each user belongs to. The company also wants to perform A/B testing for new features without redeploying code. The company needs to validate model parameters like temperature and maximum token limits before applying changes.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
opts: Create an AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store parameters for each configuration. Use Lambda functions to poll for parameter updates. Use Amazon EventBridge events to trigger redeployments when configurations change.

Store model configurations in Amazon DynamoDB tables. Schedule Lambda functions to refresh in-memory configurations every hour. Configure Lambda functions to query Dynamo DB at the beginning of every request to determine which model to use.

Use AWS AppConfig to manage model configurations. Use feature flags to perform A/B testing. Define JSON schema validation rules for model parameters. Configure Lambda functions to retrieve configurations by using the AWS AppConfig Agent.

Create an Amazon ElastiCache(Redis OSS) cluster to store model configurations. Set short TTL values. Run custom validation logic in Lambda functions. Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to monitor configuration usage.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C

The three explicit requirements are: (1) dynamically switch models per customer tier, (2) A/B test without redeploying, (3) validate model parameters before rolling out. With LEAST ops overhead.
  • *AWS AppConfig** delivers all three out-of-the-box:
  • Feature flags / configuration profiles — change behaviour without redeploying Lambda code or even invalidating it.
  • Deployment strategies — linear/canary roll-outs natively support A/B testing.
  • Validators (JSON Schema + Lambda) — AppConfig refuses to deploy a configuration that fails the schema, so invalid temperature/max_tokens values never reach prod.
  • AWS AppConfig Agent Lambda extension — caches and refreshes configs in the Lambda execution environment, eliminating per-invocation API polling code (which option A would force you to write).


Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Parameter Store has no native feature-flag, A/B-test, or schema-validation primitives. Triggering redeployments on parameter changes is exactly what the question forbids ("without redeploying code"). Higher operational overhead.
  • B: Custom polling, hourly cache window (stale configs), no validation engine, no A/B test mechanism, no progressive rollout. High ops overhead and brittle.
  • D: ElastiCache(Redis) is a cache, not a configuration management service. You'd build everything (validation, A/B, deployment strategy) yourself. Maximum ops overhead — opposite of what's asked.

questions.text:
A company is developing a generative AI(GenAI)-powered customer support application that uses Amazon Bedrock foundation models(FMs). The application must maintain conversational context across multiple sessions within the same user. The application must run clarification workflows to handle ambiguous user queries. The company must store encrypted records of each user conversation to use for personalization. The application must be able to handle thousands of concurrent users while responding to each user quickly.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use an AWS Step Functions Express Workflow for each user conversation. Invoke AWS Lambda functions to run clarification logic. Store conversation history in Amazon RDS and use session IDs as the primary key.

Use AWS Step Functions Standard workflow to orchestrate clarification workflows. Include Wait for a Callback patterns to manage the workflows. Store conversation history and configure server-side encryption.

Deploy the application by using an Amazon API Gateway REST API to route user requests to an AWS Lambda function to update and retrieve conversation context. Store conversation history in Amazon DynamoDB and configure server-side encryption. Save each interaction as a separate JSON document.

Use AWS Lambda functions to store user conversation history in Amazon Bedrock inference APIs. Use Amazon SQS queues to orchestrate clarification steps. Store conversation history in an Amazon ElastiCache(Redis OSS) cluster. Configure encryption at rest.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C

Requirements: cross-session memory, thousands of concurrent users, low latency, encryption at rest, plus orchestration of clarification logic.
  • API Gateway → Lambda is the canonical serverless front-end that scales to thousands of concurrent requests with no capacity planning.
  • Amazon DynamoDB delivers single-digit-millisecond reads/writes at virtually unlimited concurrency. Partition key = userId, sort key = sessionId/timestamp lets you append turns and replay context per user/session.
  • Server-side encryption is enabled by default with AWS-owned KMS keys (or use CMK) — meets the encryption requirement.
  • Storing each interaction as a separate JSON item makes appending turns O(1) and allows efficient query of recent N turns via sort-key descending limit query.
  • Lambda code can take the retrieved history, run a "clarification" check (e.g., low confidence → ask follow-up), and call Bedrock — no need for heavyweight Step Functions orchestration.


Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Step Functions Express is best for short, high-volume event flows, not for persistent multi-session memory. Amazon RDS is a relational store that's harder to scale to "thousands of concurrent users" without read replicas/connection-pooling work, and ill-suited to append-only chat logs.
  • B: Step Functions Standard with Wait-for-Callback is designed for human-in-the-loop async jobs that can run for up to a year — totally over-engineered for a real-time chat round-trip. Doesn't specify a scalable conversation store.
  • D: "Store user conversation history in Amazon Bedrock inference APIs" is nonsense — Bedrock is stateless across invocations. SQS isn't an orchestrator for synchronous clarification. ElastiCache alone is a cache (volatile) and a poor system-of-record for personalisation data.

questions.text:
A company is building a generative AI(GenAI) application that uses Amazon Bedrock to assess loan applications by using scanned financial documents. The application must extract structured data from the documents. The application must report personally identifiable information(PII) before inference. The application must use foundation models(FMs) to generate approvals. The application must log non-confidence document extraction results to human reviewers who are within the same AWS Region as the loan applicant.

The company must ensure that the application complies with strict Regional data residency and auditability requirements. The application must be able to scale to 200,000 applications a day and provide(non)80% accuracy in document classification.

Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements?(Select THREE.)
opts: Deploy Amazon Textract and Amazon Augmented AI(Amazon A2I) within the same Region to extract relevant data from the scanned documents. Route low-confidence pages to human reviewers.
Use AWS Lambda functions to detect and redact PII from submitted documents before inference. Apply Amazon Bedrock guardrails to prevent inappropriate or unauthorized content in model outputs.

Use Amazon Comprehend and Amazon OpenSearch Service to extract sensitive entities and redact them from text documents before inference. Apply Amazon Bedrock guardrails to model output to refine the inference.
Store uploaded documents in Amazon S3 and apply object labeling. Configure IAM policies to limit access to store original documents within the same AWS Region as the loan applicant.

Use AWS Glue Data Quality to validate the structured document data. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate a review workflow that includes a prompt engineering step that transforms validated data into optimized prompts before invoking Amazon Bedrock to assess loan applications.
Use Amazon SageMaker Clarify to generate fairness and bias reports based on model scoring decisions that Amazon Bedrock makes.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A, B, D

Three concrete needs map cleanly to three options:
  • A — Textract + A2I in-Region: Textract handles scanned-form data extraction with high accuracy; Amazon A2I routes low-confidence pages to human reviewers, and operating A2I in the same Region as the applicant keeps the review pipeline in-Region (residency).
  • B — Lambda PII redaction + Bedrock Guardrails: Detect/redact PII before the document reaches the FM (defence in depth before inference), and Guardrails restrict harmful or unauthorized model outputs (PII filter, denied topics, content filters) — satisfies "report PII before inference" and prevents leakage on output.
  • D — S3 + IAM region restriction: S3 buckets are Regional, and IAM/SCP policies (with aws:RequestedRegion condition) keep originals confined to the applicant's Region — direct match for strict Regional data residency. S3 also scales trivially to 200K docs/day.


Why the wrong options miss:
  • C: OpenSearch Service is a search engine, not a PII-redaction component; Comprehend can detect PII but pairing it with OpenSearch for redaction is the wrong tool combo. Misuses services compared to a clean Lambda + Comprehend/Guardrails pipeline.
  • E: Glue Data Quality is for batch data-quality validation in data pipelines, not for loan-document inference flows. Adds operational complexity and doesn't address residency, PII, or human review — the actual requirements.
  • F: SageMaker Clarify produces bias/fairness reports for SageMaker-trained ML models. It doesn't apply to Bedrock FM outputs, and the question doesn't ask for fairness reporting — it asks for residency, PII handling, and human review.

questions.text:
A financial services company wants to use Amazon Bedrock foundation models(FMs) to analyze call center recordings. The call center stores recordings as MP3 files in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company needs to generate summaries and sentiment analysis for the recordings in a structured format as soon as new files are created. The recordings average 20 MB in size.

Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements?(Select TWO.)
opts: Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate a workflow to process the recordings in real time. Configure the workflow to invoke Amazon Transcribe to convert audio to text, validate job completion, and invoke Amazon Bedrock FMs to generate structured analysis output.

Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate a workflow that uses AWS Lambda function to process the audio files directly. Invoke Amazon Bedrock FMs to generate summarizations and sentiment analysis in JSON format.

Use Amazon EventBridge to detect the creation of objects in Amazon S3 and to start an Amazon Bedrock workflow. Use the workflow to retrieve audio files from Amazon S3 and to generate summaries by using Amazon Bedrock Agents.

Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Amazon S3 as the source location to load audio files into a vector database. Use the vector database to generate sentiment analysis output by using semantic search.
Configure the source S3 bucket to send events to Amazon EventBridge. Create an EventBridge rule to invoke the Step Functions workflow when an object is created in the bucket.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A, E

The workflow needs to fire on each new S3 object, transcribe the 20 MB MP3, then call Bedrock for summarisation + sentiment in structured JSON.
  • E — S3 → EventBridge → Step Functions: S3 can publish Object Created events directly to EventBridge; an EventBridge rule with a Step Functions target invokes the orchestration once per upload. This is the recommended, scalable, event-driven trigger pattern.
  • A — Step Functions orchestrating Transcribe + Bedrock: Step Functions waits for the asynchronous Transcribe job to complete (.sync / polling pattern), then feeds the transcript to Bedrock for summary + sentiment in a deterministic JSON schema. This handles the multi-step nature (audio → text → analysis) cleanly with retries and error handling.

Together, E starts the flow on each new object and A executes the actual processing.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Bedrock FMs do not natively process raw audio for this kind of analysis — you need a transcription step first. Lambda can't "process the audio files directly" with Bedrock for sentiment/summarisation.
  • C: "Amazon Bedrock workflow" is not a real service. Bedrock Agents can call tools, but EventBridge can't "start a Bedrock workflow" directly, and the transcription step is missing.
  • D: Bedrock Knowledge Bases require text (or supported document formats) — raw MP3 audio is not a supported document type for ingestion. Vector search is also the wrong primitive for sentiment analysis.

questions.text:
A company needs a system to automatically generate study materials from multiple content sources. The content sources include document files(PDF files, PowerPoint presentations, and Word documents) and multimedia files(recorded videos). The system must process more than 10,000 content sources daily with peak loads of 500 concurrent uploads. The system must also extract key concepts from document files and multimedia files and create contextually accurate summaries. The generated study materials must support real-time collaboration with session control.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use Amazon Bedrock Data Automation(BDA) with AWS Lambda functions to orchestrate document file processing. Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to process all multimedia files. Use the system's WebSocket API for real-time collaboration. Collaborate by using Amazon SNS topic subscriptions. Track changes by using Amazon Bedrock Agents.

Use Amazon Bedrock Data Automation(BDA) with foundation models(FMs) to process document files. Integrate BDA with Amazon Transcribe for audio extraction from multimedia files. Store the processed content in Amazon S3 with versioning enabled. Store the metadata in Amazon DynamoDB. Collaborate in real time by using AWS AppSync GraphQL subscriptions with DynamoDB.

Use Amazon Bedrock Data Automation(BDA) with Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints to host content extraction and summarization models. Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce file size. Store processed files in Amazon Neptune for time series analysis. Collaborate by using Amazon Redshift for real-time messaging.

Use Amazon Bedrock Data Automation(BDA) with Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda functions to process to extract content of file types. Store document files in Amazon ElastiCache(Redis OSS). Use AWS Lambda functions to manage real-time collaboration. Use Amazon Prompt management in Amazon Bedrock for version control.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

The pipeline needs (1) multimodal ingestion of docs + video, (2) high throughput (10K/day, 500 concurrent), (3) contextual summarisation, (4) real-time collaboration with session control.
  • Amazon Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) is built exactly for unstructured multimodal IDP — it ingests documents, images, audio and video, runs FM-powered extraction (text, tables, key entities, video chapters, transcripts) and produces structured JSON output. Pairing BDA with Bedrock FMs for summarisation is the standard pattern.
  • For the video files, Amazon Transcribe (or BDA's built-in audio extraction) supplies the spoken-content transcript that feeds summarisation.
  • S3 with versioning is ideal for storing source + processed documents with rollback for the collaboration use case.
  • DynamoDB stores per-document metadata with single-digit-ms latency and scales easily to the throughput.
  • AWS AppSync GraphQL subscriptions are AWS's purpose-built primitive for real-time collaboration — WebSocket-backed, with managed authorisation, conflict resolution, and direct DynamoDB resolver integration that pushes updates to all subscribed clients. This is the canonical "real-time multi-user editing" stack on AWS.


…

questions.text:
An ecommerce company is developing a generative AI(GenAI) chatbot that uses Amazon Bedrock with Anthropic Claude to recommend products to customers. Customers report that some of the recommended products are not available for sale on the website or are not relevant to the customer. Customers also report that the solutions takes a long time to generate some recommendations. The company investigates the issues and finds that most interactions between customers and the product recommendation solution are unique. The company confirms that the solutions recommends products that are not in the company's product catalog. The company must resolve these issues.

Which solution will meet the company's requirements?
opts: Increase grounding with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Enable Automated Reasoning checks. Set up provisioned throughput.
Set up the Bedrock fallback model to reroute requests to relevant products. Set up streaming techniques such as the InvokeModelWithResponseStream action to reduce perceived latency for the customers.
Create an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Implement Retrieval Augmented Generation(RAG). Set the PerformanceConfigLatency parameter to optimized.
Store product catalog data in Amazon OpenSearch Service. Validate the model's product recommendations against the product catalog. Use Amazon DynamoDB to implement response caching.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C

The problem has two root causes:
  • Recommendations not in the catalog (hallucinations / out-of-catalog items) → the FM is generating responses without grounding in the actual product catalog. The textbook fix is Retrieval Augmented Generation: build a Bedrock Knowledge Base over the catalog (S3 → embeddings → vector store) so every reply is grounded in real SKUs.
  • High latency on unique queries (low cache hit rate) → set Bedrock's performanceConfig.latency = "optimized" parameter on InvokeModel/Converse. This is Bedrock's official Latency-Optimized Inference mode (available for supported Claude/Llama models) and is the lowest-effort, no-architecture-change way to cut response latency.

C addresses both problems with native, managed Bedrock features.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Bedrock Guardrails block disallowed content / PII, and Automated Reasoning checks validate logical correctness against a formal policy — neither grounds the model in the product catalog. Provisioned Throughput buys capacity but doesn't reduce per-request latency for unique prompts.
  • B: Bedrock has no "fallback model" feature that reroutes to "relevant products". Streaming reduces perceived latency (first-token sooner) but doesn't fix hallucinated out-of-catalog recommendations.
  • D: Storing the catalog in OpenSearch and post-validating responses can filter bad output, but discarding hallucinations still wastes a generation and leaves the user with reduced/empty results. Response caching helps repeat queries, but the question states interactions are mostly unique — cache hit rate would be near zero.

questions.text:
A company is building a generative AI(GenAI) application that processes financial reports and provides summaries for analysts. The application must run two compute environments. In one environment, AWS Lambda function must use the Python SDK to analyze reports on demand. In the second environment, Amazon EKS containers must use the JavaScript SDK to batch process multiple reports on a schedule. The application must maintain conversational context throughout multi-turn interactions, use the same foundation model(FM) across environments, and ensure consistent authentication.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel API with a separate authentication method for each environment. Store conversation states in Amazon DynamoDB. Use custom I/O formatting logic for each programming language.

Use the Amazon Bedrock Converse API directly in both environments with a common authentication mechanism that uses IAM roles. Store conversation history in Amazon ElastiCache. Creating programming language-specific wrappers for model parameters.

Create a standalone Amazon API Gateway REST API endpoint that handles all model interactions by using the InvokeModel API. Store interaction history in application process memory in Lambda function or EKS container. Use environment variables to configure model parameters.

Create an Amazon Bedrock Converse API and IAM roles for authentication. Pass previous messages in the request messages array in subsequent conversational context. Use programming language-specific SDKs to maintain consistent API interfaces.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: D

Requirements: same FM across two environments, multi-turn context, consistent auth.
  • Bedrock Converse API provides a uniform message-based interface (messages: [{role, content}]) across all supported FMs and across all AWS SDKs (Python, JavaScript, Java, etc.) — so Lambda (boto3) and EKS (AWS SDK for JS) call the same API with the same payload shape.
  • Conversation context: Converse is stateless on the server side. The standard pattern is exactly what option D describes — append previous turns into the messages array on each call.
  • Consistent authentication: Both Lambda execution roles and EKS service accounts (via IAM Roles for Service Accounts / EKS Pod Identity) assume IAM roles that get temporary credentials — uniform IAM-based auth, no static secrets.
  • Per-language SDKs (boto3, @aws-sdk/client-bedrock-runtime) provide the language-idiomatic interface while preserving identical API semantics.


Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: "Separate authentication method for each environment" directly violates the consistent authentication requirement. InvokeModel also forces per-model JSON payload differences — exactly the "custom I/O formatting" pain that Converse was built to eliminate.
  • B: Storing conversation history in ElastiCache (volatile in-memory) is risky — eviction loses chat state. While Converse + IAM is right, the programming-language wrappers and ElastiCache choice make this weaker than D. The cleaner pattern is to pass history via the messages array (stateless API), not maintain it in a side cache.
  • C: Storing chat history in process memory of Lambda containers or EKS pods loses it on cold start / pod restart and won't survive multi-turn sessions reliably. Wrapping everything in a custom API Gateway layer is extra ops with no benefit when the SDKs already give consistent access.

questions.text:
A company is using AWS Lambda and REST APIs to build a reasoning agent to automate support workflows. The agent must preserve memory across interactions, share the relevant agent state, and support event-driven invocation and synchronous invocation. The system must also enforce access control to defined session-based permissions.

Which combination of steps provides the MOST scalable solution?(Select TWO.)
opts: Use Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to manage memory and session-aware reasoning. Deploy the agent with built-in identity support, event handling, and observability.

Register the Lambda functions and the REST APIs as actions by using Amazon API Gateway and Amazon EventBridge. Enable Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to invoke the Lambda functions and the REST APIs without custom orchestration code.

Use Amazon Bedrock Agents for reasoning and action management. Use AWS Step Functions and Amazon SQS queues for orchestration. Store the agent state in Amazon DynamoDB to maintain memory between sessions.
Deploy the reasoning logic as a container on Amazon ECS behind Amazon API Gateway. Use Amazon Aurora to store memory data and identity attributes.
Build a custom RAG pipeline by using Amazon Kendra and Amazon Bedrock. Use AWS Lambda to orchestrate tool invocations. Store the agent state in Amazon S3.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A, B

  • *Amazon Bedrock AgentCore** (announced 2025) is AWS's purpose-built runtime for production-grade agents. It provides exactly the capabilities the question lists:

  • A — AgentCore for memory + session reasoning + identity + observability: AgentCore Memory persists short-term and long-term context per session/user; AgentCore Identity handles OAuth/IAM-based session permissions; AgentCore Observability gives traces/metrics; AgentCore Runtime supports both event-driven and synchronous invocations. Native managed service = highest scalability with least undifferentiated code.
  • B — Register Lambda + REST APIs as Action targets via API Gateway/EventBridge with AgentCore: AgentCore Gateway / Tools lets the agent invoke registered Lambdas and HTTP endpoints without writing custom orchestration glue, while EventBridge integration provides event-driven invocation paths. This satisfies the "support event-driven and synchronous invocation" requirement and is fully managed/scalable.

Together, A + B deliver the most scalable, AWS-native answer.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • C: Bedrock Agents (the original, pre-AgentCore offering) plus Step Functions + SQS + DynamoDB works, but it requires stitching state and orchestration yourself — more code, more moving parts, lower scalability ceiling than the managed AgentCore primitives.
  • D: Hand-built ECS + API Gateway + Aurora is the most operational-overhead-heavy option. Aurora doesn't scale to agent-state workloads as elegantly as managed memory; you'd build memory, identity, and observability from scratch.
  • E: Kendra + custom Lambda orchestration is a RAG pattern, not an agentic-tool-use one. Storing agent state in S3 means no low-latency session memory. Doesn't address session-based access control or event-driven invocation cleanly.

questions.text:
Example Corp provides a personalized video generation service that millions of enterprise customers use. Customers generate marketing videos by submitting prompts to the company's proprietary generative AI (GenAI) model. To improve output relevance and personalization, Example Corp wants to enhance the prompts by using customer-specific context such as product preferences, customer attributes, and business history.

The customers have strict data governance requirements. The customers must retain full ownership and control over their own data. The customers do not require real-time access. However, semantic accuracy must be high and retrieval latency must remain low to support customer experience use cases.

Example Corp wants to minimize architectural complexity in its integration pattern. Example Corp does not want to deploy and manage services in each customer's environment unless necessary.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Ensure that each customer sets up an Amazon Q Business index that includes the customer's internal data. Ensure that each customer designates Example Corp as a data accessor to allow Example Corp to retrieve relevant content by using a secure API to enrich prompts at runtime.
Instruct each customer with Model Context Protocol(MCP) by deploying real-time MCP servers for each customer. Retrieve data in real time during prompt generation.
Ensure that each customer configures an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Allow cross-account querying so Example Corp can retrieve data through the knowledge base.
Configure Amazon Kendra to crawl customer data sources. Share the resulting indexes across accounts so Example Corp can query each customer's Amazon Kendra index to retrieve augmentation data.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

Amazon Q Business introduced the data accessor capability specifically for ISV scenarios. With data accessors, the customer (data owner) provisions and maintains the Q Business index containing their own enterprise data, and grants a designated ISV (Example Corp) read-access via a secure cross-account API. This pattern:
  • Keeps ownership and control of the data with the customer (strict governance requirement satisfied).
  • Avoids Example Corp deploying or managing infrastructure inside each customer's environment (minimizes architectural complexity).
  • Provides semantic search with low retrieval latency through Q Business's managed retriever.
  • Works for prompt-time enrichment (RAG-style context fetch) without requiring real-time streaming, matching the stated need.

This is the AWS-recommended pattern for ISVs that want to enrich their GenAI prompts with customer data while preserving customer-side governance.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: MCP requires Example Corp to deploy and operate MCP servers per customer (or the customer to operate them), adding significant per-tenant operational complexity. The question explicitly says Example Corp wants to avoid deploying services in each customer's environment.
  • C: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases do not natively support cross-account multi-tenant sharing of the same KB to an external ISV the way Q Business data accessors do. Even if hacked together with cross-account IAM and S3 sharing, every customer would have to build and maintain a KB and a complex IAM trust setup — high architectural complexity.
  • D: Amazon Kendra indexes are not designed to be "shared across accounts" as a tenancy pattern. Each customer would need to provision and manage Kendra (expensive) and replicate index access to Example Corp manually. High cost and high complexity.

questions.text:
A company is creating a workflow to review customer-facing communications before the company sends the communications.
