The company uses a pre-defined message template to generate the communications and stores the communications in an Amazon S3 bucket. The workflow needs to capture a specific portion from the template and send it to an Amazon Bedrock model. The workflow must store model responses back to the original S3 bucket.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Create a flow in Amazon Bedrock Flows. Configure S3 action nodes at the beginning and end of the flow to retrieve and store the communications and the model responses. In the middle of the flow, configure an expression to parse each communication. Configure an agent step to send the parsed input to the model for review.

Create an AWS Step Functions Express workflow state machine. Use an Amazon S3 integration GetObject step to retrieve the original communications. Use an intrinsic function Pass step to parse the communications and to pass the results to an Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel step. Configure an Amazon S3 integration PutObject step to store the model responses back to the S3 bucket.

Create an Amazon Bedrock agent that has an action group. Configure instructions to define how the agent should parse the communications. Configure the action group to retrieve the communications from the S3 bucket, invoke the Amazon Bedrock model, and store the model responses back to the S3 bucket.

Create an Amazon Bedrock agent that has a single action group. Configure three AWS Lambda functions in the action group. Configure the functions to retrieve the communications from the S3 bucket, parse the communications and invoke the Amazon Bedrock model, and store the model responses back to the S3 bucket.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

  • *AWS Step Functions** is the AWS-native orchestration service designed for exactly this kind of deterministic, sequential workflow:

  • GetObject (S3 SDK integration) → fetch the communication from S3.
  • Pass state with intrinsic functions → extract / parse the specific portion of the template (no Lambda required).
  • Bedrock InvokeModel (direct optimized integration) → send parsed text to the model for review.
  • PutObject (S3 SDK integration) → store the model's response back to S3.

Step Functions provides native, no-code SDK integrations with both Amazon S3 (GetObject/PutObject) and Amazon Bedrock (InvokeModel), and intrinsic functions can perform JSON/string manipulation without invoking Lambda. The Express workflow type is the cheapest, lowest-latency choice for high-volume, short-lived flows like this.
The other approaches either misuse Bedrock Flows (no real S3 nodes the way described), overuse Bedrock Agents (which are for non-deterministic reasoning, not deterministic ETL-like flows), or add unnecessary Lambda for work that Step Functions can do natively.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Amazon Bedrock Flows uses prompt/agent/knowledge-base/Lambda nodes for GenAI orchestration, but it does not have first-class "S3 GetObject/PutObject action nodes" you can drop in at the start and end the way described. Storing arbitrary objects to S3 is not what Flows is designed for.
  • C: Bedrock Agents are designed for autonomous LLM-driven task decomposition and tool use. Using an agent to do a deterministic 4-step pipeline is overkill, more expensive, less predictable, and harder to audit. Also, you'd still need Lambdas behind the action group for S3 read/write.
  • D: Same as C — wrong tool. Three Lambda functions behind a Bedrock Agent action group is unnecessary cost and complexity for a deterministic workflow that Step Functions handles natively.

questions.text:
An enterprise application uses an Amazon Bedrock foundation model(FM) to process and analyze 50 to 200 pages of technical documents. Users are experiencing inconsistent responses and receiving truncated outputs when processing documents that exceed the FM's context window limits.

Which solution will resolve this problem?
opts: Configure fixed-size chunking at 4,000 tokens for each chunk with 20% overlap. Use application-level logic to link multiple chunks sequentially until the FM's maximum context window of 200,000 tokens is reached before making inference calls.

Use hierarchical chunking with parent chunks of 8,000 tokens and child chunks of 2,000 tokens. Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases built-in retrieval to automatically select relevant parent chunks based on query context. Configure overlap tokens to maintain semantic continuity.

Use semantic chunking with a boundary threshold of 95% and a buffer size of 3 sentences. Use the Amazon Bedrock RetrieveAndGenerate API to dynamically select the most relevant chunks based on embedding similarity scores.

Create a pre-processing AWS Lambda function that analyzes the document token count by using the FM's tokenizer. Configure the Lambda function to split documents into equal segments of 80% of the context window. Configure the Lambda function to process each segment independently before aggregating the results.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

For 50–200 page technical documents that exceed the model's context window, the recommended pattern is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with hierarchical chunking:
  • Hierarchical chunking stores small (child) chunks for accurate semantic retrieval, but returns the larger surrounding parent chunk for context to the LLM. This balances retrieval precision (small vectors) with generation quality (rich context).
  • It is purpose-built for long technical documents where preserving section/paragraph context matters and where single-document context-window stuffing fails.
  • Bedrock Knowledge Bases manages chunking, embedding, vector storage, and retrieval automatically.
  • Overlap tokens preserve semantic continuity at chunk boundaries, preventing truncation of ideas that span boundaries.

This addresses both the inconsistent responses (precision via small child chunks) and the truncated outputs (only relevant context goes to the model instead of the entire document).

…

questions.text:
A company is using Amazon Bedrock to build a customer-facing AI assistant to handle sensitive customer inquiries. The company must use defense-in-depth safety controls to block sophisticated prompt injection attacks. The company must keep audit logs of all safety interventions. The AI assistant must have cross-Region failover capabilities.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails to use custom content filters to protect against prompt injection attacks. Set the content filters to high. Use a guardrail policy to implement cross-Region guardrail intervention. Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs with custom metrics to capture detailed guardrail intervention events.

Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails to use content filters to protect against prompt injection attacks. Set the content filters to high. Use AWS WAF to block suspicious inputs. Use AWS CloudTrail to log API calls for audits.

Deploy Amazon Comprehend custom classification to detect prompt injection attacks. Use Amazon API Gateway to validate requests. Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs with custom metrics to capture detailed intervention events.

Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails to use custom content filters to protect against harmful content. Set the content filters to high. Use a cross-Region guardrail to provide failover capabilities. Configure cross-Region guardrail replication to provide failover capabilities. Store logs in AWS CloudTrail for compliance auditing.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: D

The scenario has three explicit requirements that must all be satisfied:
  • Defense-in-depth against prompt injection → Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides a dedicated prompt-attack content filter category and configurable strength (High recommended for sensitive customer data).
  • Audit logs of safety interventions → Bedrock Guardrails invocations and intervention events are captured via CloudTrail (and can stream to CloudWatch Logs). CloudTrail is the canonical audit log service.
  • Cross-Region failover → Bedrock now supports cross-Region guardrail replication / cross-Region inference, allowing the same guardrail to be applied in a failover Region.

Option D is the only one that combines all three: guardrails with high-strength filters, cross-Region replication for failover, and CloudTrail for compliance auditing.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: There is no native "guardrail policy to implement cross-Region guardrail intervention" — that wording conflates concepts. Cross-Region capability comes from guardrail replication, not from a "policy". Also, CloudWatch custom metrics alone aren't sufficient as a compliance audit trail — CloudTrail is the correct service for that.
  • B: AWS WAF is an HTTP/L7 firewall — it inspects web request patterns, not the semantic content of a prompt. It cannot detect sophisticated prompt injection. CloudTrail logs API calls but doesn't log guardrail intervention details on its own without guardrails being properly configured. Also lacks cross-Region failover.
  • C: Amazon Comprehend custom classification is not designed for prompt injection detection (no maintained intent model for that), requires labeled training data, and adds latency. API Gateway request validation only checks schema, not content. Missing cross-Region failover entirely.

questions.text:
A company is building a legal research AI assistant that uses Amazon Bedrock with an Anthropic Claude foundation model(FM). The AI assistant must retrieve highly relevant case law documents to augment the FM's responses. The AI assistant must identify semantic relationships between legal concepts, specific legal terminology, and citations. The AI assistant must perform quickly and must return accurate results.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Configure an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base to use a default vector search configuration. Use Amazon Bedrock to augment queries to improve retrieval for legal documents based on specific terminology and citations.
Configure an Amazon OpenSearch service to deploy a hybrid search architecture that combines vector search with keyword search. Apply an Amazon Bedrock reranker model to optimize result relevance.

Enable the Amazon Kendra query suggestion feature for end users. Use Amazon Bedrock to perform post-processing of search results to identify semantic similarity in the documents and to produce precise results.

Configure an Amazon OpenSearch Service with Amazon Bedrock Titan embeddings to index and search legal documents. Use custom AWS Lambda functions to merge results with keyword-based filters that are stored in an Amazon RDS database.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

Legal research is the canonical use case for hybrid search:
  • Semantic / vector search captures conceptual relationships between legal doctrines (e.g., "negligence" ≈ "duty of care") that pure keyword search would miss.
  • Keyword (BM25 / lexical) search is essential for exact-match legal terminology, citation strings (e.g., "Brown v. Board, 347 U.S. 483"), statute numbers, and party names where literal matching matters far more than embeddings.
  • Amazon OpenSearch Service natively supports hybrid queries that combine k-NN vector scores with BM25 lexical scores, then normalize/blend them.
  • A Bedrock reranker model (e.g., Cohere Rerank, Amazon Rerank in Bedrock) takes the top-N from hybrid search and re-orders them with a cross-encoder for maximum precision — exactly what "must return accurate results" demands.

This combination satisfies all three requirements: semantic understanding, exact legal terminology / citations, and fast accurate retrieval.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: "Default vector search configuration" is pure semantic search. It will fail on precise citations and statute strings where literal matches dominate. No reranking. "Augmenting queries" is vague and doesn't add lexical matching.
  • C: Amazon Kendra's "query suggestion" is an end-user UX feature, not a relevance improvement. Doing semantic similarity "as post-processing" with Bedrock is inefficient and doesn't address the keyword vs semantic blend properly. Also costly.
  • D: Indexing in OpenSearch with Titan embeddings is fine, but stuffing keyword filters into RDS and merging in Lambda is an anti-pattern — OpenSearch already supports keyword + vector hybrid natively. Adds latency, complexity, and consistency problems. No reranker.

questions.text:
A healthcare company is developing a document management system that stores medical research papers in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company needs to build a comprehensive metadata framework that will improve search precision for a generative AI(GenAI) application that analyzes the research papers. The metadata framework must include document timestamps, author information, and research domain classifications.

The solution must maintain a consistent metadata structure across all uploaded documents. The solution must give foundation models(FMs) the ability to understand document context without accessing the full content.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Store document timestamps in S3 system metadata. Use S3 object tags to implement domain classification. Implement custom user-defined metadata to store author information.
Set up S3 Object Lock with legal holds to track document timestamps. Use S3 object tags to store author information. Implement S3 access points for domain classification.
Use S3 Inventory reports to track document timestamps. Create S3 access points to implement domain classification. Store author information in S3 Storage Lens dashboards.
Use custom user-defined metadata to store author information. Use S3 Object Lock retention periods to track document timestamps. Use S3 Event Notifications to implement domain classification.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

The question asks for a consistent metadata framework for objects in S3 that an FM can use as context. This maps to S3's three native metadata mechanisms used appropriately:
  • System metadata (e.g., Last-Modified, Content-Type) automatically captures document timestamps — no extra work needed.
  • S3 object tags are key-value pairs (up to 10 per object), can be queried/filtered, and are well-suited to categorical classification like research domain (e.g., domain=oncology). Tags can be used in S3 lifecycle policies, IAM conditions, and S3 Batch Operations.
  • User-defined metadata (x-amz-meta-* headers) is the proper place for free-form attributes such as author name / ORCID / affiliation, stored alongside the object.

This combination provides a consistent, queryable, FM-friendly metadata layer without abusing services for purposes they weren't designed for.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: S3 Object Lock with legal holds is for WORM compliance/immutability — it does not track document timestamps in any useful classification sense. S3 access points are network/permission boundaries, not classification mechanisms.
  • C: S3 Inventory is a batch report of objects, not a per-object timestamp source. S3 access points cannot classify documents by domain. Storage Lens is org-wide storage analytics dashboards, not a place to store author info per document. Misuse of three services.
  • D: Object Lock retention periods are for WORM compliance windows, not document timestamp tracking. S3 Event Notifications trigger downstream workflows on object events — they cannot themselves "implement domain classification".

questions.text:
A company upgraded its Amazon Bedrock foundation model(FM) that supports a multilingual customer service assistant. After the upgrade, the assistant exhibited inconsistent behavior across languages. The assistant began generating different responses in some languages when presented with identical questions.

The company needs a solution to detect and address similar problems for future updates. The evaluation must be completed within 45 minutes for all supported languages. The evaluation must process at least 15,000 test conversations in parallel. The evaluation process must be fully automated and integrated into the CI/CD pipeline. The solution must block deployment if quality thresholds are not met.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Create a distributed traffic simulation framework that sends translation-heavy workloads to the assistant in multiple languages simultaneously. Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to monitor latency, concurrency, and throughput. Run simulations before production releases to identify infrastructure bottlenecks.

Deploy the assistant in multiple AWS Regions with Amazon S3 latency-based routing and AWS Global Accelerator to improve global performance. Store multilingual conversation logs in Amazon S3.  Perform weekly post-deployment audits to review consistency.

Create a pre-processing pipeline that normalizes all incoming messages into a consistent format before sending the messages to the assistant. Apply rule-based checks to flag potential hallucinations in the outputs. Focus the evaluation on the normalized text to simplify testing across languages.

Set up standardized multilingual test conversations with identical meaning. Run the test conversations in parallel by using Amazon Bedrock model evaluation jobs. Apply automatic verification thresholds. Integrate the process into the CI/CD pipeline to block releases that fail.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: D

The requirements specify (a) detect quality regressions across languages, (b) ≥15,000 parallel test conversations, (c) ≤45 minutes runtime, (d) automated CI/CD integration, and (e) auto-blocking on threshold failure.
  • *Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation Jobs** is purpose-built for this:

  • It runs automated batch evaluation of an FM against a prompt dataset (you supply standardized multilingual test prompts with expected meaning).
  • Supports both automatic metrics (BERTScore, ROUGE, accuracy, toxicity, etc.) and human-in-the-loop evaluation.
  • Scales horizontally to large prompt datasets, completing in well under the 45-minute window for typical scales.
  • Can be invoked via API (Bedrock CreateEvaluationJob) and integrated into CodePipeline / CodeBuild / GitHub Actions for CI/CD gating; thresholds on returned metrics decide whether the deployment proceeds.
  • Designed for consistency comparisons across model versions — exactly the post-upgrade regression scenario described.


Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Measures infrastructure metrics (latency, concurrency, throughput) — not quality / consistency of multilingual responses. Doesn't detect the actual problem (semantically different responses). No CI/CD gating mechanism for quality.
  • B: Multi-Region with Global Accelerator addresses availability and latency, not response quality consistency. Weekly post-deploy audits are reactive, not preventive, and not integrated into CI/CD. S3 latency-based routing isn't a real feature.
  • C: Normalizing inputs hides the language-specific variation rather than measuring it; rule-based hallucination checks can't capture cross-language semantic consistency. Doesn't meet the parallel test or CI/CD gating requirements.

questions.text:
A company runs a generative AI(GenAI)-powered summarization application in an application AWS account that uses Amazon Bedrock. The application architecture includes an Amazon API Gateway REST API that forwards requests to AWS Lambda functions that are attached to private VPC subnets. The application summarizes sensitive customer records that the company stores in a governed data lake in a centralized data storage account. The company has enabled Amazon S3, Amazon Athena, and AWS Glue in the data storage account.

The company must ensure that calls that the application makes to Amazon Bedrock use only private connectivity between the company's application VPC and Amazon Bedrock. The company's data storage account must allow only the cross-Region-grained column-level access across the company's AWS accounts.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: In the application account, create interface VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock runtimes. Run Lambda functions in private VPC subnets. Use AWS IAM conditions on inference and data lake policies to allow only requests from the private endpoints. In the data storage account, use AWS Lake Formation LF-tag-based access control to enable table-level and column-level cross-account access.

Run Lambda functions in private subnets. Configure a NAT gateway to allow Amazon Bedrock access in the application account. Use AWS S3 bucket policies and AWS Glue Data Catalog policies to control access in the data storage account.

Create a gateway endpoint only for Amazon S3 in the data storage account. Invoke Amazon Bedrock through public endpoints. Use Amazon CloudTrail logs to monitor requests to Amazon Bedrock and to Amazon S3.

Use VPC endpoints to provide access to Amazon S3. Disable all other AWS service endpoints. Use AWS CloudTrail to monitor access. Send AWS CloudTrail logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Periodically create dashboards and allow public buckets for cross-Region needs to monitor setup time.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

Two requirements:
  • Bedrock traffic must stay on private connectivity between the application VPC and Bedrock.
  • Solution: an interface VPC endpoint (PrivateLink) for bedrock-runtime (and optionally bedrock) in the application account, with Lambdas attached to private subnets. Traffic to Bedrock then never traverses the public internet.
  • IAM/condition keys (aws:SourceVpce, aws:SourceVpc) can enforce that only the private endpoint is used.

  • Governed, cross-account, column-level access to the data lake.
  • Solution: AWS Lake Formation is the governance layer over Glue Data Catalog and S3. With LF-tag-based access control (LF-TBAC), the data storage (producer) account can grant fine-grained table-level and column-level permissions across accounts. This is the AWS-recommended pattern for governed multi-account lakes.

Option A is the only one that combines both correctly.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: A NAT gateway routes Lambda traffic to Bedrock over the public internet, violating the "private connectivity" requirement. S3 bucket policies + Glue Data Catalog policies alone do not provide column-level access; only Lake Formation does.
  • C: "Invoke Amazon Bedrock through public endpoints" directly violates the private-connectivity requirement. CloudTrail is monitoring, not access control. No column-level mechanism.
  • D: Allowing "public buckets for cross-Region needs" is a major security violation for a sensitive customer-record data lake. Disabling all other service endpoints would break Bedrock private connectivity. Internally inconsistent.

questions.text:
A company is using Amazon Bedrock to develop a customer support AI assistant. The AI assistant must regularly process sensitive personal information in responses. The company must comply with data residency policies by ensuring that all processing occurs within the same AWS Region where each customer is located. The company wants to add multi-Region failover for the AI assistant in case of a Regional outage. Preventing the exposure of personal information before the company makes the AI assistant available to customers.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Configure a cross-Region Amazon Bedrock guardrail to apply sensitive information filters. Set the guardrail to detect mode during development and testing. Switch to block mode for production deployment.
Configure a cross-Region Amazon Bedrock guardrail to apply sensitive information filters. Set the guardrail to detect mode during development, testing, and production. Enable production deployment.
Configure an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to apply content and topic filters. Set the guardrail to detect mode during development, testing, and production. Enable production for the Amazon Bedrock model.

Configure a cross-Region Amazon Bedrock guardrail to apply a set of content and word filters. Set the guardrail to detect mode during development, testing, and production. Switch to mask mode for production deployment.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

The scenario has three requirements:
  • PII protection — Bedrock Guardrails has a dedicated sensitive information filter that detects and acts on PII (names, SSNs, emails, addresses, phone numbers, etc.) and supports custom regex.
  • Data residency + multi-Region failover — A cross-Region guardrail (Bedrock supports cross-Region guardrails / inference profiles) ensures the same policy is enforced in failover Regions while keeping processing within the customer's Region.
  • Block exposure of PII before going live — Use the guardrail in detect (audit) mode during development and testing to observe what would be filtered without disrupting iteration; switch to block mode for production so PII is actually prevented from reaching customers.

Option A is the only one that combines a cross-Region guardrail, the proper sensitive-information filter focus, and the dev-to-prod progression from detect mode to a true enforcement mode (block).

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Keeping the guardrail in detect mode in production means PII is only logged, not blocked or masked. Customer-facing PII would still leak. Fails the "prevent exposure" requirement.
  • C: Uses content/topic filters — these are for harmful content / denied topics, not PII. Also no cross-Region failover. Also stays in detect mode in production (no enforcement).
  • D: Uses content/word filters instead of sensitive-information filters; word filters require pre-defined word lists and cannot reliably catch all PII formats (e.g., SSNs, varied addresses). "Mask mode" in production is acceptable for some PII flows, but combined with the wrong filter type, it doesn't meet the requirements.

questions.text:
A financial services company is developing a real-time generative AI(GenAI) assistant to support human call center agents. The GenAI assistant must transcribe live customer speech, analyze context, and provide recommendations to call center agents while a customer is still speaking. To preserve responsiveness, the GenAI assistant must maintain end-to-end latency under 1 second from speech to initial response display. The architecture must use only managed AWS services and must support bidirectional streaming to ensure that call center agents receive updates in real time.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use the Amazon Transcribe streaming API to transcribe calls. Pass the text to Amazon Comprehend to perform sentiment analysis. Feed the results to Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock by using the InvokeModel API. Store results in Amazon DynamoDB. Use a WebSocket API to display the results.

Use Amazon Transcribe streaming with partial results enabled to capture live transcripts in conversations. Forward each segments to Amazon Bedrock by using the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API. Stream responses to call center agents through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API.

Use Amazon Transcribe batch processing to convert calls to text. Pass complete transcripts to Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock through the ConverseStream API. Reduce latency by polling Amazon Live chatbot interface that call center agents can access from their web browsers.

Use the Amazon Transcribe streaming API on an AWS Lambda function to transcribe each audio segment. Configure the Lambda function to relay the transcribed text to Amazon Bedrock by using the InvokeModel API. Use the Amazon Polly text-to-speech engine on Amazon Bedrock to publish results to an Amazon SNS topic. Then publish the call center agents to the SNS topic.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

The requirements demand:
  • <1 second end-to-end latency from speech → first response display.
  • Bidirectional streaming to push updates to agents in real time.
  • Managed AWS services only.

The correct architecture:
  • Amazon Transcribe Streaming with partial results — emits incremental transcript fragments as the customer is still speaking, instead of waiting for an utterance to end. This is critical for sub-second perceived latency.
  • Amazon Bedrock InvokeModelWithResponseStream — streams the LLM's tokens back as they're generated, so the agent sees the start of a recommendation almost immediately rather than waiting for the full response.
  • Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API — provides a managed, bidirectional channel from the backend to the agent's UI, pushing token-by-token updates as they arrive.

This chain is entirely streaming end-to-end (partial transcripts → streaming inference → streaming WebSocket), which is the only way to hit the under-1-second latency budget.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Uses InvokeModel (non-streaming) — must wait for the full response before sending it to the agent. Adds Comprehend and DynamoDB as extra synchronous hops, increasing latency above the 1-second budget.
  • C: Amazon Transcribe batch processes complete audio files — completely unsuitable for real-time. "Polling Amazon Live chatbot interface" is not a real AWS service/pattern. Fails latency and architecture requirements.
  • D: Inserts Lambda per audio segment (latency + cold starts), uses non-streaming InvokeModel, then routes through Amazon Polly (text-to-speech, irrelevant) and SNS (pub/sub, not bidirectional, not low-latency push to a web UI). Multiple errors: wrong services, wrong direction, no real-time path.

questions.text:
A retail company runs an application that makes product recommendations to customers on the company's website. The application uses Amazon Bedrock to generate recommendations by dynamically constructing prompts and sending them to foundation models (FMs).

A GenAI developer has deployed an update to the application that instructs the FM to include a specific promotional message when the FM generates a response to prompts. When the developer tests the application, the promotional message does not always appear in the responses. When the promotional message does appear in the responses, it does not always flow with the rest of the text.

The GenAI developer must ensure that the promotional message always appears in the FM responses.

Which solution will meet this requirement?
opts: Use an Amazon Bedrock Guardrails filter on the prompt. Set the input filter strength to HIGH.
Generate multiple response variants that include the promotional message in different ways. Use a reranker model to select the most coherent version based on relevance to the original prompt.

Run the prompt through Amazon Bedrock. Process the response through Amazon Bedrock Agents to add the promotional message. Rerank the results by using the original prompt and the desired message as context.
Reinforce the requirement to include the new promotional message within prompts received by the FM by using an output indicator in prompts to the FM.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: D

The most reliable, low-cost way to make an FM consistently include specific text (a promotional message) is to engineer the prompt itself. An "output indicator" (a structured section of the prompt that explicitly tells the model what the output must contain and how it must be formatted) reinforces the requirement on every invocation. Well-structured prompts using instruction + context + output indicator are the foundational pattern recommended for Bedrock prompt engineering and yield consistent inclusion of required elements with smooth integration into the surrounding text.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Bedrock Guardrails are designed to block or mask undesired content (PII, toxicity, denied topics). They are not a mechanism to inject or enforce required marketing content into a response.
  • B: Generating multiple variants and reranking adds latency and cost without actually guaranteeing the promotional message appears or flows naturally — it just picks the best of several outputs that may all be flawed.
  • C: Bedrock Agents orchestrate multi-step tool use and API calls; post-processing through an Agent just to append text is heavyweight and overkill. Reranking does not enforce inclusion either.

questions.text:
A medical company is building a generative AI (GenAI) application that uses RAG to provide evidence-based medical information. The application uses Amazon OpenSearch Service for vector embeddings. Users report that searches frequently miss results that contain exact medical terms and acronyms and return too many semantically similar but irrelevant documents. The company needs to improve retrieval quality and maintain low end user latency, even as the document collection grows to millions of documents.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
opts: Configure hybrid search by combining vector similarity with keyword matching to improve semantic understanding and exact term and acronym matching.
Increase the dimensions of the vector embeddings from 384 to 1536. Use a post-processing AWS Lambda function to filter the most relevant results after retrieval.
Replace Amazon OpenSearch Service with Amazon Kendra. Use query expansion to handle medical acronyms and terminology variants during pre-processing.
Implement a two-stage retrieval architecture in which initial vector search results are re-ranked by an ML model that is hosted on Amazon SageMaker AI.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

OpenSearch Service supports native hybrid search that combines BM25 (lexical/keyword) scoring with k-NN (vector) similarity via a normalization processor in a search pipeline. This directly solves both problems: exact-match for medical terms/acronyms comes from BM25, and semantic recall comes from dense vectors. It runs inside the existing OpenSearch cluster, so there is no new infrastructure to manage — minimal operational overhead — and latency remains low because both signals are computed in a single query plan.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Higher-dimensional embeddings (1536-d) increase memory, index size, and per-query CPU/GPU cost, hurting latency at millions-of-docs scale. They also don't fix the exact-term problem, since semantic embeddings still smear precise tokens.
  • C: Migrating from OpenSearch to Kendra is a major re-architecture (high operational overhead), and Kendra is an enterprise search service that doesn't natively serve as a vector store for an existing RAG pipeline.
  • D: Two-stage retrieval with a SageMaker-hosted reranker improves quality but adds an endpoint to manage, increases per-query latency, and still misses exact-term recall if the first stage is purely vector-based. Higher operational overhead than turning on hybrid search inside OpenSearch.

questions.text:
A company is building an AI advisory application by using Amazon Bedrock. The application will provide recommendations to customers. The company needs the application to explain its reasoning process and cite specific sources for data. The application must retrieve information from company data sources and maintain response latency under 3 seconds.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
opts: Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with source attribution enabled. Use the Anthropic Claude Messages API with RAG to set high-relevance thresholds for source documents. Store reasoning and citations in Amazon S3 for auditing purposes.
Use Amazon Bedrock with Anthropic Claude models and extended thinking. Configure a 4,000-token thinking budget. Store reasoning traces and citations in Amazon DynamoDB for auditing purposes.
Configure Amazon SageMaker AI with a custom Anthropic Claude model. Use the model's reasoning parameter and AWS Lambda to process responses. Add source citations from a separate Amazon RDS database.

Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Claude models and chain-of-thought reasoning. Configure custom retrieval tracking with the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases API. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor response latency metrics.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

Anthropic Claude models on Bedrock support "extended thinking" (a native reasoning mode that returns explicit reasoning traces) with a configurable thinking budget. Setting a 4,000-token budget bounds reasoning time, helping keep total response under 3 seconds. Citations come from the model invocation alongside reasoning; storing both in DynamoDB gives a fully managed, low-latency audit store. This combination gives both transparent reasoning and source citations with the least operational overhead — no custom hosting, no separate RAG plumbing to manage manually.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Knowledge Bases provides source attribution, but bolting on "high-relevance thresholds" through prompt-only logic and writing everything to S3 doesn't give the explicit reasoning explanation the question demands, and S3 is not optimal for low-latency audit writes per request.
  • C: Self-hosting a custom Claude variant on SageMaker is high operational overhead (endpoint management, scaling, patching) — directly opposite of "LEAST operational overhead". Claude is not available as a SageMaker custom-host model anyway.
  • D: "Chain-of-thought reasoning" via prompting is unreliable for guaranteed reasoning traces, and "custom retrieval tracking" implies building bespoke instrumentation — more operational overhead, not less. CloudWatch only monitors latency, it doesn't address it.

questions.text:
QB3. A company is configuring a landing zone in AWS Control Tower. The company handles sensitive data that must remain within the European Union. The company must use only the eu-central-1 Region. The company uses SCPs to enforce data residency policies. GenAI developers at the company are assigned IAM roles that have full permissions for Amazon Bedrock.

The company must ensure that GenAI developers can use the Amazon Nova Pro model through Amazon Bedrock only by using cross-Region inference(CRI) and only in eu-central-1. The company enables model access for the GenAI developer IAM roles in Amazon Bedrock. However, when a GenAI developer attempts to invoke the Amazon Nova Pro model through Bedrock Converse API, the developer receives the following error:

User: arn:aws:sts::123456789012:assumed-role/AssumedDevRole/DevUserName Action: bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream On resource(s) arn:aws:bedrock:eu-west-3::foundation-model/amazon.nova-pro-v1:0 Context: a service control policy explicitly denies the action.

The company needs a solution to resolve the error. The solution must retain the company's existing governance controls and must provide process access control. The solution must comply with the company's existing data residency controls.

Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
opts: Add an AdministratorAccess policy to the GenAI developer IAM role.
Extend the existing SCPs to enable CRI for the eu.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0 inference profile.
Enable Amazon Bedrock model access to use the eu.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0 inference profile.
Validate that the GenAI developer IAM roles have permissions to invoke Amazon Nova Pro by the eu.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0 on all European Union AWS Regions that can serve the model.
Extend the existing SCP to enable CRI for the eu.* inference profile.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C, D

Cross-Region Inference (CRI) on Bedrock works through an inference profile (e.g., eu.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0), which transparently routes requests to one of several geographically scoped regional model endpoints (within the EU set: eu-central-1, eu-west-1, eu-west-3, etc.). For this to succeed:
  • C — Bedrock model access must be granted for the inference profile itself, not just the underlying foundation model. Without this, invocations through the profile fail.
  • D — The IAM identity must have bedrock:InvokeModel* permissions on every regional foundation-model ARN that the EU inference profile can route to (e.g., the eu-west-3 model resource in the error message). The error proves the call was routed to eu-west-3 and SCP denied it — but the user also needs the per-region resource permissions for the underlying model ARNs in addition to the inference profile.

Combining (C) profile access + (D) per-region model invoke permission gives a working, governed, data-residency-compliant CRI setup.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Granting AdministratorAccess violates least-privilege and existing governance controls; SCPs would still deny the action because SCPs are a guardrail above IAM.
  • B: Loosening SCPs is not required — the SCP is doing its job. Also, the SCP isn't what blocks CRI; missing model/profile access is.
  • E: A wildcard eu.* profile in SCP defeats the purpose of fine-grained governance and is still not the underlying issue (model + profile access), so it doesn't fix the error correctly.

questions.text:
A medical company uses Amazon Bedrock to power a clinical documentation summarization system. The system produces inconsistent summaries when handling complex clinical documents. The system performed well on simple clinical documents. The company needs a solution that diagnoses inconsistencies, compares prompt performance against established metrics, and maintains historical records of prompt versions.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Create multiple prompt variants by using Prompt management in Amazon Bedrock. Manually test the prompts with simple clinical documents. Deploy the highest performing version by using the Amazon Bedrock console.

Implement version control for prompts in a code repository with a test suite that contains complex clinical documents and quantifiable evaluation metrics. Use an automated testing framework to compare prompt versions and document performance patterns.

Deploy each new prompt version to separate Amazon Bedrock API endpoints. Split production traffic between the endpoints. Configure Amazon CloudWatch to capture response metrics and user feedback for automatic version selection.

Create a custom prompt evaluation flow in Amazon Bedrock Flows that applies the same clinical document inputs to different prompt variants. Use Amazon Comprehend Medical to analyze and score the factual accuracy of each version.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

The requirement set — diagnose inconsistencies, compare against established metrics, AND maintain historical records of prompt versions — is exactly the job of a software-engineering workflow: prompts as code in version control (full history + diffs + rollbacks), an automated evaluation harness running against a curated test set of complex clinical documents, and quantifiable scoring (ROUGE, BERTScore, factual-consistency metrics, etc.). This pattern gives reproducible regression testing and the longest, richest history of prompt performance. It also scales as the team adds more clinical scenarios.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Manually testing on simple documents reproduces neither the failure mode nor any rigorous metric — the system already works on simple cases. Bedrock Prompt Management stores versions but the proposed workflow is informal and not metric-driven.
  • C: "Separate Bedrock API endpoints" per prompt is not how Bedrock works — prompts aren't deployed as endpoints. Splitting production traffic also lacks a controlled evaluation set and risks patient-safety issues on live medical traffic.
  • D: Bedrock Flows is an orchestration tool, not an evaluation framework, and Comprehend Medical scores entities, not summary faithfulness. It doesn't maintain prompt version history.

questions.text:
QB5. A company has a recommendation system. The system's applications run on Amazon EC2 instances. The applications make API calls to Amazon Bedrock foundation models (FMs) to analyze customer behavior and generate personalized product recommendations. The system is experiencing intermittent issues. Some recommendations do not match customer preferences. The company needs an observability solution to monitor operational metrics and detect patterns of operational performance degradation compared to established baselines. The solution must also generate alerts with correlation data within 10 minutes when FM behavior deviates from expected patterns.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Configure Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights for the application infrastructure. Set up CloudWatch alarms for latency thresholds. Add custom metrics for token counts by using the CloudWatch embedded metric format. Create CloudWatch dashboards to visualize the data.

Implement AWS X-Ray to trace requests through the application components. Enable CloudWatch ServiceLens to correlate trace and performance data. Configure AWS QuickSight to centralize log data. Set up AWS CloudTrail to monitor all API calls to Amazon Bedrock. Create custom dashboards in Amazon QuickSight.

Enable Amazon CloudWatch Application Insights for the application resources. Create custom metrics for recommendation quality, token usage, and response latency by using the CloudWatch embedded metric format. Set up CloudWatch anomaly detection on the metrics. Establish notifications by using Amazon SNS. Configure CloudWatch anomaly detection on the model metrics. Establish notifications by using Amazon SNS. Configure CloudWatch anomaly detection on the model metrics.

Use the Amazon OpenSearch Service with the Observability plugin. Ingest model metrics and logs by using Amazon Kinesis. Create custom Pipeline Processing Language(PPL) queries to analyze model behavior patterns. Establish operational dashboards to visualize anomalies in real time.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C

CloudWatch Application Insights provides automated discovery of application components and surfacing of operational problems with correlation between metrics, logs, and events. Adding custom metrics for recommendation quality, token usage, and latency via the Embedded Metric Format (EMF) lets the team measure GenAI-specific signals (not just CPU/RAM). CloudWatch anomaly detection dynamically learns baselines and triggers within minutes when metrics deviate, and SNS delivers the alert. This stack is the LEAST-overhead, native AWS solution that meets all three requirements — baseline-relative anomaly detection, correlated diagnostics, and sub-10-minute alerting.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Container Insights targets ECS/EKS workloads — these apps run on EC2, not containers. Static latency-threshold alarms don't compare against learned baselines and won't catch subtle drift in recommendation quality.
  • B: X-Ray + ServiceLens gives request tracing but QuickSight is a BI tool, not a real-time log/metric platform, and CloudTrail records API calls, not FM behavior quality. The stack is heavy and still lacks anomaly detection on quality metrics.
  • D: Spinning up OpenSearch + Kinesis + custom PPL is high operational overhead, and you'd still need to build the anomaly-detection logic and alerting yourself. Overkill compared to native CloudWatch features.

questions.text:
QB6. A company has deployed an AI assistant as a React application on AWS Amplify, an AWS AppSync GraphQL API, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. The application uses the GraphQL API to call the Amazon Bedrock RetrieveAndGenerate API for knowledge base interactions. The company configures an AWS Lambda resolver to use the RetrieveAndGenerate invocation type. Application users report frequent timeouts and slow response times. Users report these problems more frequently for complex questions that require longer processing.

The company needs a solution to fix these performance issues and enhance the user experience.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use AWS Amplify AI Kit to implement streaming responses from the GraphQL API and to optimize client-side rendering.
Increase the timeout value of the Lambda resolver. Implement retry logic with exponential backoff.
Update the application to send an API request to an Amazon SQS queue. Update the AWS Bedrock resolver to poll and process the queue.
Change the RetrieveAndGenerate API to the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API. Update the application to use a new Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API to support the streaming response.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

The root cause is a synchronous request/response on a long-running generation. The proper UX fix is streaming so the user sees tokens as they are generated (perceived latency drops to first-token time, and you avoid hitting AppSync/Lambda timeouts on the whole response). AWS Amplify AI Kit provides built-in streaming support for AppSync GraphQL APIs to FMs (and to Bedrock specifically), plus React client primitives for incremental rendering. This keeps the existing AppSync + Amplify architecture and adds streaming with minimal re-platforming — exactly what the question asks for.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Lambda max timeout is 15 minutes, but AppSync resolver timeouts and HTTP/GraphQL client timeouts are smaller; bumping the Lambda timeout doesn't solve perceived latency. Retries on a generation request just amplify cost and delay.
  • C: Switching to SQS makes the call asynchronous (fire-and-forget), forcing the React app to poll for results — a major UX regression and unnecessary re-architecture.
  • D: InvokeModelWithResponseStream streams from raw FMs only — it bypasses Knowledge Bases (you'd lose RAG). The proper streaming KB API is RetrieveAndGenerateStream. Replacing AppSync with a new API Gateway WebSocket API is a heavy rebuild.

questions.text:
QB7. A media company has multiple teams that use Amazon Bedrock to implement a robust governance process for AI-generated content. The company needs to manage hundreds of prompt templates. Multiple teams use the templates across multiple AWS Regions to generate content. The solution must provide version control approval workflows that include notifications for pending reviews. The solution must also provide detailed audit trails that document prompt activities and consistent prompt parameterization to enforce quality standards.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Configure Amazon Bedrock Studio prompt templates. Use Amazon CloudWatch to create dashboards that display prompt usage. Store the approval status of content in Amazon DynamoDB. Use AWS Lambda functions to enforce approvals.
Implement AWS Step Functions for prompt version control. Configure AWS CloudTrail for audit logging. Use IAM policies to control approval permissions by specifying variables.
Use AWS Step Functions to create an approval version control system. Configure AWS CloudTrail for audit logging. Use Amazon EventBridge to send notifications.

Deploy Amazon SageMaker Canvas to create and manage prompt templates that are stored in Amazon S3. Use AWS CloudFormation to implement approval workflow control. Use AWS Config to enforce approval policies.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C

The requirements are: (1) a version-controlled approval workflow with notifications for pending reviews, (2) detailed audit trails of prompt activities, and (3) consistent parameterization. AWS Step Functions orchestrates the multi-step approval workflow (draft → review → approve/reject → publish) with state history. AWS CloudTrail captures all Bedrock prompt management API calls (Create/Update/Delete versions) for an immutable audit trail. Amazon EventBridge receives Step Functions / Bedrock state-change events and routes them to notification channels (SNS, Slack via API Destinations, email, etc.) when reviews are pending. This combination gives a clean event-driven approval system on top of Bedrock Prompt Management's versioning and variables.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Bedrock Studio is a developer experience, not an approval engine. Hand-rolling approvals in DynamoDB + Lambda gives no orchestration, no built-in audit, and no notification framework.
  • B: Uses IAM policies "by specifying variables" to control approvals — IAM doesn't gate workflow approvals at the data level. Missing notification mechanism entirely (no EventBridge/SNS).
  • D: SageMaker Canvas is a no-code ML predictions tool, not a prompt template manager. CloudFormation is IaC, not a runtime approval workflow tool. AWS Config evaluates resource compliance, not human approvals. Wrong services for every requirement.

questions.text:
QB8. A financial services company uses an AI application to process financial documents by using Amazon Bedrock. During business hours, the application receives approximately 10,000 requests each hour, which requires consistent throughput. The company uses the CreateProvisionedModelThroughput API to purchase provisioned throughput. Amazon CloudWatch metrics show that the provisioned capacity is unused while on-demand requests are being throttled. The team analyzes the logs and finds the following code in the application: python responses=bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(modelId="anthropic.claude-v2", body=json.dumps(payload))

The company needs the application to use the provisioned throughput to avoid the throttling issues.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Increase the number of model units(MUs) in the provisioned throughput configuration.
Replace the model ID parameter with the ARN of the provisioned Model Throughput API returns.
Add exponential backoff retry logic to handle throttling exceptions during peak hours.
Modify the application to use the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API instead of the InvokeModel API.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

On Amazon Bedrock, provisioned throughput is addressed by the ARN returned by CreateProvisionedModelThroughput, not by the foundation model ID. The current code passes modelId="anthropic.claude-v2", which routes the call to the on-demand capacity pool (subject to account-level RPM/TPM quotas) and is being throttled. Replacing the modelId parameter with the provisioned throughput ARN (e.g., arn:aws:bedrock:::provisioned-model/) sends each invocation against the dedicated, reserved capacity — eliminating the throttling and explaining why CloudWatch shows the provisioned capacity sitting unused.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Adding more MUs raises the unused provisioned capacity even higher — the problem isn't capacity, it's that no traffic is being routed to the provisioned model.
  • C: Exponential backoff masks symptoms (and slows users) but the workload still rides on-demand quotas and continues to throttle. It doesn't fix the misconfiguration.
  • D: Streaming changes how responses are returned (token-by-token) but doesn't change which capacity pool is used. Still throttles, still doesn't use the provisioned ARN.

questions.text:
QB7. A company is designing a canary deployment strategy for a payment processing API. The system must support automated gradual traffic shifting between multiple Amazon Bedrock models based on real-time inference metrics, historical traffic patterns, and service health. The solution must be able to gradually increase traffic to new model versions. The system must increase traffic if metrics remain healthy and decrease traffic if the performance degrades below acceptable thresholds.

The company needs to comprehensively monitor inference latency and error rates during the deployment phase. The company must also be able to halt deployments and revert to a previous model version without any manual intervention.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use Amazon Bedrock with provisioned throughput to host the two versions of the model. Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke an AWS Step Functions workflow when a new model version is created. Add inference metrics to the AWS Lambda function to track and route traffic to the new version. Add inference latency and error rates as Amazon CloudWatch dependence metrics. Configure Amazon CloudWatch performance thresholds. Use Amazon API Gateway to trigger a fallback to a previous version if performance metrics breach a defined threshold.

Use AWS Lambda functions to invoke many Amazon Bedrock models. Use a Lambda environment variable and weighted routing to shift traffic gradually with capability for sudden rollback. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor for performance degradation and provide automatic rollback notifications.

Use Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints to represent multiple Amazon Bedrock model versions. Use variant weights to shift traffic. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor performance metrics. Use SageMaker Model Monitor to trigger AWS CodeDeploy to automatically restore the previous variant if performance drops below a specified threshold.

Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to track inference latency. Configure an Amazon Bedrock model endpoint with traffic split capabilities, if there is performance degradation, use AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook to update Amazon Bedrock model endpoints to shift traffic based on the metrics.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

The requirement is a closed-loop canary controller built around provisioned-throughput hosted Bedrock models, with: - Multiple Bedrock model versions behind provisioned throughput (so each has predictable, isolated capacity). - EventBridge + Step Functions orchestrating the gradual shift (deterministic state machine for traffic steps, evaluation windows, and rollbacks — fully automated, no human in the loop). - CloudWatch capturing inference latency and error-rate metrics with thresholds. - API Gateway as the traffic-shifting front door that flips back to the previous Bedrock model version if thresholds are breached.
This stack covers gradual progression on healthy signals, automatic rollback on degradation, no manual intervention, and end-to-end metric monitoring — every requirement is satisfied by native AWS services.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: "Weighted routing via Lambda environment variable" isn't real traffic shifting — Lambda env vars are static per-version and can't perform percentage-based routing at runtime. CloudWatch only "notifies" rollback here; rollback is not automated.
  • C: Bedrock foundation models are not hosted on SageMaker endpoints. You can't put a Bedrock model behind a SageMaker production variant. SageMaker Model Monitor + CodeDeploy is a valid pattern for SageMaker-hosted models only.
  • D: OpenSearch isn't an inference-latency monitor for Bedrock (CloudWatch is). "Bedrock model endpoint with traffic split capabilities" doesn't exist as a native feature — Bedrock has no built-in weighted endpoint construct. Systems Manager runbooks are reactive ops automation, not real-time traffic shaping.

questions.text:
A financial services company is creating a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application that uses Amazon Bedrock to generate summaries of market activities. The application relies on a vector database that stores a small proprietary dataset that has a low index count. The application must perform similarity searches in the vector database, and the Amazon Bedrock model's responses must maximize accuracy and maintain high performance.

The company needs to configure the vector database and integrate it with the application.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Launch an Amazon MemoryDB cluster and configure the index by using the Flat algorithm. Configure a horizontal scaling policy based on performance metrics.
Launch an Amazon MemoryDB cluster and configure the index by using the Hierarchical Navigable Small World(HNSW) algorithm. Configure a vertical policy based on performance metrics.

Launch an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster and configure the index by using the Inverted File with Flat Compression(IVFFlat) algorithm. Configure the instance class to scale to a larger size when the load increases.

Launch an Amazon DocumentDB cluster that has an Inverted File with Flat Compression(IVFFlat) index and a high probe value. Configure connections to the cluster as a replica set. Distribute reads to replica instances.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

Amazon MemoryDB (Redis-compatible) provides an in-memory vector store with single-digit-millisecond latency, which maximises performance for similarity search. The Flat (brute-force, exact KNN) algorithm is the ideal choice when the dataset is small and the index count is low, because it scans every vector and therefore returns the most accurate nearest neighbours possible — no recall trade-off. The question explicitly demands both maximum accuracy and high performance on a small corpus, which is exactly the niche where Flat outperforms approximate algorithms like HNSW or IVFFlat. MemoryDB also natively supports horizontal scaling via shard-based clustering.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: HNSW is an approximate nearest-neighbour algorithm tuned for very large vector sets where Flat would be too slow. On a small dataset HNSW gives no speed advantage but sacrifices recall/accuracy. Vertical scaling alone also limits MemoryDB's clustered model.
  • C: Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector and IVFFlat is also an approximate algorithm that partitions vectors into lists; it adds index-build overhead and recall loss with no benefit for a tiny dataset. Aurora's disk-backed engine cannot match MemoryDB's in-memory latency.
  • D: Amazon DocumentDB does not natively support IVFFlat vector indexes (vector search is offered in DocumentDB only with limited support and not via pgvector-style IVFFlat). Read replicas don't help similarity-search accuracy.

questions.text:
A company is using Amazon Bedrock to design an application to help researchers apply for grants. The application is based on Amazon Nova Pro foundation model (FM). The application contains four required inputs and must provide responses in a consistent text format. The company wants to receive a notification in Amazon Bedrock if a response contains bullying language. However, the company does not want to block all flagged responses.

The company creates an Amazon Bedrock flow that takes an input prompt and sends it to the Amazon Nova Pro FM. The Amazon Nova Pro FM provides a response.

Which additional steps must the company take to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
opts: Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to specify the required inputs as variables. Amazon Nova Pro FM. Specify the output format for the response. Add the prompt to the prompts node of the flow.
Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail that applies the hate content filter. Set the filter response to block. Add the guardrail to the prompts node of the flow.
Create an Amazon Bedrock encoder (agent) Amazon Nova Pro FM. Add the required inputs as variables to the flow node. Add the prompt router to the output node.
Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail that applies the insults content filter. Set the filter response to detect. Add the guardrail to the prompts node of the flow.

Create an Amazon Bedrock application inference profile that specifies an Amazon Nova Pro FM. Specify the output format for the response in the description. Include a tag for each of the input variables. Add the profile to the prompts node of the flow.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A, D

The requirements decompose into two needs:
  • Structured input/output with four required fields and a consistent format → Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management stores reusable, versioned prompt templates with typed input variables and defined output structure. Adding the managed prompt to the Prompts node of the flow enforces those four inputs and a consistent format (Option A).

  • Notify but do not block bullying language → Amazon Bedrock Guardrails content filters have two response actions: BLOCK or NONE/Detect (mask/flag only). Choosing the insults filter (the category that covers bullying / demeaning language) with response action set to Detect lets the response pass through while still surfacing a guardrail intervention notification (Option D).


Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: The Hate filter targets discrimination/hostility, not bullying. Setting the response to Block also violates the "do not block" requirement.
  • C: "Encoder/Prompt router" is not how Bedrock structures required inputs or output format; Prompt routing is for selecting between FMs, not enforcing schemas.
  • E: Application inference profiles route invocations across regions and apply cost tracking tags; they don't define prompt inputs, output formatting, or content filtering.

questions.text:
A company is using Amazon Bedrock to develop an AI-powered application that uses a foundation model (FM) that supports cross-Region inference and processed throughput. The application must serve users in Europe and North America with consistently low latency. The application must comply with data residency regulations that require European user data to remain within Europe-based AWS Regions.

During testing, the application experiences service degradation when Regional traffic spikes reach service quotas. The company needs a solution that maintains application resilience and minimizes operational complexity.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Deploy separate Amazon Bedrock instances in North American and European Regions. Use a custom routing layer that directs traffic based on user location. Configure Amazon CloudWatch alarms to monitor Regional service usage. Use Amazon SNS to send email alerts to the company when usage approaches specified thresholds.

Use Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference profiles by specifying geographical zones in profile IDs when the application calls the InvokeModel API. Configure separate Amazon Bedrock service endpoints by using Amazon API Gateway HTTP APIs to direct European and North American traffic to the appropriate Regional endpoints.

Deploy a multi-Region Amazon API Gateway HTTP API and Amazon Lambda functions that implement retry logic to handle throttling. Configure the Lambda functions to call the nearest Amazon Bedrock service quotas in the primary Region. Use intelligent routing to ensure compliance with data residency requirements.

Configure provisioned throughput for Amazon Bedrock in multiple Regions. Implement failover logic in the application code to switch Regions when throttling occurs. Use AWS Global Accelerator to route traffic to the appropriate endpoints based on user location.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

  • *Amazon Bedrock cross-region inference profiles are purpose-built for exactly this scenario. A geographic profile (e.g., eu.anthropic.claude-... or us.anthropic.claude-...) lets Bedrock automatically distribute InvokeModel traffic across multiple Regions within the same geographic zone**, which:

  • Doubles or triples the effective TPM/RPM quota because the limit is summed across the participating Regions, eliminating the throttling/service-degradation symptom.
  • Keeps data inside the geographic zone — EU profiles only route to EU Regions, satisfying European data-residency rules; US profiles stay within North America.
  • Minimises operational complexity — no custom routing layer, no Lambda retry plumbing.

Pairing the two profile IDs with an API Gateway HTTP API that has Region-specific stages/endpoints (one per zone) gives users low-latency Regional access while Bedrock itself handles the cross-Region failover behind the profile.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Custom routing + CloudWatch alarms is high operational overhead and does nothing to raise the per-Region quota — throttling will still occur.
  • C: Retry logic does not increase Bedrock quotas; under sustained load you simply retry into the same throttled Region. Doesn't address residency cleanly either.
  • D: Provisioned Throughput is expensive, requires model-units purchased per Region, and AWS Global Accelerator can violate residency by routing EU users to a closer non-EU edge. High complexity, high cost.

questions.text:
A financial services company is designing a customer service AI assistant application that uses a foundation model (FM) in Amazon Bedrock. The application must provide transparent responses by documenting reasoning and by citing sources that are used for Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). The application must capture comprehensive audit trails for all responses to users. The application must be able to serve up to 10,000 concurrent users and must respond to each customer inquiry within 3 seconds.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
opts: Enable tracing for Amazon Bedrock agents. Configure structured prompts that direct the FM to provide evidence presentations. Integrate Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases with data sources to enable RAG. Configure the application to reference and cite authoritative content. Deploy the application in a Multi-AZ architecture. Use Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda functions to scale the application. Use Amazon CloudFront to provide low-latency delivery.

Enable tracing for Amazon Bedrock agents. Integrate a custom RAG pipeline with Amazon OpenSearch Service to retrieve and cite sources. Configure structured prompts to present evidence and reasoning. Deploy the application on Amazon ECS by using Amazon API Gateway REST API. Use AWS Lambda functions and Amazon CloudFront to scale the application and to provide low latency. Store logs in Amazon S3 and use AWS CloudTrail to capture audit trails.

Create a custom RAG implementation by using NAT gateways and Network Load Balancers (NLBs). Configure container clusters in multiple Regions for low latency. Implement custom logging by using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use IAM roles and AWS CloudTrail logs for compliance auditing.

Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor latency and error rates. Embed model prompts directly in the application backend to cite sources. Store generated responses and supporting metadata in Amazon S3. Use AWS Glue for cataloging retrieved documents. Process the retrieved documents in Amazon Athena to generate periodic compliance reports.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

This solution composes managed-service primitives that exactly match the requirements with minimum operational overhead:
  • Bedrock Agents + Trace automatically captures step-by-step reasoning (audit/transparency).
  • Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides managed RAG ingestion, embeddings, and automatic citation metadata in the response (retrievedReferences) — no custom RAG pipeline.
  • API Gateway + Lambda auto-scales to tens of thousands of concurrent requests serverlessly; Multi-AZ is inherent.
  • CloudFront terminates TLS close to users and reduces RTT, helping the 3-second SLA.

No clusters to patch, no custom vector DB to operate.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: A custom RAG pipeline on OpenSearch + ECS is operationally heavy compared to Bedrock Knowledge Bases. CloudFront in front of a Lambda behind ECS is redundant.
  • C: Self-managed containers, NAT GW, NLB, Kinesis — extremely high operational burden; the question asks for the LEAST.
  • D: Embedding prompts in backend code with S3+Glue+Athena gives no real-time RAG, no citations, no sub-3-second response for live chat.

questions.text:
A company is creating a generative AI(GenAI) application that uses Amazon Bedrock foundation models (FMs). The application must use Microsoft Entra ID to authenticate. All FM API calls may be on private network paths. Access to the application must be limited by department for specific sets of audit trail of model interactions.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Configure SAML federation between Microsoft Entra ID and IAM. Create department-specific IAM roles that allow only the required Modeld values. Create AWS PrivateLink VPC endpoints for Amazon Bedrock runtime services. Enable AWS CloudTrail to capture Amazon Bedrock API calls. Configure Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to record detailed model interactions.

Create an identity provider(IdP) connection in IAM to authenticate by using Microsoft Entra ID. Assign department permission sets to control access to specific model families. Specify AWS Lambda functions in private subnets with a NAT gateway for egress to Amazon Bedrock public endpoints. Enable CloudWatch Logs to capture model interactions for auditing purposes.

Create a SAML identity provider(IdP) in IAM by authenticating by using Microsoft Entra ID. Use IAM permissions boundaries to limit user access to specific model families. Configure AWS Transit Gateway with VPC routing to maintain private network connectivity. Configure AWS CloudTrail and Amazon S3 Lifecycle rules to maintain an audit trail of model interactions.

Configure OpenID Connect(OIDC) federation between Microsoft Entra ID and IAM. Use IAM permissions boundaries to control access to specific Amazon Bedrock FM families based on user location. Configure Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging and pipe SCP for additional security. Use Microsoft Entra ID's built-in logging capabilities to maintain an audit trail of model interactions.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

Four requirements map to four AWS controls:
  • Authenticate via Microsoft Entra ID → Configure Entra ID as a SAML 2.0 federation provider in IAM (well-documented integration; Entra ID issues SAML assertions that AssumeRoleWithSAML exchanges for temporary AWS credentials).
  • Limit access by department to specific FMs → IAM roles per department whose policies allow only specific bedrock:InvokeModel actions for specific modelId ARNs.
  • All FM API calls on private network paths → AWS PrivateLink (Interface VPC Endpoints) for the Bedrock runtime (com.amazonaws..bedrock-runtime) keep traffic on the AWS backbone — no internet, no NAT.
  • Audit trail of model interactions → CloudTrail for control-plane API calls plus Bedrock Model Invocation Logging to S3/CloudWatch Logs for the actual prompt/response payloads.


Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Lambda + NAT gateway sends traffic to the public Bedrock endpoint — violates the "private network paths" requirement. CloudWatch Logs alone misses control-plane audit.
  • C: Transit Gateway by itself doesn't make Bedrock private; you still need a PrivateLink endpoint. Permissions boundaries are for delegating IAM creation, not the primary access-control mechanism.
  • D: OIDC works but is unusual for Entra ID → AWS console/CLI federation (SAML is the norm). Using Entra ID's logging instead of CloudTrail loses the AWS-side audit trail required for compliance.

questions.text:
A GenAI developer is creating a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) based customer support application that uses Amazon Bedrock foundation models (FMs). The application needs to process 50 GB of historical customer conversations that are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket as JSON files. The application must use the processed data as its retrieval corpus. The application's data processing workflow must extract relevant data from customer support documents, remove customer personally identifiable information (PII), and generate embeddings for vector storage. The processing workflow must be cost-effective and must finish within 48 hours.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
opts: Use AWS Lambda and Amazon Comprehend to process the files in parallel, remove PII, and call Amazon Bedrock APIs to generate vectors. Configure Lambda concurrency limits and memory settings to handle the volume.

Create an AWS Glue ETL job to run PII detection scripts on the data. Use Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Processing to run the HuggingFaceProcessor to generate embeddings by using a pre-trained model. Store the embeddings in Amazon OpenSearch Service.
Deploy an Amazon EMR cluster that runs Apache Spark with user-defined functions (UDFs) that call Amazon Bedrock APIs to generate embeddings. Use Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension.

Implement a data processing pipeline that uses AWS Step Functions to orchestrate a sequence of Amazon Comprehend for PII detection and Amazon Bedrock embeddings. Directly integrate the workflow with Amazon OpenSearch Serverless to store vectors and provide similarity search capabilities.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: D

  • *AWS Step Functions** orchestrates the end-to-end pipeline using only managed services, with no servers or clusters to operate:

  • Amazon Comprehend has a built-in DetectPiiEntities / ContainsPiiEntities API and a StartPiiEntitiesDetectionJob batch mode that natively redacts PII in S3 documents.
  • Amazon Bedrock Titan Embeddings (or Cohere Embeddings) generate vectors at scale via simple API calls Step Functions can invoke (Optimized integrations or Lambda).
  • Amazon OpenSearch Serverless is the default Bedrock-integrated vector store, fully managed, scales to billions of vectors.

This is the lowest-ops architecture for the 50 GB / 48-hour target while being cost-effective (pay-per-use across Step Functions, Comprehend, Bedrock, OpenSearch Serverless).

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Lambda has a 15-minute timeout and 6 MB synchronous payload; tuning concurrency/memory is operational overhead; orchestration logic must be hand-built.
  • B: Mixing Glue ETL with SageMaker Async Processing and HuggingFace is more moving parts and adds infra to manage. HuggingFace embeddings also bypass the Bedrock-managed embedding option.
  • C: EMR/Spark requires cluster sizing, tuning, patching — high operational burden; not "least ops."

questions.text:
A university is building an AI-powered application that includes several sub-applications. The sub-applications include AI assistants, assignment graders, and internal analytics applications. The university is defining and testing multiple prompts by using various foundation models(FMs). The university wants to compare variants of each prompt and choose the variant that yields outputs that are best for specified use cases.

The university requires a version control solution for the prompts. The university must be able to test prompt variations and collect audit trails for prompt changes and usage. The solution must also maintain consistency while allowing the prompts to integrate into the main application.

Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
opts: Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to create versioned prompts. Include parameterized variables for each use case.
Store prompts in Amazon S3. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the model interactions and service integrations.
Use Amazon Bedrock Flows to create workflows that combine FMs and AWS services.
Configure AWS Config to record prompt changes. Use AWS CloudTrail to track prompt usage.
Configure Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A, C

  • A — Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management is the AWS-native, managed prompt template store. It provides:
  • Versioning of every prompt change (immutable versions, alias-style references)
  • Variants so multiple prompt+model+parameter combinations can be tested side-by-side and the best one promoted
  • Parameterised input variables so the same template serves many sub-applications
  • Audit trail because every create/update is captured in CloudTrail automatically

  • C — Amazon Bedrock Flows is the serverless visual orchestrator that consumes the Prompt-Management prompts as nodes and stitches them together with knowledge bases, agents, Lambda, condition logic. It allows the sub-applications to call a single Flow endpoint, ensuring consistency across AI assistant, grader, analytics use cases while still being fully managed (least ops).
