Together they give versioning + testing + governance + low-ops integration.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Storing raw prompt files in S3 means hand-building versioning, variant testing, and audit, increasing operational overhead.
  • D: AWS Config tracks resource configuration drift, not prompt text. CloudTrail records API calls but Prompt Management already integrates with CloudTrail natively — this option duplicates work and still lacks variant testing.
  • E: Intelligent Prompt Routing dynamically picks the cheapest/fastest model per request; it does not version prompts, run variants, or audit content.

questions.text:
A company provides a service that helps users from around the world discover new restaurants. The service has 7 million monthly active users. The company wants to implement a semantic search solution across a database that contains 20 million restaurants and 200 million reviews. The company currently stores the data in a PostgreSQL database. The solution must support complex natural language queries and return results for at least 95% of queries within 500 ms. The solution must maintain data freshness for frequent updates that update hourly. The solution must also scale cost-effectively during peak usage periods.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
opts: Migrate the restaurant data to Amazon OpenSearch Service. Implement custom keyword-based search functionality based on user input. Add a tuning to text analyzers to optimize search performance for restaurant queries and reviews. Use Amazon CloudWatch for performance and to transform user queries into structured search queries.

Migrate the restaurant data to Amazon OpenSearch Service. Use a foundation model (FM) in Amazon Bedrock to generate vector embeddings from restaurant descriptions, reviews, and metadata. When users enter natural language queries, convert the queries to embeddings, and perform vector similarity search by using k-NN search on the the FM.

Keep the restaurant data in PostgreSQL. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service. Grant the AI agent Lambda functions permission to invoke the Lambda function that hosts the MCP server. Configure the AI agent's MCP server to invoke the MCP server synchronously.

Deploy a custom fine-tuned model on Amazon SageMaker AI. Train the model on the company's restaurant and review data. Configure the application to use the SageMaker endpoint to convert natural language queries to SQL. Run the SQL queries against the existing PostgreSQL database.

Migrate the restaurant data to Amazon DynamoDB. Use Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases to generate test queries that have known answers on a regular schedule, and track model success for edge cases. Use Amazon SageMaker Feature Store to maintain evaluation datasets. Use a built-in Amazon Bedrock evaluation to track retrieval precision and hallucination rates.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

The requirements demand semantic search ("complex natural-language queries"), sub-500 ms p95 over a 220 M-record corpus, hourly freshness, and cost-effective scaling — all with least development effort.
  • Amazon OpenSearch Service has a native k-NN vector engine with HNSW that comfortably serves p95 < 500 ms at 200 M-vector scale.
  • Bedrock Titan/Cohere embeddings can vectorise restaurant descriptions and reviews — embedding generation is a managed API call, no model training.
  • Hourly delta updates to OpenSearch are well supported via streaming pipelines (DMS, OpenSearch Ingestion).
  • No custom model, no SQL translation — natural language is encoded once and compared via cosine similarity.

This is dramatically less effort than fine-tuning a text-to-SQL model.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Keyword search alone (BM25) cannot satisfy "complex natural language queries" semantically.
  • C: Adds MCP server + Lambda plumbing without explaining how PostgreSQL would serve sub-500 ms semantic search; also high dev effort.
  • D: Fine-tuning a text-to-SQL model on SageMaker is high effort, requires labelled training data, and PostgreSQL is unlikely to meet 500 ms p95 at this scale for complex queries.
  • E: DynamoDB is key-value; no semantic search. The rest of the option describes evaluation tooling, not the actual search solution.

questions.text:
A company uses AWS Lambda functions to build an AI agent solution. A GenAI developer must set up a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that accesses user information. The GenAI developer must ensure that also configure the AI agent to use the new MCP server. The GenAI developer must ensure that only authorized users can access the MCP server.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use a Lambda function to host the MCP server. Grant the AI agent Lambda functions permission to invoke the Lambda function that hosts the MCP server. Configure the AI agent's MCP server to invoke the MCP server asynchronously.

Use a Lambda function to host the MCP server. Create an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API that proxies requests to invoke the Lambda function. Configure the AI agent to use the STDIO transport with the MCP server.

Use a Lambda function to host the MCP server. Create an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API that provides requests to invoke the Lambda function. Configure the API gateway to use a NAT gateway for egress to Amazon Bedrock public endpoints. Use Amazon Cognito to authorize OAuth 2.0.

Use a Lambda layer to host the MCP server. Create the Lambda layer for the AI agent Lambda functions. In the AI agent's MCP configuration, specify the Lambda layer ARN as the command. Specify the user credentials as environment variables.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C

The MCP specification supports two transports: STDIO (local subprocess) and HTTP/SSE (remote). When the MCP server runs inside a Lambda function, the client (the AI agent) cannot speak STDIO to it because Lambda is an event-driven runtime, not a subprocess. The correct architecture is:
  • Lambda hosts the MCP server logic.
  • Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) exposes it over HTTPS so the agent can connect via the MCP HTTP/SSE transport.
  • Amazon Cognito (or an OAuth 2.0 authoriser) sits in front of API Gateway to enforce that only authorised users can invoke the MCP server — exactly the security requirement.
  • The agent's outbound calls reach the Bedrock/agent endpoints; option C mentions a NAT gateway for any required egress.

This is the only option that pairs a remote, HTTPS-fronted MCP server with proper end-user authorisation.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Synchronous request/response is what MCP needs; asynchronous Lambda invocation doesn't fit MCP's request/response model and IAM-only auth doesn't authenticate end users.
  • B: STDIO transport requires launching a local subprocess; you cannot use STDIO over an API Gateway HTTP endpoint. Wrong transport.
  • D: Lambda layers package shared libraries; they do not "host" an MCP server. Specifying a layer ARN as a command is meaningless, and storing user credentials in env vars violates the authorisation requirement.

questions.text:
A healthcare company is using Amazon Bedrock to build a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application that helps practitioners make clinical decisions. The application must achieve high accuracy, identify hallucinations in generated content, and manage evaluation costs.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use Amazon Comprehend to analyze and report RAG responses and to extract medical entities and relationships. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate automated evaluations. Configure Amazon CloudWatch metrics to track confidence scores. Configure CloudWatch to send an alert when accuracy falls below specified thresholds.

Implement automated large language model(LLM)-based evaluations that use a specialized model that is fine-tuned for medical content to assess responses. Deploy AWS Lambda functions to perform automated batch evaluations. Publish results to Amazon CloudWatch metrics that track relevance and factual accuracy.

Configure Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics to generate test queries that have known answers on a regular schedule, and track model success for edge cases. Use Amazon SageMaker Feature Store to maintain evaluation datasets. Use a built-in Amazon Bedrock evaluation to track retrieval precision and hallucination rates.

Deploy a hybrid evaluation system that uses an automated LLM-as-a-judge evaluation to obtain large-scale evaluation for initially flagged response and uses human evaluation through Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth for nuanced clinical accuracy assessment. Use a built-in Amazon Bedrock evaluation with built-in expert capabilities to track retrieval and hallucination scores.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: D

Clinical AI demands a two-tier evaluation because:
  • Automated LLM-as-a-judge (built into Amazon Bedrock Evaluations and Knowledge Base Evaluations) scales to thousands of responses cheaply and screens for hallucination, faithfulness, answer relevance, and context precision.
  • Human evaluation via SageMaker Ground Truth captures nuanced clinical correctness that an LLM judge cannot reliably assess. Only responses pre-flagged by the LLM judge are escalated to clinicians, managing evaluation cost.

Bedrock's built-in evaluation features (Model Evaluation and Knowledge Base Evaluation) already provide retrieval precision, faithfulness, and hallucination metrics out of the box, so this hybrid stacks managed automation on top of expert human review — best accuracy and bounded cost.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Comprehend Medical extracts entities but cannot judge whether a generated answer is factually correct or hallucinated.
  • B: A custom fine-tuned medical judge model is heavy to build, validate, and maintain, and a pure-LLM judge alone is insufficient for clinical safety.
  • C: CloudWatch Synthetics is a website/API canary tool — wrong service. Generating test queries on a schedule doesn't measure hallucination on real production traffic.

questions.text:
A software company is using Amazon Q Business to build an AI assistant that allows employees to access company information and personal information by using natural language prompts. The company stores this information in an Amazon S3 bucket. Each department in the company has a dedicated prefix in the S3 bucket. Each object name includes the S3 prefix of the department that it belongs to. Each department can belong to only a single group in AWS IAM Identity Center. Each employee belongs to a single department. The company configures Amazon Q Business to access data stored in an S3 bucket as a data source. The company needs to ensure that the AI assistant respects access controls based on the user's IAM Identity Center group membership.

Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
opts: Create a JSON file named acl.json in each department folder. In each file, create access control entries that specify the IAM Identity Center group that should have access to that department's data. Indicate the location of the JSON file in the Access Control section of the data source settings.

Create a single JSON file named acl.json at the top level of the S3 bucket. Add access control entries that map each department's S3 prefix to its corresponding IAM Identity Center group. Indicate the location of the JSON file in the Access Control section of the data source settings.

For each IAM Identity Center group, create a separate permissions set that denies access to all prefixes in the S3 bucket. Add a StringNotEquals condition key to the permissions set for each group that specifies the department each group is associated with. Attach the permissions sets to the Identity Center groups.

Create a metadata file named metadata.json at the top level of the S3 bucket. Add an AccessControlList object to the file that specifies the S3 path for each department's prefix. Reference the metadata file in the Amazon Q Business data source settings.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

Amazon Q Business honors document-level Access Control Lists (ACLs) supplied alongside ingested S3 documents. For the S3 connector the supported pattern is per-prefix/per-document acl.json metadata that lists IAM Identity Center principals (users or groups) allowed to view each document. Putting one acl.json inside each department folder maps that folder's documents to that department's IDC group with zero code and zero IAM policy churn. Q Business uses these ACLs at query time so an employee only sees results their group can access.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: A single top-level acl.json is not a supported Q Business connector format; per-document/per-prefix ACL metadata is.
  • C: IAM permissions sets in IAM Identity Center govern AWS console/CLI access, not Q Business document filtering. Q Business uses its own ACL filter, not S3 IAM denies.
  • D: "metadata.json with AccessControlList object" at bucket root is fabricated — not a Q Business S3 connector convention.

questions.text:
An elevator service company has developed an AI assistant application by using Amazon Bedrock. The application generates elevator maintenance recommendations to elevator technicians. The company uses Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to collect the elevator sensor data.

New regulatory rules require that a human technician must review all AI generated recommendations. The company needs to establish human oversight workflows to review and approve the AI recommendations. The company must store all human technician review decisions in Amazon DynamoDB.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Create a custom approval workflow by using AWS Lambda functions and Amazon SQS queues for human review of AI recommendations. Store all review decisions in Amazon DynamoDB for auditing purposes.

Create an AWS Step Functions workflow that has a human approval step that uses the waitForTaskToken API to pause execution. After a human technician completes a review, use an AWS Lambda function to call the SendTaskSuccess API. Then call the approval decision. Store all review decisions in Amazon DynamoDB.

Create an AWS Glue workflow with a human approval step. After a human technician review, integrate the application with an AWS Lambda function that calls the SendTaskSuccess API. Store all human technician review decisions in Amazon DynamoDB.

Configure Amazon EventBridge rules with custom event patterns to route AI recommendations to human technicians for review. Create AWS Lambda functions to process the human technician's decision. Use Amazon ElastiCache to cache all human technician review decisions.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

AWS Step Functions provides a first-class human-approval pattern via the .waitForTaskToken integration. The state machine pauses, hands a task token to an out-of-band UI/email/SQS task, and resumes only when SendTaskSuccess (or SendTaskFailure) is called with that token. This is the AWS-recommended way to gate an automated pipeline on a human decision. Lambda then writes the recorded decision to DynamoDB for the audit trail.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: A homegrown Lambda+SQS approval loop reinvents what Step Functions already provides natively; more operational overhead and no built-in pause/resume semantics.
  • C: AWS Glue is an ETL service — it doesn't offer human approval steps or task token integration.
  • D: EventBridge can fan out, but ElastiCache is volatile cache, not a durable audit store. Requirement says DynamoDB.

questions.text:
A retail company is using Amazon Bedrock to develop a customer service AI assistant. Analysis shows that 70% of customer inquiries are simple product questions that a smaller model can effectively handle. However, 30% of inquiries are complex return policy questions that require advanced reasoning. The company wants to implement a cost-effective model selection framework to automatically route customer inquiries to appropriate models based on inquiry complexity. The framework must maintain high customer satisfaction and minimize response latency.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST implementation effort?
opts: Create a multi-stage architecture that uses a Small Language Model (SLM) to classify the complexity of each inquiry. Route simple inquiries to a smaller, more cost-effective model. Route complex inquiries to a larger, more capable model. Use AWS Lambda functions to handle the routing logic.

Use Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing to automatically analyze inquiries. Route simple product inquiries to smaller models, and route complex return policy inquiries to more capable larger models.

Implement a single-model solution that uses an Amazon Bedrock mid-sized foundation model(FM) with on-demand pricing. Include special instructions in model prompts to handle both simple and complex inquiries.

Create separate Amazon Bedrock endpoints for simple and complex inquiries. Implement a rule-based routing system based on keyword detection. Use on-demand pricing for the smaller model and provisioned throughput for the larger model.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing is a managed feature (GA in 2025) that dynamically routes each prompt to the most cost-effective model within a configured family (e.g., Claude Haiku vs Sonnet, or Llama 8B vs 70B) while preserving response quality. It's a single API call, no custom classifier, no Lambda glue — minimum implementation effort that directly satisfies the "cost-effective + low latency + auto routing" requirements.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Functional but requires you to build, train (or prompt) a classifier SLM, host it, and wire Lambda routing — far more effort than the managed feature in B.
  • C: Single model means you pay big-model price for the 70% of simple queries, defeating cost optimization.
  • D: Keyword rules are brittle (return policy questions don't always say "return"); also more code than B.

questions.text: A legal research company has a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application that uses Amazon Bedrock and Amazon OpenSearch Service. The application stores 788-dimensional vector embeddings for 15 million legal documents, including statutes, court rulings, and case summaries. The company's current chunking strategy segments text into fixed-length blocks of 500 tokens. The company chunking strategy often splits contextually linked information such as legal arguments, court opinions or statute references across separate chunks. Researchers report that generated outputs frequently omit key context or cite outdated legal information. Recent application logs show a 40% increase in response times. The p95 latency metric exceeds 2 seconds. The company expects storage needs for the application to grow from 90 GB to 360 GB within a year. The company needs a solution to improve retrieval response speed and content management of legal documents. Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Increase the embedding vector dimensionality from 768 to 4,096 without changing the existing chunking or pre-processing strategy.
Replace dynamic retrieval with static, pre-written summaries that are stored in Amazon S3. Use Amazon CloudFront to serve the summaries to reduce compute demand and improve predictability.

Update the chunking strategy to use semantic boundaries such as complete legal arguments, clauses, or sections rather than fixed token limits. Regenerate vector embeddings to align with the new chunk structure.
Migrate from OpenSearch Service to Amazon DynamoDB. Implement keyword-based indexes to enable faster lookups for legal concepts.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: C

The root cause of "outputs omit context / cite outdated info" is that the fixed 500-token chunker splits coherent legal units (arguments, opinions, statute references) so retrieval returns partial context. Switching to a semantic / structural chunker (paragraph, section, argument boundaries) keeps legally coherent units intact, which (a) reduces the number of irrelevant chunks pulled per query (lower latency), (b) improves recall@k and answer quality, and (c) keeps embeddings aligned to retrievable units of meaning. Re-embedding is required because old vectors are tied to old chunk boundaries.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Raising dimensionality to 4096 makes ANN search slower and storage bigger — worse latency, not better; doesn't fix the context-splitting problem.
  • B: Pre-written static summaries throw away the whole point of RAG (fresh, citable retrieval) and won't keep up with new legal documents.
  • D: DynamoDB is a key-value/document store with no native vector ANN search. Keyword lookups regress to lexical search and lose semantic recall.

questions.text:
A healthcare company is using Amazon Bedrock to build a system to help practitioners make clinical decisions. The system must provide treatment recommendations to physicians based only on approved medical documentation and must cite specific sources. The system must not hallucinate or produce factually incorrect information.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
opts: Integrate Amazon Bedrock with Amazon Kendra to retrieve approved documents. Implement custom post-processing to compare generated responses against source documents and to include citations.
Deploy an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Use Amazon Bedrock RetrieveAndGenerate API to return citations from the knowledge base.
Use Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Comprehend Medical to extract medical entities. Implement verification logic against a medical terminology database.

Use an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with Retrieve API calls and InvokeModel API calls to retrieve approved clinical source documents. Implement verification logic to compare against retrieved sources and to cite sources.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases combined with the RetrieveAndGenerate API delivers grounded answers and built-in source citations in a single managed call. The KB ingests the approved clinical corpus (S3), handles chunking + embeddings + vector store (OpenSearch Serverless / Aurora / Pinecone), and the RetrieveAndGenerate response object includes the cited passages and document URIs. There's no need to write your own retrieval, prompt assembly, or citation-stitching logic — that's the lowest operational overhead.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Kendra is a strong search engine, but you'd still write custom prompt construction, generation, citation matching, and verification — high overhead.
  • C: Comprehend Medical only extracts entities; it does not generate grounded responses or cite documents. You'd still need an LLM step and a verification database — more overhead.
  • D: Using Retrieve + InvokeModel separately is the manual two-step that RetrieveAndGenerate replaces; adds custom verification logic = more overhead than B.

questions.text:
A software as a service (SaaS) company is building a recommendation model that uses Amazon SageMaker. AI models on Amazon Bedrock by using Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import. Airline companies will use the application to sort customized offers to customers.

The model must examine the travel history of customers to help make more relevant recommendations. The company stores customer travel history data in an Amazon RDS database. The company must ensure that the application delivers consistent, relevant, and accurate results across multiple airline customer populations.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to implement a RAG architecture to analyze customer travel history. Use the integration with vector search capabilities to generate personalized cabin upgrade recommendations. Apply Amazon Bedrock guardrails to filter responses. Use AWS Step Functions and AWS Lambda functions to orchestrate validation to reduce hallucinations.

Implement text-to-SQL transformations with SQL validations to accurately retrieve relevant information from the RDS database. Use the results to generate personalized cabin upgrade recommendations. Apply Amazon Bedrock guardrails to filter content. Use AWS Step Functions and AWS Lambda functions to orchestrate validation to reduce hallucinations.

Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to separately search across customer travel history for embedding similarities. Use the results to generate personalized cabin upgrade recommendations. Apply Amazon Bedrock guardrails to filter content. Implement custom validation by using AWS Lambda functions to reduce hallucinations.

Implement text-to-SQL transformations with SQL validations to accurately retrieve relevant information from the RDS database. Use the results to generate personalized cabin upgrade recommendations. Apply Amazon Bedrock guardrails to filter responses. Use conference scoring and semantic similarly measures to reduce hallucinations.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

Customer travel history lives in a relational (RDS) store with structured rows (flights, dates, fares, classes). The right grounding pattern is text-to-SQL: convert the user / agent prompt into a validated SQL query, execute it against RDS, and feed the deterministic rows back to the model for recommendation generation. SQL validation (allow-list of tables/columns, parameterized statements, syntax check before execution) prevents both injection and hallucinated columns. Bedrock Guardrails filter unsafe/off-topic outputs, and a Step Functions + Lambda orchestration enforces a validation step (e.g., schema check, row sanity, business rules) before responses are returned — the layered approach that reduces hallucinations on structured data.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Bedrock Knowledge Bases / vector search are designed for unstructured text (PDFs, docs). Embedding rows of a transactional RDS schema loses structure and produces fuzzy matches — wrong tool for structured customer history.
  • C: Same problem as A: OpenSearch vector similarity over relational rows is semantically lossy and won't reliably reflect "show me flights >Y miles in 2024". No orchestrated validation step either.
  • D: Drops Step Functions orchestration in favor of ad-hoc "conference scoring" (likely a typo for "confidence scoring") plus similarity measures, but you still need a validated control flow. Less robust than B's explicit validation orchestration.

A healthcare company is building a generative AI (GenAI) application to answer patient questions based on patient medical records and published treatment guidelines. To comply with healthcare regulations, the application must provide transparent citations for all information sources. The application must also maintain an audit trail for all data access and ensure that responses reference only authorized medical information.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
opts: Deploy Amazon Bedrock Agents and Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to generate patient responses. Use AWS CloudTrail to log the application model(FM) interactions for audits.
Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to connect the application to authorized data sources. Use Amazon CloudWatch to collect comprehensive logs for all queries and approved sources.
Configure Amazon Bedrock guardrails to filter patient information. Create a custom vector database outside of AWS to store medical records. Use AWS Lambda functions to track citations.

Use Amazon SageMaker AI to fine-tune Amazon Bedrock with proprietary medical data. Use a custom attribution mechanism in an Amazon API Gateway layer to cite data sources. Store data lineage records in Amazon DynamoDB.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides authorized-source-only RAG out of the box: documents are ingested from a controlled S3 location, RetrieveAndGenerate returns citations to specific source chunks, and IAM/CloudTrail logs every invocation. Pairing the KB with CloudWatch (KB ingestion logs, model invocation logs that Bedrock can write to CloudWatch Logs/S3) yields a complete audit trail with essentially no custom code. This combination satisfies all three regulatory requirements — citations, audit trail, authorized-only sources — with the least operational overhead.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Agents + Prompt Management orchestrate tool calling and template versioning but don't inherently restrict answers to authorized sources or return citations. CloudTrail records API calls, not LLM prompts/responses, so audit is incomplete.
  • C: Hosting a vector DB outside AWS adds infra and security overhead; custom Lambda citation tracking is more code.
  • D: Fine-tuning bakes data into model weights — you lose source attribution entirely and can't selectively revoke sources. High overhead, opposite of "least".

A financial services company wants to develop an Amazon Bedrock application that gives analysts the ability to query quarterly earnings reports and financial statements. The financial documents are typically 5-100 pages long and contain both tabular data and text. The application must provide contextually accurate responses that preserve the relationship between financial metrics and their explanatory text. To support accurate and scalable retrieval the application must incorporate document segmentation and context management strategies.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use a direct model invocation approach that uses Anthropic Claude to process each financial document as a single input. Use fine-tuned models that instruct the model to parse tables and text separately.

Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to create a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application that retrieves relevant information from contextually chunked sections of financial documents. Segment the documents based on their structural layout. Include citations that reference the original input.

Deploy an Amazon Bedrock agent that has an action group that calls AWS Lambda functions to analyze financial documents. Configure the Lambda functions to perform fixed-size chunking when a user submits a query about financial metrics.

Create one specialized Amazon Bedrock application for structured for structured data. Create a second application for unstructured data. Use applications for a generic relational database to store data, the structure of each application to use a centralized management strategy.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides scalable, citation-grounded RAG which is exactly what's required: ingest 5-100 page reports, chunk by structural layout (sections, headings, tables), embed, store in OpenSearch Serverless, and serve RetrieveAndGenerate calls that return the answer plus citations to the exact passages. Structural / hierarchical chunking preserves the relationship between a metric (often in a table) and the surrounding narrative, satisfying the "preserve metric ↔ explanation" requirement. KBs scale across an entire document corpus where single-document invocation cannot.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: Feeding entire 100-page docs as raw input is expensive, hits context limits, and doesn't scale across many filings or analysts. Fine-tuning doesn't add retrieval.
  • C: Fixed-size chunking is exactly the wrong choice — it splits tables away from their explanatory text. Agents are also overkill for pure Q&A.
  • D: Two separate apps with a relational DB store don't address chunking, semantic retrieval, or citations; the description is also incoherent.

questions.text: A financial services company is developing a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application to help investment researchers query complex financial relationships across multiple investment vehicles, market sectors, and regulatory environments. The dataset contains highly interconnected entities that have multi-hop relationships. The analysts must be able to examine the relationships holistically to provide accurate investment guidance. The application must deliver comprehensive answers that capture indirect relationships between financial entities. The application must produce responses in less than 3 seconds. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
opts: Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with GraphRAG and Amazon Neptune Analytics to store the financial data. Analyze the multi-hop relationships between entities and automatically identify related information across documents.

Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases and an Amazon OpenSearch Service vector store to implement custom relationship identification logic that uses AWS Lambda functions to query multiple vector embeddings in sequence.

Use an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector database with a nearest neighbor(k-NN) searches. Implement manual relationship mapping in an application layer that runs in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group.
Use Amazon DynamoDB to store financial data in a custom indexing system. Use an AWS Lambda function to query relevant records based on input questions. Use Amazon SageMaker AI to generate responses.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

Bedrock Knowledge Bases now supports GraphRAG backed by Amazon Neptune Analytics. It automatically builds a knowledge graph from your ingested documents and uses graph traversal during retrieval so multi-hop relationships (e.g., issuer → parent company → sector → regulator) are surfaced in a single managed call. This delivers the "comprehensive answers capturing indirect relationships" the question demands, without any custom traversal code — the lowest operational overhead. Managed Neptune Analytics is built for fast in-memory graph queries (sub-second), supporting the <3 s response budget.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Custom Lambda sequencing of multiple vector queries is fragile, slow (chained calls add latency), and requires you to build the relationship logic yourself — opposite of "least overhead".
  • C: Manual relationship mapping in EC2 Auto Scaling = the most operational overhead possible: capacity planning, scaling rules, code maintenance.
  • D: DynamoDB has no native multi-hop traversal; SageMaker generation adds model-hosting overhead. Doesn't model graph relationships at all.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon Bedrock to implement a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)-based system to serve medical information to users. The company needs to compare multiple chunking strategies, evaluate the generation quality of two foundation models(FMs), and enforce quality thresholds for deployment. Which Amazon Bedrock evaluation configuration will meet these requirements?
opts: Create a whole-only evaluation job that uses a supported version of Anthropic Claude Sonnet as the evaluator model. Configure metrics for context relevance and context coverage. Define deployment thresholds in a separate CICD pipeline.

Create a retrieve-and-generate evaluation job that uses custom prompt datasets at metrics and an LLM-as-a- judge metric that uses a scale of 1-5. Include each chunking strategy in the evaluation dataset. Use a supported version of Anthropic Claude Sonnet to evaluate responses from both FMs.

Create a separate evaluation job for each chunking strategy and FM combination. Use Amazon Bedrock built-in metrics for correctness and completeness. Manually review scores before deployment approval.

Set up a pipeline that uses multiple service jobs to assess retrieval quality. Create separate evaluation jobs for both FMs that use the LLM-as-a-judge model. Evaluate based on faithfulness and citation precision metrics.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: B

Amazon Bedrock Evaluations offers a retrieve-and-generate (RAG) evaluation job type that can compare different KB configurations (including chunking strategies) and different generation FMs in the same job, scored by an LLM-as-a-judge evaluator (Claude Sonnet supported) on a 1-5 scale across metrics like correctness, helpfulness, faithfulness, relevance, completeness. Putting each chunking strategy variant into the evaluation dataset and choosing both FMs lets you produce comparable scores in one configuration, then enforce a quality threshold (e.g., judge score ≥ 4) before promoting to production.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • A: "Whole-only evaluation job" isn't a Bedrock job type. Context-relevance/coverage alone don't measure generation quality of two FMs. Defers thresholding entirely to CI/CD, missing built-in eval gating.
  • C: Spinning up an evaluation job per combination is unnecessary overhead and manual review violates the "enforce quality thresholds" requirement programmatically.
  • D: Splits FMs into different jobs (hard to compare apples-to-apples) and doesn't address chunking-strategy comparison.

A medical company is creating a generative AI (GenAI) system by using Amazon Bedrock. The system processes data from various sources and must maintain end-to-end data lineage. The system must also use real-time personally identifiable information (PII) filtering and audit trails to automatically report compliance.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use AWS Glue Data Catalog to register all data sources and track lineage. Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails PII logging for all Amazon Bedrock API calls. Use Amazon Macie to scan stored data for compliance and to publish AWS Audit Manager reports for compliance frameworks.

Use AWS Lake Formation to track data lineage of model interactions and changes. Use AWS Config to track model configuration changes. Use Amazon CloudWatch to capture logging activities and generate an automated compliance report.

Use AWS CloudTrail to track data source configurations and changes. Use AWS WAF with custom rules to filter PII for the application layer before. Amazon Comprehend Medical to capture and route audit events to Amazon S3 for compliance.

Use AWS Systems Manager to register service requests, validate data, and ensure that Amazon Bedrock complies with industry regulations. Configure Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to capture and route audit events to Amazon S3 to establish AWS Lambda functions to identify with and inspect PII from generated responses.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

The combination directly maps to each requirement: - AWS Glue Data Catalog is the standard AWS metadata + lineage store; registering all data sources gives end-to-end lineage. - Bedrock Guardrails provides real-time PII detection and masking on prompts and completions, with PII filter logging on every Bedrock API call. - Amazon Macie continuously scans S3 data sources for PII/PHI compliance. - AWS Audit Manager automates evidence collection and produces compliance reports against frameworks (HIPAA, SOC 2, etc.).
Together these deliver lineage + real-time PII filtering + automated compliance reporting end-to-end.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Lake Formation handles data-lake permissions, not model-interaction lineage. AWS Config tracks resource config changes (useful) but neither it nor CloudWatch alone can generate compliance-framework reports automatically. No PII filtering.
  • C: AWS WAF inspects HTTP traffic; not a real-time PII filter for LLM I/O. CloudTrail tracks API calls but not data source lineage. Comprehend Medical extracts entities, doesn't route audit events.
  • D: Systems Manager is operations tooling, not a compliance lineage solution. Custom Lambda PII inspection misses the managed Guardrails capability and is high overhead.

A medical company is creating a generative AI (GenAI) system by using Amazon Bedrock. The system processes data from various sources and must maintain end-to-end data lineage. The system must use real-time personally identifiable information (PII) filtering and audit trails to automatically report compliance.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
opts: Use AWS Glue Data Catalog to register all data sources and track lineage. Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails PII logging for all Amazon Bedrock API calls. Enable AWS CloudTrail logging to track Amazon Bedrock API access and use Amazon Macie to scan stored data for compliance and to publish AWS Audit Manager reports for compliance frameworks.

Use AWS Lake Formation to track data lineage of model interactions and changes. Use Amazon Macie to inspect Amazon Bedrock model outputs in real time. Use Amazon Comprehend to filter PII data. Use AWS Lambda functions to compile automated compliance reports.

Use AWS X-Ray to track data source configurations and changes. Configure Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to capture and route audit events to Amazon S3. Configure Amazon CloudWatch with AWS Step Functions workflows to identify and report PII from generated responses.

Use AWS DataSync to register data sources to track changes. Use Amazon CloudWatch custom metrics to monitor PII exposure in Amazon Bedrock responses. Use an Amazon S3 Lifecycle policy to establish audit trails and use AWS X-Ray to generate an audit trail. Use an Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels model to detect sensitive information in the data that Amazon Bedrock processes.
questions.exp:
Correct answer: A

This is the same scenario as Q91 with slightly different distractors and an explicit CloudTrail step. The winning answer remains the same architecture, now strengthened by adding CloudTrail for Bedrock API access auditing: - Glue Data Catalog — registers data sources and tracks lineage. - Bedrock Guardrails (PII filter + logging) — real-time PII detection/masking on every Bedrock API call. - CloudTrail — records every Bedrock API access for forensic audit. - Macie — scans S3-stored data for PII/PHI compliance. - Audit Manager — automatically assembles evidence into framework reports (HIPAA, SOC 2, etc.).
All four requirements (lineage, real-time PII filtering, audit trail, automated compliance reporting) are met using the AWS-native, fit-for-purpose services.

Why the wrong options miss:
  • B: Lake Formation governs lake permissions, not GenAI model-interaction lineage. Macie cannot inspect live Bedrock outputs (it scans S3, not API streams). Comprehend can detect PII but is not the real-time guardrail layer; custom Lambdas for compliance reports = high overhead vs Audit Manager.
  • C: AWS X-Ray traces distributed application calls, not data-source configuration changes. Routing Guardrails events to S3 and reconstructing compliance via CloudWatch + Step Functions is a high-overhead rebuild of Audit Manager.
  • D: DataSync moves data, doesn't register sources. CloudWatch custom metrics don't filter PII. S3 Lifecycle is for retention, not audit. Rekognition Custom Labels is for image classification — wrong tool for textual PII.
